alaska.name: Chugach State Park
alaska.shortDescription: One of the largest state parks in the country, offering dramatic wilderness right on Anchorages doorstep.
alaska.fullDescription: Chugach State Park is an incredible 495,000-acre wilderness preserve located immediately east of Anchorage, Alaska. It encompasses towering alpine peaks, colossal glaciers, massive lakes, and pristine spruce-birch forests. The park is a world-class destination for hiking, backcountry skiing, wildlife viewing, and rugged mountaineering. It is one of the most accessible wild areas in North America, allowing visitors to step from urban amenities directly into raw, spectacular sub-arctic ecosystems.

hikingTrails.name: Flattop Mountain Trail
hikingTrails.description: The most climbed mountain in Alaska, offering a rocky scramble to a flat summit with breathtaking panoramic views of Anchorage, Cook Inlet, and the Aleutian Range.

hikingTrails.name: Albert Loop Trail
hikingTrails.description: A beautiful loop trail starting at the Eagle River Nature Center, winding through scenic boreal forests and river flats with excellent birdwatching.

alaska.campingInfo: The park has three developed campgrounds: Eklutna Lake Campground (50 sites), Eagle River Campground (57 sites), and Bird Creek Campground (28 sites). Primitive backcountry camping is permitted throughout most of the park.
alaska.fishingBoating: Eklutna Lake is a hub for non-motorized boating, kayaking, and paddleboarding. Fishing is popular in the Eagle River and Eklutna Lake for Dolly Varden and salmon (with state permits).
wildlife: Dall sheep (frequently seen on high rocky cliffs)

visitorCenter.name: Eagle River Nature Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides park information, interactive wildlife displays, trail maps, and host guided naturalist programs.

alaska.hours: Open 24/7 year-round.
alaska.entranceFees: $5.00 daily parking fee at developed trailheads.
alaska.bestTimeToVisit: June to August for pleasant hiking weather, and September for stunning autumn tundra colors.
tips: Always carry bear spray and make plenty of noise while hiking on the trails.
Weather can change rapidly in the mountains; always dress in layers and carry a rain jacket.
Start early if hiking Flattop Mountain on sunny weekends, as the Glen Alps parking lot fills up quickly.

alaska.name: Denali State Park
alaska.shortDescription: Bordering the national park, Denali State Park offers some of the absolute best viewpoints of Mt. Denali.
alaska.fullDescription: Denali State Park is a 325,240-acre park located adjacent to Denali National Park & Preserve. It is bisected by the Parks Highway, offering incredibly scenic road access. The park's terrain varies from low-lying river valleys to alpine tundra and steep mountain ridges. It is renowned for offering unparalleled vistas of Mount Denali (formerly Mt. McKinley) and the Alaska Range, often considered superior and less crowded than the viewpoints within the national park.
thingsToDo: Scenic driving and photography along the Parks Highway
Canoeing and kayaking on Byers Lake

hikingTrails.name: Kesugi Ridge Trail
hikingTrails.description: A world-famous alpine ridge trail offering continuous, jaw-dropping views of Mount Denali and the Alaska Range across the Susitna Valley.

hikingTrails.name: Byers Lake Loop Trail
hikingTrails.description: A flat, peaceful loop tracing the shores of Byers Lake, passing through birch groves and crossing suspension bridges over rushing creeks.

alaska.campingInfo: Byers Lake Campground offers 73 beautifully wooded campsites, plus three public-use cabins available for reservation. Lower Troublesome Creek offers an additional 20 campsites.
alaska.fishingBoating: Byers Lake is a beautiful, quiet body of water. No motors are allowed, making it pristine for kayaking and canoeing. Rentals are available seasonally. Fishing is excellent for rainbow trout and salmon.

visitorCenter.name: Byers Lake Ranger Station
visitorCenter.info: Provides visitor information, hiking guides, canoe rentals, and registration for public-use cabins.

alaska.hours: Open 24/7 year-round.
alaska.address: Mile 147 Parks Hwy, Trapper Creek, AK 99683
alaska.bestTimeToVisit: June to August for clear mountain days, and early September for spectacular fall tundra colors.
tips: Bring a high-quality camera with a zoom lens; the views of Mount Denali on a clear day are once-in-a-lifetime.
Rent a canoe at the Byers Lake landing to explore the quiet shoreline under the shadow of the mountains.
Be alert for bears around the salmon streams in late summer; carry bear spray.

arizona.name: Slide Rock State Park
arizona.shortDescription: A world-famous natural water slide located inside Sedona's red rock Oak Creek Canyon.
arizona.fullDescription: Slide Rock State Park, located in Sedona's Oak Creek Canyon, is a spectacular 43-acre historic apple orchard turned natural water park. It features a world-famous natural water slide formed by the slick sandstone bed of Oak Creek. Flanked by high red rock cliffs, the park offers refreshing swimming holes, sunbathing on flat rocks, scenic canyon trails, and historic buildings dating back to the early 1900s.
thingsToDo: Sliding down the natural sandstone water slide
Swimming and wading in Oak Creek
Exploring the historic Pendley Apple Homestead
Picnicking under the shade of giant sycamores

hikingTrails.name: Slide Rock Clifftop Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short scenic pathway climbing above the creek bed, offering a bird's-eye view of the swimmers and Oak Creek Canyon.

hikingTrails.name: Pendley Homestead Trail
hikingTrails.description: A flat paved trail passing through the historic apple orchard, rustic barns, and early farming equipment.

arizona.campingInfo: No camping is permitted in Slide Rock State Park, but numerous campgrounds are located nearby in the Coconino National Forest.
arizona.fishingBoating: Oak Creek is stocked with rainbow trout, offering excellent stream-side fishing. No boating is allowed due to shallow rapids.

visitorCenter.name: Slide Rock Park Ranger Station
visitorCenter.info: Provides historical exhibits on the Pendley apple homestead, canyon geology, and safety guidelines for the water slide.

arizona.hours: 8:00 AM to 6:00 PM daily (Hours vary by season).
arizona.entranceFees: $20.00 - $30.00 per vehicle (depending on season and day of the week).
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: Late May to September for warm water sliding, and October for the historic apple harvest and beautiful fall foliage.
tips: The sandstone slide can be extremely slippery; water shoes with good grip are highly recommended.
Arrive before 9:00 AM during the hot summer months, as the parking lot frequently fills to capacity and closes early.
Bring your own refreshments, as purchasing options inside the park are limited.

arizona.name: Lost Dutchman State Park
arizona.shortDescription: Nestled at the base of the majestic Superstition Mountains, famous for the legendary lost gold mine.
arizona.fullDescription: Lost Dutchman State Park is a stunning 320-acre desert park located in the Sonoran Desert, just 40 miles east of Phoenix. It is named after the legendary "Lost Dutchman" gold mine that is rumored to be hidden deep within the rugged Superstition Mountains. Flanked by massive saguaro cacti and volcanic rock formations, the park offers hiking trails ranging from easy desert walks to strenuous mountain scrambles, alongside modern campground facilities.

hikingTrails.name: Flatiron Siphon Draw Trail
hikingTrails.description: A demanding, rugged climb up Siphon Draw into the sheer volcanic cliffs of Flatiron, offering a spectacular, high-altitude lookout over the Phoenix valley.

hikingTrails.name: Treasure Loop Trail
hikingTrails.description: Winds through desert saguaro forests at the base of the mountain, leading to rocky scenic viewpoints.

arizona.campingInfo: Features 134 modern campsites (68 with water and 50/30 amp electricity), a dump station, clean restrooms with hot showers, and 5 rustic camping cabins available for rent.
arizona.fishingBoating: No lakes or rivers are inside the park, but Canyon Lake is located just 15 miles north for extensive boating and fishing.

visitorCenter.name: Lost Dutchman Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Features educational displays about the legend of the Lost Dutchman Gold Mine, Sonoran Desert survival, and native desert flora.

arizona.hours: 6:00 AM to 8:30 PM daily.
arizona.address: 6109 N Apache Trail, Apache Junction, AZ 85119
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: October to April for perfect, comfortable daytime temperatures and beautiful spring wildflower blooms.
tips: The Flatiron trail is an unmaintained mountain scramble; always wear robust boots and carry at least 3 liters of water.
Sunset behind the Superstition Mountains is incredibly dramatic; set up your camera near the Saguaro trail loop for iconic photos.
Always check under your boots and camping gear for desert insects like scorpions or beetles.

california.name: Emerald Bay State Park
california.shortDescription: One of Lake Tahoes most iconic and photographed bays, featuring Fannette Island and the historic Vikingsholm Castle.
california.fullDescription: Emerald Bay State Park is a jaw-dropping national natural landmark nestled on Lake Tahoe's west shore. Known for its brilliant blue-green waters, steep pine-clad granite peaks, and Tahoe's only island (Fannette Island), it is one of the most scenic gems in California. The park is home to Vikingsholm, a stunning 38-room mansion constructed in 1929, which stands as one of the finest examples of Scandinavian architecture in the United States. Visitors can hike, kayak, and take in the majestic clifftop vistas.
thingsToDo: Kayaking or paddleboarding to Fannette Island
Scuba diving in the Emerald Bay Maritime Heritage Trail

hikingTrails.name: Rubicon Trail
hikingTrails.description: A beautiful trail tracing the lakeside cliffs from Emerald Bay to D.L. Bliss State Park, offering continuous, stunning vistas of Lake Tahoe's crystal-clear waters.

hikingTrails.name: Vikingsholm Trail
hikingTrails.description: A steep downhill walk from the highway parking lot to the shoreline of the bay, leading directly to the historic Vikingsholm mansion.

california.campingInfo: The park features the Eagle Point Campground (94 sites, closed in winter) and a unique, boat-in campground situated on the lake shoreline with primitive campsites.
california.fishingBoating: Boating is highly popular inside Emerald Bay. Motorized boat speed is strictly regulated. Kayak and paddleboard rentals are available at the beach. Fishing is excellent for Mackinaw and Rainbow trout.

visitorCenter.name: Vikingsholm Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides park details, historical information about Mrs. Lora Knight's estate, and tickets for castle tours.

california.hours: Sunrise to Sunset daily (Road closures can occur in winter).
california.address: 138 Emerald Bay Rd, South Lake Tahoe, CA 96150
california.bestTimeToVisit: June to September for lake sports and castle tours, and October for quiet hiking and beautiful crisp weather.
tips: The hike down to Vikingsholm is 1 mile long and drops 400 feet; the walk back up is steep, so pace yourself.
Rent a kayak early in the morning from South Lake Tahoe or Baldwin Beach to enjoy flat, glassy water inside the bay.
Strictly store all food inside bear-proof lockers, as active black bears roam the campgrounds.

california.name: Big Basin Redwoods State Park
california.shortDescription: Californias oldest state park, famous for its ancient, towering coast redwood trees.
california.fullDescription: Big Basin Redwoods State Park, established in 1902, is California's oldest state park. Located in the Santa Cruz Mountains, it is home to the largest continuous stand of ancient Coast Redwoods south of San Francisco. Some of these colossal trees are over 1,000 to 1,800 years old, reaching heights of more than 300 feet and circumferences of 50 feet. The park is a lush, mossy coastal rainforest with cascading waterfalls, bubbling streams, and over 80 miles of hiking trails.

hikingTrails.name: Redwood Loop Trail
hikingTrails.description: A flat, fully accessible loop leading past some of the park's most famous giant trees, including the Mother of the Forest and Father of the Forest.

hikingTrails.name: Skyline-to-the-Sea Trail (Section)
hikingTrails.description: Winds downhill through redwood groves and lush fern canyons, tracing Waddell Creek towards the Pacific ocean.

california.campingInfo: Campgrounds are recovering from wildfire; limited drive-in campsites and walk-in tent sites are available by reservation only. Backpacking sites on the Skyline-to-the-Sea route require wilderness permits.
california.fishingBoating: No boating is available. Limited stream-side fishing is permitted in Waddell Creek seasonally, subject to California Department of Fish and Wildlife rules.
wildlife: Banana slugs (the iconic yellow mascot of the redwood forest)

visitorCenter.name: Big Basin Temporary Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides trail updates, park maps, and educational exhibits on redwood ecology and forest fire recovery.

california.hours: 8:00 AM to Sunset daily.
california.entranceFees: $10.00 per vehicle parking fee (Day-use reservations are highly recommended).
california.address: 21600 Big Basin Way, Boulder Creek, CA 95006
california.bestTimeToVisit: April to June for roaring waterfalls and lush ferns, or October for crisp, quiet mountain trail walks.
tips: Keep an eye out on the damp trail beds for bright yellow Banana Slugs—they are a beloved, unique symbol of the old-growth forest.
Due to post-fire recovery, some trails may have detours; check in with rangers at the visitor center for the latest map updates.
Cell service is non-existent in the deep canyons; download offline maps and trails before departing.

colorado.name: Eldorado Canyon State Park
colorado.shortDescription: A world-renowned rock climbing destination featuring sheer sandstone cliffs and scenic hiking trails.
colorado.fullDescription: Eldorado Canyon State Park is a treasure of Colorado, located just south of Boulder. Famed globally for its gold-colored, sheer sandstone cliffs, the canyon attracts rock climbers from all over the world who tackle over 1,000 technical routes. For hikers, the park offers beautiful trails winding along the rushing waters of South Boulder Creek, climbing through dense pine forests to reveal spectacular panoramic views of the continental divide.
thingsToDo: Technical rock climbing on golden sandstone walls
Hiking through lush foothills and dense pine forests
Fly fishing in South Boulder Creek
Watching climbers tackle historic, sheer routes

hikingTrails.name: Eldorado Canyon Trail
hikingTrails.description: Climbs steadily through evergreen forests, passing old homestead ruins and offering spectacular views of the red-rock canyon and distant peaks.

hikingTrails.name: Fowler Trail
hikingTrails.description: A flat, wheelchair-accessible path clinging to the canyon wall, providing incredible close-up views of rock climbers.

colorado.campingInfo: No camping is permitted in Eldorado Canyon State Park to protect the delicate environment, but camping is available at nearby Golden Gate Canyon State Park.
colorado.fishingBoating: South Boulder Creek offers excellent trout fishing, particularly for brown and rainbow trout. No boating is allowed due to rocky rapids and shallow creek depths.
wildlife: Golden eagles (nesting on the canyon cliffs)

visitorCenter.name: Eldorado Canyon Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides rock climbing guides, historical photos, geologic maps, and displays on the canyon's industrial mining history.

colorado.hours: Sunrise to Sunset daily (Vehicle timed-entry reservations required on summer weekends).
colorado.entranceFees: $10.00 daily vehicle pass (or $4.00 per person for walk-ins).
colorado.bestTimeToVisit: September to October for comfortable hiking temperatures, and April to May for rushing creek flows.
tips: Timed-entry reservations are mandatory on weekends and holidays from mid-May through mid-September; book early!
Sit on one of the wooden benches along the Fowler Trail with a pair of binoculars to watch world-class climbers ascend the Bastille wall.
South Boulder Creek flows fast in spring; keep children and pets well away from the banks during the high run-off.

hawaii.name: Waimea Canyon State Park
hawaii.shortDescription: Kauaʻi park overlooking Waimea Canyon, the 'Grand Canyon of the Pacific', up to 3,000 feet deep.
hawaii.fullDescription: Waimea Canyon State Park on Kauaʻi's west side overlooks Waimea Canyon, about ten miles long and up to 3,000 feet deep, known as the Grand Canyon of the Pacific. Its name means 'reddish water', for the canyon's red soil. The park has a scenic drive, canyon lookouts, a viewpoint toward Niʻihau, and the Iliau Nature Loop and Kukui Trail.

hikingTrails.name: Iliau Nature Loop
hikingTrails.description: One of the trails named on the official Waimea Canyon State Park page.

hikingTrails.name: Kukui Trail
hikingTrails.description: One of the trails named on the official Waimea Canyon State Park page.

hawaii.fishingBoating: The official park page lists seasonal trout fishing.

visitorCenter.name: Waimea Canyon State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

hawaii.entranceFees: Non-residents $5/person (children 3 and under free) plus $10/vehicle parking; Hawaii residents free with HI ID/DL
hawaii.bestTimeToVisit: Go on a clear morning once the park has reopened, because canyon views depend on the weather and trails can be muddy after rain.
tips: Status as of Oct 2026: closed (hurricane recovery, official notice 10/19/26). Check the official page before going.
Parking tickets are valid at both the Waimea Canyon State Park and Kokee State Park parking lots, so you only need to pay once.
Non-residents pay the entry and parking fees at an automatic ticket booth, and no reservation is needed.
Trails in the area can be slippery, muddy and dangerous, so wear shoes with good traction.

hawaii.name: ʻAkaka Falls State Park
hawaii.shortDescription: Hawaiʻi Island park north of Hilo with 442-foot ʻAkaka Falls, seen from a short rainforest loop.
hawaii.fullDescription: ʻAkaka Falls State Park lies about 11 miles north of Hilo, above Honomū at the end of Route 220. A 0.4-mile paved loop through tropical vegetation leads to viewpoints of ʻAkaka Falls, which plunges 442 feet into a stream-eroded gorge, and of 300-foot Kahūnā Falls.

hikingTrails.name: ʻAkaka Falls Loop Trail
hikingTrails.description: A paved, self-guided loop through lush tropical vegetation to vista points overlooking Kahuna Falls and the 442-foot ʻAkaka Falls.

hawaii.campingInfo: Check the official park website for current camping details.
hawaii.fishingBoating: Check the official park website for current boating and fishing details.

visitorCenter.name: ʻAkaka Falls State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

hawaii.entranceFees: Non-residents $5/person plus $10 parking per non-commercial vehicle; Hawaii residents free with ID or driver's license; children 3 and under free; credit card only
hawaii.bestTimeToVisit: The park is open year-round from 8:30am to 5:00pm, so arrive early to explore the rainforest loop before the busier part of the day.
tips: Status as of Oct 2026: open, part of the loop trail closed (fallen trees, notice 10/19/26). Check the official page before going.
Pay parking and entrance fees before you arrive because cell reception at the park is limited; payment is credit card only.
Allow about half an hour for the full loop. To see only ʻAkaka Falls, take the left (south) path at the first junction.
Stay on the trail. Mountain biking and open fires are not allowed, and you should pack out what you pack in.

hawaii.name: Hāʻena State Park
hawaii.shortDescription: 'End of the road' park on Kauaʻi's north shore with Keʻe Beach and the Kalalau Trail trailhead.
hawaii.fullDescription: Hāʻena State Park covers 230 acres at the end of the Kūhiō Highway on Kauaʻi's north shore. It has Keʻe Beach, ancient Hawaiian sites including sea caves estimated at more than 4,000 years old, and the trailhead of the 11-mile Kalalau Trail, the only land access to the Nā Pali Coast. A parking or entry reservation is required, with a daily limit of 900 people.

hikingTrails.name: Kalalau Trail
hikingTrails.description: Hāʻena State Park is home to the trailhead of the world-famous Kalalau Trail, and hiking past Hanakāpīʻai Valley requires a Nāpali Coast State Wilderness Park camping permit.

hikingTrails.name: Hanakāpīʻai Falls trail
hikingTrails.description: Following part of the Kalalau Trail to Hanakāpīʻai Valley, the hike from Hāʻena SP to Hanakāpīʻai Waterfalls is 8 miles round trip and is included with a park entry or parking reservation.

hawaii.campingInfo: As of the official 10/19/2026 park notice, all Kauaʻi state park camping remains closed.
hawaii.fishingBoating: The park offers beach-related activities including shore fishing and swimming at Kēʻē Beach.

visitorCenter.name: Hāʻena State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

hawaii.hours: Summer (from Apr 1): 7:00am–7:45pm; Winter (from day after Labor Day): 7:00am–6:45pm
hawaii.entranceFees: Non-residents: $5/person entry plus $10/vehicle parking, advance reservation required. Hawaii residents free with HI DL/ID. Children 3 and under free.
hawaii.address: End of Kūhiō Highway (Hwy 56), Hāʻena, Kauaʻi, HI 96714
hawaii.bestTimeToVisit: The park is open year-round with daily visitor limits, so plan any visit around a reservation booked up to 30 days ahead. In autumn 2026, also check the Park Notices site because of recent hurricane-related closures.
tips: Status as of Oct 2026: reopened Oct 15, 2026. Check the official page before going.
Non-residents must buy both entry and parking reservations in advance. Reservations open 30 days ahead, and parking reservations no longer cover passengers.
Parking reservations are only valid for the time slots you purchase. Staying from opening to closing requires buying all three slots.
Bring a valid parking voucher (print or digital) to show on arrival. Miloliʻi camping permits are not accepted for park entry.

hawaii.name: Na Pali Coast State Wilderness Park
hawaii.shortDescription: A breathtaking wilderness park featuring towering emerald cliffs, hidden sea caves, and pristine beaches along Kauai's rugged northern coastline.
hawaii.fullDescription: Na Pali Coast State Wilderness Park encompasses 6,175 acres of rugged land along the northwest coast of Kauai. The park is defined by its dramatic pali, or cliffs, which rise up to 4,000 feet above the Pacific Ocean. Historically, the valleys were home to ancient Hawaiian settlements, and today the area remains a protected wilderness accessible primarily by foot, boat, or helicopter, preserving its pristine natural beauty and geological significance.
thingsToDo: Boat tours for snorkeling and sea cave exploration
Photography of the dramatic cliff faces

hikingTrails.name: Kalalau Trail
hikingTrails.description: A world-famous, challenging trek that traverses five valleys and ends at the secluded Kalalau Beach.

hikingTrails.name: Hanakapi'ai Trail
hikingTrails.description: The first section of the Kalalau Trail leading to a beautiful beach and a nearby waterfall.

hawaii.campingInfo: Camping is allowed only at Kalalau Beach and requires a valid state-issued permit. There are no facilities, and campers must pack out all trash.
hawaii.fishingBoating: Boating is permitted via licensed commercial tour operators; private vessels require specific permits and adherence to strict environmental regulations.

visitorCenter.name: Kokee State Park Ranger Station
visitorCenter.info: Provides information, safety warnings, and permit assistance for the Na Pali Coast region.

hawaii.hours: Open 24 hours for permitted hikers; access is weather-dependent.
hawaii.entranceFees: Entry is free, but camping permits require a fee of $30 per person per night for non-residents.
hawaii.bestTimeToVisit: May through September when ocean conditions are calmer.
tips: Always check the weather forecast as flash floods can make trails dangerous.
Secure your camping permits months in advance as they sell out quickly.
Bring plenty of water and a filtration system, as there is no potable water on the trail.

hawaii.name: Makapuʻu Point State Scenic Shoreline
hawaii.shortDescription: Experience breathtaking panoramic views of Oahu's eastern coastline and the historic Makapuʻu Lighthouse from this scenic coastal trail.
hawaii.fullDescription: Makapuʻu Point State Scenic Shoreline offers visitors a unique opportunity to explore the rugged volcanic landscape of southeastern Oahu. The park is home to the iconic Makapuʻu Point Lighthouse, built in 1909, and provides excellent vantage points for whale watching during the winter months. The area is geologically significant, featuring dramatic sea cliffs and tide pools formed by ancient lava flows.

hikingTrails.name: Makapuʻu Point Lighthouse Trail
hikingTrails.description: A paved, steady incline trail that offers spectacular views of the Pacific Ocean and the offshore islands.

hikingTrails.name: Makapuʻu Tide Pools Trail
hikingTrails.description: A steep, unpaved descent from the main trail leading down to the natural tide pools along the shoreline.

hawaii.campingInfo: Camping is not permitted at Makapuʻu Point State Scenic Shoreline.

visitorCenter.name: Makapuʻu Point Information Kiosk
visitorCenter.info: Informational signage regarding the lighthouse history and local marine life.

hawaii.bestTimeToVisit: Winter months for whale watching or early morning to avoid midday heat.
tips: Bring plenty of water as there is no shade along the paved trail.
Wear sturdy shoes if you plan to hike down to the tide pools.
Arrive early in the morning to secure parking in the limited lot.

hawaii.name: Kōkeʻe State Park
hawaii.shortDescription: Perched high above the Waimea Canyon, Kōkeʻe State Park offers cool mountain air, lush rainforests, and breathtaking vistas of the Na Pali Coast.
hawaii.fullDescription: Kōkeʻe State Park encompasses 4,345 acres of mountainous terrain on the island of Kauaʻi. Located at elevations ranging from 3,200 to 4,200 feet, the park is characterized by its native koa and ʻōhiʻa forests, diverse birdlife, and dramatic overlooks. The area is geologically significant for its proximity to the Alakaʻi Swamp, one of the highest elevation swamps in the world, and its role as a gateway to the rugged cliffs of the Na Pali Coast.

hikingTrails.name: Pihea Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail offers stunning views of the Kalalau Valley and connects to the Alakaʻi Swamp Trail.

hikingTrails.name: Awaʻawapuhi Trail
hikingTrails.description: A challenging descent through native forest that ends at a dramatic cliff-top overlook of the Na Pali Coast.

hawaii.campingInfo: The park offers tent camping at the Kōkeʻe Campground and cabin rentals managed by the Kōkeʻe Lodge. Permits are required for all camping activities.
hawaii.fishingBoating: Fishing is permitted in designated streams during specific seasons with a valid Hawaii freshwater fishing license.

visitorCenter.name: Kōkeʻe Natural History Museum
visitorCenter.info: Provides educational exhibits on the park's unique flora, fauna, and history, along with trail maps and weather updates.

hawaii.entranceFees: Free entrance for Hawaii residents; non-residents must pay a parking fee of $10.00 per vehicle.
hawaii.bestTimeToVisit: Early morning to avoid afternoon clouds and mist.
tips: Bring layers as temperatures can be significantly cooler than at sea level.
Check trail conditions at the museum before heading out, as paths can be very muddy.
Pack plenty of water and snacks as there are limited services within the park.

hawaii.name: Diamond Head State Monument
hawaii.shortDescription: Diamond Head State Monument offers iconic panoramic views of the Honolulu coastline and the Pacific Ocean from the summit of a historic volcanic crater.
hawaii.fullDescription: Diamond Head, known to Native Hawaiians as Lēʻahi, is a volcanic tuff cone that was formed approximately 300,000 years ago. The park encompasses over 475 acres and features a challenging trail that leads to the summit, where visitors can explore historic military bunkers and observation decks built in the early 20th century as part of Oahu's coastal defense system.

hikingTrails.name: Diamond Head Summit Trail
hikingTrails.description: A steep, paved and dirt trail that climbs 560 feet from the crater floor to the summit, featuring stairs and a tunnel.

hikingTrails.name: Crater Floor Loop
hikingTrails.description: A gentle walk around the base of the interior crater, offering views of the surrounding volcanic walls.

hawaii.campingInfo: Camping is not permitted within the Diamond Head State Monument.
hawaii.fishingBoating: Not applicable as the park is located inland within a volcanic crater.

visitorCenter.name: Diamond Head Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides educational exhibits on the geology and military history of the crater, along with park information and souvenirs.

hawaii.hours: Daily: 6:00 AM - 6:00 PM (Last entry at 4:00 PM)
hawaii.entranceFees: $5.00 per person entry fee and $10.00 per vehicle parking fee.
hawaii.bestTimeToVisit: Early morning to avoid the midday heat and peak crowds.
tips: Reservations are required for all visitors and vehicles.
Bring plenty of water and wear sturdy hiking shoes.
The trail is steep and involves climbing stairs, so prepare accordingly.

hawaii.name: Palaʻau State Park
hawaii.shortDescription: Palaʻau State Park offers breathtaking views of the Kalaupapa Peninsula and a glimpse into Molokaʻi's rich cultural history.
hawaii.fullDescription: Located on the northern coast of Molokaʻi, Palaʻau State Park is a 234-acre park known for its dramatic cliffs and historical significance. The park features the famous Phallic Rock, a site of cultural importance, and provides a stunning overlook of the Kalaupapa National Historical Park, where the historic leper colony was established. The area is characterized by its lush eucalyptus and ironwood forests, offering a cool, serene environment for visitors.
thingsToDo: Picnicking in the shaded forest areas

hikingTrails.name: Kalaupapa Lookout Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short, paved path leading to a spectacular overlook of the Kalaupapa Peninsula and the world's highest sea cliffs.

hikingTrails.name: Phallic Rock Trail
hikingTrails.description: A brief walk through a beautiful ironwood forest to reach the culturally significant Phallic Rock formation.

hawaii.campingInfo: Camping is currently not permitted at Palaʻau State Park.

visitorCenter.name: Palaʻau State Park Information Kiosk
visitorCenter.info: The park provides informational signage regarding the history of the Kalaupapa settlement and local cultural sites.

hawaii.bestTimeToVisit: Early morning for the clearest views of the Kalaupapa Peninsula before afternoon clouds roll in.
tips: Bring a light jacket as the elevation makes the park significantly cooler than the coast.
Check the weather forecast, as the lookout is often obscured by fog or low clouds.
Respect the cultural significance of the Phallic Rock and do not climb on or disturb the site.

idaho.name: Farragut State Park
idaho.shortDescription: North Idaho park on Lake Pend Oreille, on the site of a World War II naval training station.
idaho.fullDescription: Farragut State Park covers 4,000 acres at the southern tip of Lake Pend Oreille in the Coeur d'Alene Mountains, about 30 miles northeast of Coeur d'Alene. It was the Farragut Naval Training Station during World War II, where over 293,000 sailors trained; the Museum at the Brig occupies its former confinement building. The park offers camping, boating, swimming, hiking and disc golf.

hikingTrails.name: Shoreline Trail
hikingTrails.description: An easy, fairly flat loop trail with very little elevation gain.

hikingTrails.name: Squirrel Cache Trail
hikingTrails.description: An easy loop suitable for casual walkers and families.

hikingTrails.name: Highpoint Trail
hikingTrails.description: The park recommends taking the Highpoint Trail to the Scout Trail for hikers who like a challenge.

idaho.campingInfo: The park has 223 individual campsites, 10 camping cabins and 7 group camps; in fall 2026 Waldron campground is open with vault toilets only, and water to the sites is turned off.
idaho.fishingBoating: Fishing and boating are offered at the park, which sits on the southern tip of Lake Pend Oreille.

visitorCenter.name: Farragut State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

idaho.hours: Day-use 7am–10pm; Visitor Center 9am–4pm (Fall/Winter 2026); Museum at the Brig open Memorial Day–Labor Day
idaho.entranceFees: $7 resident / $14 non-resident motor vehicle entrance fee, due on arrival year-round (per IDPR guide; confirm current rate)
idaho.bestTimeToVisit: Summer, between Memorial Day and Labor Day, is best for the full experience, since the Museum at the Brig is open and campground services are on; fall is quieter but cool, with seasonal closures.
tips: State Highway 54 construction through the park means detours and alternate entrances; flaggers direct arriving visitors.
The Museum at the Brig is closed for the season and reopens Memorial Day weekend 2027.
Dogs must be confined or on a leash no longer than 6 feet and never left unattended.

idaho.name: Ponderosa State Park
idaho.shortDescription: McCall park on a forested peninsula in Payette Lake, with trails, beaches and cabins.
idaho.fullDescription: Ponderosa State Park covers 1,515 acres on a peninsula in Payette Lake at the northeast edge of McCall, plus a North Beach unit at the lake's northern end. It has hiking and biking trails, beaches, guided walks, evening programs, a visitor center and cabins, with skiing and snowshoeing in winter.

hikingTrails.name: Peninsula Trail
hikingTrails.description: AllTrails lists it as the best place to hike in the park, with about 134 ft of elevation gain.

hikingTrails.name: Meadow Marsh Trail
hikingTrails.description: It is temporarily closed after the Meadow Marsh 2 under burn and will reopen once the park deems it safe for pedestrians.

idaho.campingInfo: The park offers 163 serviced campsites, 22 standard sites, 7 serviced ADA sites, 9 deluxe cabins and 1 camper cabin, and no overnight parking or camping in vehicles is allowed in the campgrounds.
idaho.fishingBoating: The park has boat ramps and handling docks, canoe and kayak rentals for paddling the North Fork of the Payette River, and fishing supplies sold at the Visitor Center.

visitorCenter.name: Ponderosa State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

idaho.hours: Day-use 7 am–10 pm (may change at park manager discretion)
idaho.entranceFees: $7–$14 per vehicle, single-day entry (per Visit Idaho)
idaho.bestTimeToVisit: Summer brings Junior Ranger and naturalist programs on Payette Lake, while winter offers groomed Nordic ski and snowshoe trails at this 5,050-ft mountain park.
tips: Pets must be on a leash no longer than 6 feet, electronic shock collars do not meet this requirement, and pets are not allowed in cabins.
Expect brief road closures in October near the Water Tower 2 area during forest restoration work.
Book campsites and cabins through park reservations at 1-888-9-CAMPID, and note there is no camping in your vehicle in any campground.

idaho.name: Bruneau Dunes State Park
idaho.shortDescription: Idaho park home to North America's tallest single-structured sand dune, about 470 feet high.
idaho.fullDescription: Bruneau Dunes State Park covers 4,800 acres in Owyhee County, fifteen miles south of Mountain Home. It has large sand dunes and small lakes, including North America's tallest single-structured dune at about 470 feet. Visitors climb and sandboard the dunes (no vehicles allowed), and a public observatory opens for stargazing on weekend evenings.

hikingTrails.name: 6 Mile Dune Trail
hikingTrails.description: A six-mile interpretive trail that crosses the country's tallest single-structured sand dune, rated moderately strenuous on the dune tops and taking 3–6 hours.

hikingTrails.name: Bruneau Dunes Loop
hikingTrails.description: A moderate loop with 538 ft of elevation gain that takes about 1–1.5 hours.

idaho.campingInfo: The park has 82 serviced and 35 standard campsites plus 2 cabins; reservations are required for the Broken Wheel and Eagle Cove campgrounds (1-888-922-6743), while the 19-site Equestrian Campground is first-come, first-served.
idaho.fishingBoating: You can fish for bluegill and bass in the lakes at the foot of the dune, and the boat ramps allow electric-motor boats only.

visitorCenter.name: Bruneau Dunes State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

idaho.hours: Day-use areas, including the dunes, open 7 am–10 pm. Hours may change at the park manager's discretion. Visitor Center and entrance kiosk hours vary.
idaho.entranceFees: $7 Motor Vehicle Entrance Fee per vehicle (bring cash or check)
idaho.address: 27608 Sand Dunes Rd, Mountain Home, ID 83647
idaho.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and fall are most comfortable because summer heat on the dunes is intense; peak season starts in mid-March, and winter brings Saturday-night observatory programs.
tips: Bring cash or a check for the $7 vehicle entrance fee, because Visitor Center and kiosk hours vary and not paying can result in a citation.
For the 6 Mile Dune Trail, pack 1–2 quarts of water per person and sturdy shoes, and avoid the intense summer heat.
Sandboards (stand-up and sled styles) rent at the Visitor Center for $15/day for one or $25/day for two, and renters must be 18 or older.

idaho.name: Harriman State Park
idaho.shortDescription: Nestled within an 11,000-acre wildlife refuge in the heart of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, Harriman State Park offers stunning landscapes and world-class fly fishing.
idaho.fullDescription: Harriman State Park is located inside the Harriman Wildlife Refuge, featuring the famous Henrys Fork of the Snake River. Once a private retreat for the Union Pacific Railroad investors, the park preserves historic buildings and provides a sanctuary for trumpeter swans, moose, and elk. The landscape is defined by lodgepole pine forests, lush meadows, and volcanic geology.
thingsToDo: Fly fishing on the Henrys Fork

hikingTrails.name: Railroad Ranch Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic, relatively flat trail that winds through the historic ranch grounds and offers excellent views of the river.

hikingTrails.name: Thayer Creek Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail leads hikers through dense forests and open meadows, providing frequent opportunities to spot local wildlife.

idaho.campingInfo: The park offers several yurts for rent and a group camp area, but does not provide traditional RV hookup sites.
idaho.fishingBoating: The Henrys Fork is world-renowned for fly fishing; however, motorized boating is prohibited to protect the wildlife refuge.

visitorCenter.name: Harriman State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on park history, wildlife conservation, and trail maps.

idaho.address: 3489 Green Canyon Rd, Island Park, ID 83429
idaho.bestTimeToVisit: June through September for hiking and fishing; December through March for winter sports.
tips: Bring binoculars for excellent bird watching opportunities near the river.
Be prepared for rapidly changing weather conditions due to the high elevation.
Purchase a day-use permit at the entrance station upon arrival.

idaho.name: Castle Rocks State Park
idaho.shortDescription: A stunning high-desert landscape featuring massive granite rock formations and rich historical significance near Almo, Idaho.
idaho.fullDescription: Castle Rocks State Park is a geological wonderland located in the Albion Mountains. The park is renowned for its towering granite spires and boulders, which attract rock climbers from across the globe. Historically, the area served as a landmark for pioneers traveling the California Trail, and the park preserves remnants of this rich frontier history alongside its unique natural rock architecture.

hikingTrails.name: Castle Rocks Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic loop that winds through the base of the massive granite formations, offering excellent views of the rock spires.

hikingTrails.name: Emigrant Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle path that follows the historic route used by pioneers, featuring interpretive signs about the area's history.

idaho.campingInfo: The park offers a variety of camping options, including tent sites, RV sites with electrical hookups, and unique yurts available for reservation.
idaho.fishingBoating: Fishing is not a primary activity at this park, as there are no major lakes or rivers within the park boundaries.

visitorCenter.name: Castle Rocks State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on climbing routes, park history, and trail maps.

idaho.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for the best weather and climbing conditions.
tips: Bring plenty of water as the high-desert climate is very dry.
Check in at the visitor center for current climbing route closures.
The park is a designated dark sky area, making it perfect for night photography.

idaho.name: Priest Lake State Park
idaho.shortDescription: Nestled in the Selkirk Mountains of northern Idaho, Priest Lake State Park offers crystal-clear waters and pristine forests perfect for outdoor adventure.
idaho.fullDescription: Priest Lake State Park is located in the northern panhandle of Idaho, surrounded by the majestic Selkirk Mountains. The park is renowned for its deep, clear, cold water and dense forests of cedar, fir, and hemlock. The area was shaped by glacial activity, resulting in the deep basin that holds the lake today. Visitors can explore the diverse ecosystem, which serves as a habitat for various wildlife, while enjoying recreational activities ranging from boating to winter snowshoeing.
thingsToDo: Fishing for lake trout and kokanee

hikingTrails.name: Indian Creek Nature Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle loop that winds through the forest, offering excellent opportunities to observe local flora and fauna.

hikingTrails.name: Lion Head Trail
hikingTrails.description: A challenging climb that rewards hikers with breathtaking panoramic views of Priest Lake and the surrounding Selkirk Mountains.

idaho.campingInfo: The park features multiple campgrounds including Indian Creek, Dickensheet, and Lionhead, offering a mix of tent sites, RV sites with hookups, and rustic cabins.
idaho.fishingBoating: The park offers multiple boat ramps and docks. Fishing is popular for lake trout, kokanee, and cutthroat trout.

visitorCenter.name: Indian Creek Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides park information, maps, educational displays about local ecology, and gift shop items.

idaho.address: 4223 N Indian Creek Rd, Coolin, ID 83821
idaho.bestTimeToVisit: July through September for water activities, or January through March for winter sports.
tips: Book campsites well in advance as they fill up quickly during summer months.
Bring insect repellent, especially during the early summer season.
Check the official website for current water safety conditions and boat ramp status.

idaho.name: Thousand Springs State Park
idaho.shortDescription: Thousand Springs State Park is a collection of unique units along the Snake River, famous for its dramatic waterfalls, crystal-clear springs, and rich agricultural history.
idaho.fullDescription: Thousand Springs State Park consists of several distinct units including Malad Gorge, Niagara Springs, Ritter Island, and Billingsley Creek. The park showcases the unique geology of the Snake River Plain, where water from the Eastern Snake River Plain Aquifer emerges from the canyon walls as massive springs. Visitors can explore the deep, narrow gorge of Malad Gorge, view the powerful Niagara Springs, or enjoy the historic charm of Ritter Island, which was once a world-renowned dairy farm.

hikingTrails.name: Malad Gorge Rim Trail
hikingTrails.description: A relatively flat trail that offers spectacular views of the 250-foot deep Malad Gorge and the Devil's Washbowl.

hikingTrails.name: Ritter Island Loop
hikingTrails.description: This trail winds around the historic island, providing lush greenery and close-up views of the springs emerging from the canyon walls.

idaho.campingInfo: While there is no traditional tent or RV camping within the park units, there are nearby private campgrounds and lodging options in the town of Hagerman.
idaho.fishingBoating: Fishing is permitted in the Snake River and designated areas of the park; however, there are no boat rentals available on-site.

visitorCenter.name: Thousand Springs State Park Office
visitorCenter.info: The park office provides maps, educational brochures, and information regarding the various units of the park.

idaho.entranceFees: Free entrance to most units, though some specific parking areas may require a small fee or Idaho State Parks Passport.
idaho.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and early summer when the waterfalls are at peak flow and the wildflowers are in bloom.
tips: Visit the Malad Gorge unit early in the morning to avoid crowds and capture the best light for photography.
Bring binoculars for excellent bird watching opportunities along the Snake River.
Check the official website before visiting, as some units like Ritter Island may have seasonal access restrictions.

idaho.name: Hells Gate State Park
idaho.shortDescription: Located at the gateway to the deepest river gorge in North America, this park offers stunning views of the Snake River and rich Nez Perce cultural history.
idaho.fullDescription: Hells Gate State Park is situated along the banks of the Snake River in Lewiston, Idaho. The park serves as the entrance to the Hells Canyon National Recreation Area, featuring dramatic basalt cliffs and a unique high-desert ecosystem. The area is historically significant as the homeland of the Nimiipuu (Nez Perce) people and was passed through by the Lewis and Clark Expedition in 1805.
thingsToDo: Jet boat tours of Hells Canyon
Cycling on the paved greenbelt trail
Educational programs at the visitor center

hikingTrails.name: Discovery Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle, flat path that winds through the park's riparian zone, offering excellent birdwatching opportunities.

hikingTrails.name: Jack O'Connor Center Loop
hikingTrails.description: This trail climbs slightly above the river valley, providing panoramic views of the Snake River and the surrounding canyon walls.

idaho.campingInfo: The park features 64 campsites with water and electrical hookups, as well as several tent-only sites and a group camping area.
idaho.fishingBoating: The park provides a public boat ramp with access to the Snake River, popular for fishing and recreational boating.

visitorCenter.name: Jack O'Connor Hunting Heritage and Education Center
visitorCenter.info: Features exhibits on the life of Jack O'Connor, local history, and the natural environment of the Hells Canyon region.

idaho.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Fall for mild temperatures and optimal wildlife viewing.
tips: Bring plenty of water as the canyon floor can get very hot during summer months.
Check the river conditions before planning any water-based activities.
Visit the Lewis and Clark interpretive displays to learn about the local indigenous history.

montana.name: Lewis and Clark Caverns State Park
montana.shortDescription: Explore one of the most highly decorated limestone caverns in the American Northwest, featuring spectacular stalactites, stalagmites, and helictites.
montana.fullDescription: Lewis and Clark Caverns State Park is Montana's first and best-known state park. The park features a massive limestone cavern system formed by ancient geological processes. Visitors can take guided tours through the cool, subterranean chambers to witness stunning rock formations. Above ground, the park offers rugged hiking trails through juniper forests and limestone cliffs, providing panoramic views of the Jefferson River valley.

hikingTrails.name: Cave Loop Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic loop that winds through the park's unique limestone landscape and offers great views of the surrounding mountains.

hikingTrails.name: Eastside Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail traverses the eastern side of the park, passing through diverse habitats and offering excellent opportunities for bird watching.

montana.campingInfo: The park features a campground with 40 sites, including RV-friendly spots, tent sites, and three camping cabins available for reservation.
montana.fishingBoating: While there is no direct water access for boating within the park, the nearby Jefferson River offers excellent fishing and floating opportunities.

visitorCenter.name: Lewis and Clark Caverns Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: The center provides educational exhibits on the geology and history of the caverns, as well as tour ticket sales and gift shop items.

montana.hours: 8:00 AM - 10:00 PM daily (Cavern tours are seasonal)
montana.entranceFees: Entrance is free for Montana residents with a vehicle registration fee; non-residents pay a daily vehicle entrance fee of $8.00.
montana.address: 25 Lewis & Clark Caverns Rd, Whitehall, MT 59759
tips: Book your cavern tour tickets well in advance as they sell out quickly during peak season.
Wear comfortable walking shoes with good grip, as the cave paths can be slippery.
Bring a light jacket, as the temperature inside the caverns remains a constant 50 degrees Fahrenheit year-round.

montana.name: Makoshika State Park
montana.shortDescription: Montana's largest state park, Makoshika features spectacular badlands formations and a rich history of dinosaur fossil discoveries.
montana.fullDescription: Makoshika State Park encompasses over 11,000 acres of badlands, characterized by dramatic rock formations, deep ravines, and hoodoos. The park is world-renowned for its paleontological significance, having yielded numerous fossils of dinosaurs such as Tyrannosaurus rex and Triceratops. Visitors can explore the rugged landscape that tells a story of the Cretaceous period, offering a unique blend of geological wonder and scientific discovery.

hikingTrails.name: Cap Rock Nature Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short, accessible loop that offers excellent views of the badlands and unique geological formations.

hikingTrails.name: Hungry Joe Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail winds through scenic coulees and offers a more immersive experience into the heart of the badlands.

montana.campingInfo: The park offers two campgrounds, Cains Coulee and Hungry Joe, with a total of 28 campsites. Amenities include fire rings, picnic tables, and vault toilets, but no water or electrical hookups are available.
montana.fishingBoating: Fishing is not a primary activity within the park, though the nearby Yellowstone River offers excellent fishing opportunities.

visitorCenter.name: Makoshika Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Features impressive dinosaur fossil displays, a gift shop, and educational information about the park's geology.

montana.entranceFees: $8.00 daily vehicle fee for non-residents; free for Montana residents.
montana.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for the best weather and trail conditions.
tips: Bring plenty of water as there is no potable water available in the backcountry.
Wear sturdy hiking boots to navigate the loose, uneven terrain of the badlands.
Visit during the early morning or late evening to avoid the intense midday heat and see more wildlife.

montana.name: Bannack State Park
montana.shortDescription: Bannack State Park is a remarkably well-preserved ghost town that offers a vivid glimpse into Montana's gold rush history.
montana.fullDescription: Bannack was the site of Montana's first major gold discovery in 1862. Today, it stands as one of the best-preserved ghost towns in the United States, featuring over 60 original structures that visitors can explore. The park provides a unique historical experience, showcasing the rugged life of early settlers, miners, and outlaws in the Montana Territory.

hikingTrails.name: Bannack Bench Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle trail offering panoramic views of the historic townsite and the surrounding Grasshopper Valley.

hikingTrails.name: Bannack Creek Loop
hikingTrails.description: A short, scenic walk along the creek that runs through the heart of the historic district.

montana.campingInfo: The park features the Vigilante Campground with 24 campsites, including some suitable for RVs, though no hookups are available.
montana.fishingBoating: Fishing is permitted in Grasshopper Creek, which runs through the park, primarily for trout.

visitorCenter.name: Bannack Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Located in the historic Meade Hotel, the visitor center provides maps, historical exhibits, and information on guided tours.

montana.entranceFees: $8.00 daily vehicle fee for non-residents; free for Montana residents.
montana.bestTimeToVisit: June through September for full access to historic buildings and pleasant weather.
tips: Bring comfortable walking shoes as the townsite has uneven dirt roads and boardwalks.
Visit during Bannack Days in July for historical reenactments and demonstrations.
Pack plenty of water and sunscreen as there is limited shade in the townsite.

montana.name: Giant Springs State Park
montana.shortDescription: Home to one of the largest freshwater springs in the world, this park offers stunning views of the Missouri River and lush riparian landscapes.
montana.fullDescription: Giant Springs State Park is located along the banks of the Missouri River in Great Falls, Montana. The park features one of the largest freshwater springs in the world, which flows at a rate of 156 million gallons of water per day at a constant temperature of 54 degrees Fahrenheit. The area was discovered by the Lewis and Clark Expedition in 1805 and remains a significant historical and natural landmark. The park's geology is defined by the Madison Limestone aquifer, which feeds the crystal-clear spring water into the river.
thingsToDo: Cycling on the River's Edge Trail

hikingTrails.name: River's Edge Trail
hikingTrails.description: A paved, accessible trail that follows the Missouri River, offering excellent views of the water and local wildlife.

hikingTrails.name: Springs Loop
hikingTrails.description: A short, scenic loop that takes visitors directly around the main spring head and the surrounding lush vegetation.

montana.campingInfo: There is no overnight camping available within the boundaries of Giant Springs State Park.
montana.fishingBoating: Fishing is permitted in the Missouri River within the park boundaries, provided you have a valid Montana fishing license. No boat ramps are located within the park.

visitorCenter.name: Giant Springs State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: The visitor center provides educational exhibits about the history of the springs, the Lewis and Clark expedition, and local geology.

montana.entranceFees: Free for Montana residents; $8.00 daily vehicle fee for non-residents.
montana.address: 4800 Giant Springs Rd, Great Falls, MT 59405
montana.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for the best weather and wildlife viewing.
tips: Bring a camera to capture the vibrant blue color of the spring water.
Visit the adjacent fish hatchery to feed the trout.
Wear comfortable walking shoes to explore the extensive River's Edge Trail system.
nearbyAttractions: First Peoples Buffalo Jump State Park

montana.name: Flathead Lake State Park
montana.shortDescription: Flathead Lake State Park is a collection of six unique units surrounding the largest natural freshwater lake in the western United States.
montana.fullDescription: Flathead Lake State Park consists of six distinct units: Big Arm, Finley Point, Wayfarers, West Shore, Yellow Bay, and Wild Horse Island. The park offers stunning views of the Mission Mountains and crystal-clear waters formed by glacial activity. Visitors can explore diverse ecosystems, ranging from rocky shorelines to dense forests, while enjoying the recreational opportunities provided by the massive lake.
thingsToDo: Fishing for lake trout and whitefish

hikingTrails.name: Wayfarers Nature Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short, scenic loop that winds through the forest and offers beautiful views of the lake and surrounding cliffs.

hikingTrails.name: Wild Horse Island Trail
hikingTrails.description: A trail that traverses the interior of Wild Horse Island, providing opportunities to spot wild horses, bighorn sheep, and mule deer.

montana.campingInfo: The park offers various camping options across its units, including tent sites, RV sites with electrical hookups, and group camping areas. Reservations are highly recommended during the summer season.
montana.fishingBoating: The park features multiple boat ramps and docks across its units, making it a premier destination for fishing, kayaking, and motorboating.

visitorCenter.name: Flathead Lake State Park Headquarters
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on park regulations, recreational opportunities, and educational exhibits about the lake's ecology.

montana.entranceFees: $8.00 daily vehicle fee for non-residents; free for Montana residents.
montana.bestTimeToVisit: June through September for water activities and pleasant weather.
tips: Check the specific unit you plan to visit, as they are located in different areas around the lake.
Always wear a life jacket when boating or swimming in the lake.
Book campsites well in advance, especially for weekends during the peak summer months.

montana.name: Lone Pine State Park
montana.shortDescription: Perched high above the Flathead Valley, Lone Pine State Park offers breathtaking panoramic views of the valley, Flathead Lake, and the surrounding mountain ranges.
montana.fullDescription: Lone Pine State Park is a 270-acre park located just outside of Kalispell, Montana. It serves as a gateway to the outdoors, featuring a diverse landscape of coniferous forests and open meadows. The park is renowned for its extensive trail system that caters to hikers, mountain bikers, and horseback riders, while providing educational opportunities through its visitor center which highlights the local ecosystem and wildlife.

hikingTrails.name: Lone Pine Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic loop that winds through dense forest and provides several vantage points overlooking the Flathead Valley.

hikingTrails.name: Cliff Trail
hikingTrails.description: A steeper path that leads to dramatic rock outcroppings and offers the most expansive views in the park.

montana.campingInfo: Lone Pine State Park does not offer overnight camping or RV hookups; it is strictly a day-use facility.
montana.fishingBoating: There is no fishing or boating available within the park boundaries as there are no lakes or rivers on the property.

visitorCenter.name: Lone Pine State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: The center features interactive exhibits on local flora and fauna, geology, and history, along with a gift shop and information desk.

montana.entranceFees: Free for Montana residents; non-residents pay a $8.00 daily vehicle entrance fee.
montana.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for optimal trail conditions and clear mountain views.
tips: Bring binoculars to take full advantage of the expansive valley views from the overlooks.
Check the visitor center schedule for seasonal guided nature walks and educational workshops.
Be bear aware and carry bear spray, as the park is located in active black bear habitat.

montana.name: Pictograph Cave State Park
montana.shortDescription: Explore ancient history at this archaeological site featuring rock paintings created by prehistoric hunters over 2,000 years ago.
montana.fullDescription: Pictograph Cave State Park is a 23-acre park that features three main caves: Pictograph, Middle, and Ghost caves. These caves served as a home for generations of prehistoric hunters. Archaeologists have recovered over 30,000 artifacts from the site, including stone tools, weapons, and paintings that provide a window into the lives of the people who inhabited the Yellowstone River valley thousands of years ago.

hikingTrails.name: Pictograph Cave Trail
hikingTrails.description: A paved, loop trail that leads visitors past the three main caves with interpretive signs explaining the history and geology of the site.

hikingTrails.name: Canyon Rim Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short trail offering scenic views of the surrounding sandstone cliffs and the valley below.

montana.campingInfo: There is no camping available at Pictograph Cave State Park. The park is strictly for day-use only.

visitorCenter.name: Pictograph Cave Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: The visitor center features exhibits on the archaeological findings and the history of the rock art found within the caves.

montana.entranceFees: $8.00 per vehicle for non-residents; Montana residents enter for free with their vehicle registration fee.
montana.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Fall for mild temperatures and optimal hiking conditions.
tips: Bring binoculars to get a better view of the pictographs, as they are protected and cannot be approached closely.
Wear sturdy walking shoes as the trail has some incline and uneven surfaces.
Visit during the early morning to avoid the heat of the day and see more wildlife.

montana.name: Medicine Rocks State Park
montana.shortDescription: Medicine Rocks State Park is a unique geological site featuring massive sandstone pillars and ancient petroglyphs in the heart of eastern Montana.
montana.fullDescription: Medicine Rocks State Park is renowned for its dramatic sandstone formations that rise from the prairie, sculpted by wind and water over millions of years. Historically significant to Native American tribes, the park contains numerous petroglyphs and pictographs. The site offers a surreal landscape that has captivated visitors for centuries, including Theodore Roosevelt, who famously described the area as 'as fantastically beautiful a place as I have ever seen.'

hikingTrails.name: Medicine Rocks Loop
hikingTrails.description: A gentle loop that winds through the base of the towering sandstone formations, offering close-up views of the unique rock textures.

hikingTrails.name: Prairie Vista Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail climbs to higher ground, providing panoramic views of the surrounding Montana prairie and the park's rock formations from above.

montana.campingInfo: The park offers 12 primitive campsites suitable for tents and small RVs. There are no hookups, and water is not available on-site, so visitors must pack in their own supplies.
montana.fishingBoating: There are no lakes or rivers within the park boundaries, so fishing and boating are not available.

visitorCenter.name: Medicine Rocks Information Kiosk
visitorCenter.info: Self-service information kiosk providing maps, historical context, and safety guidelines for exploring the rock formations.

montana.entranceFees: Free for Montana residents; non-residents pay a daily vehicle fee of $8.00.
montana.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for the most comfortable weather and accessible roads.
tips: Bring plenty of water as there are no potable water sources within the park.
The sandstone is fragile; please do not climb on or deface the rock formations.
The park is an excellent location for night photography due to minimal light pollution.

nevada.name: Valley of Fire State Park
nevada.shortDescription: Nevada's oldest and largest state park, famous for its stunning 40,000-year-old Aztec sandstone formations and ancient petroglyphs.
nevada.fullDescription: Valley of Fire State Park covers nearly 46,000 acres and is known for its bright red sandstone formations that appear to be on fire when reflecting the sun's rays. The park features ancient petroglyphs carved into the rock by the Basketmaker culture and later the Paiute people. Geologically, the park is a showcase of complex uplift and faulting, resulting in dramatic landscapes that have served as backdrops for numerous films and television productions.

hikingTrails.name: Fire Wave Trail
hikingTrails.description: A popular trail leading to a unique, striped sandstone formation that resembles a wave.

hikingTrails.name: White Domes Trail
hikingTrails.description: A loop trail that takes hikers through a slot canyon and past remnants of an old movie set.

nevada.campingInfo: The park offers two campgrounds, Atlatl Rock and Arch Rock, featuring a total of 72 units with water, tables, grills, and restrooms. Some sites offer electrical and water hookups.
nevada.fishingBoating: There is no fishing or boating available within the boundaries of Valley of Fire State Park.

visitorCenter.name: Valley of Fire Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides educational exhibits on the park's geology, ecology, and history, along with a gift shop and ranger assistance.

nevada.entranceFees: $10.00 per vehicle for Nevada residents, $15.00 per vehicle for non-residents.
nevada.address: 29450 Valley of Fire Hwy, Overton, NV 89040
nevada.bestTimeToVisit: October through April to avoid extreme summer heat.
tips: Bring at least one gallon of water per person if hiking during the day.
Visit the petroglyphs at Atlatl Rock early in the morning to avoid crowds.
Check the park website for seasonal road closures or extreme heat warnings.

nevada.name: Cathedral Gorge State Park
nevada.shortDescription: Experience the dramatic, towering bentonite clay spires and narrow slot canyons of this unique Nevada desert landscape.
nevada.fullDescription: Cathedral Gorge State Park is a geological wonder located in a long, narrow valley in southeastern Nevada. The park is famous for its dramatic, cathedral-like spires and narrow slot canyons carved into soft, light-colored bentonite clay. Formed by volcanic activity millions of years ago and shaped by erosion, the landscape offers a surreal, labyrinthine environment that is unlike anywhere else in the state.
thingsToDo: Stargazing in the dark desert sky

hikingTrails.name: Miller Point Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short, scenic trail leading to an overlook with panoramic views of the entire gorge.

hikingTrails.name: Moon Caves Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short but adventurous path that takes you deep into the narrow, winding slot canyons.

nevada.campingInfo: The park features 22 campsites equipped with tables, grills, and fire pits. There are restrooms with showers and a dump station available for RVs.
nevada.fishingBoating: Fishing and boating are not available at Cathedral Gorge State Park, as it is a land-based geological park.

visitorCenter.name: Cathedral Gorge Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on the park's geology, history, and trail maps, along with interpretive exhibits.

nevada.hours: Open 24 hours daily for day use and camping.
nevada.entranceFees: $5.00 per vehicle for Nevada residents, $10.00 per vehicle for non-residents.
nevada.address: 111 Cathedral Gorge State Park Rd, Panaca, NV 89042
nevada.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Fall, when temperatures are mild and comfortable for hiking.
tips: Bring plenty of water as the desert air is very dry.
Wear sturdy shoes for navigating the sandy and uneven canyon floors.
Visit during the golden hour for the best photography lighting on the clay spires.

nevada.name: Lake Tahoe Nevada State Park
nevada.shortDescription: Lake Tahoe Nevada State Park features pristine alpine scenery, crystal-clear waters, and rugged mountain terrain along the eastern shore of Lake Tahoe.
nevada.fullDescription: Spanning over 14,000 acres, Lake Tahoe Nevada State Park encompasses diverse landscapes ranging from the sandy beaches of Sand Harbor to the high-altitude wilderness of the Marlette-Hobart backcountry. The park is renowned for its unique geology, including massive granite boulders and glacial-carved valleys, and serves as a vital habitat for diverse Sierra Nevada wildlife.
thingsToDo: Swimming and sunbathing at Sand Harbor
Mountain biking on the Flume Trail

hikingTrails.name: Sand Harbor Nature Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short, accessible boardwalk trail offering beautiful views of the shoreline and interpretive signs about the local ecosystem.

hikingTrails.name: Marlette Lake Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic trek that leads visitors through forested terrain to the stunning, high-altitude Marlette Lake.

nevada.campingInfo: There is no developed camping within the park boundaries; however, backcountry camping is permitted in the Marlette-Hobart area with a valid permit.
nevada.fishingBoating: Fishing is permitted in accordance with Nevada Department of Wildlife regulations; boat launches are available at Sand Harbor.

visitorCenter.name: Sand Harbor Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on park history, safety, and recreational opportunities, along with a gift shop.

nevada.entranceFees: $10.00 per vehicle for Nevada residents, $15.00 for non-residents.
nevada.bestTimeToVisit: Summer for water activities and fall for cooler hiking temperatures.
tips: Arrive early during summer weekends as parking lots fill up quickly.
Bring plenty of water and sunscreen, as the high altitude increases sun exposure.
Practice Leave No Trace principles to protect the fragile alpine environment.

nevada.name: Spring Mountain Ranch State Park
nevada.shortDescription: Nestled in the Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area, this historic ranch offers a unique blend of lush green pastures and dramatic desert mountain scenery.
nevada.fullDescription: Spring Mountain Ranch State Park is a 520-acre oasis located at the base of the Wilson Cliffs. Originally established in the 1860s, the ranch has a colorful history involving early settlers, wealthy socialites, and even Hollywood stars like Vera Krupp and Howard Hughes. The park preserves historic ranch buildings, including the main ranch house, and provides a cool, green retreat from the nearby Las Vegas heat.

hikingTrails.name: Sandstone Canyon Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic trail that leads hikers through beautiful sandstone formations and offers panoramic views of the valley.

hikingTrails.name: Overlook Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short, accessible path that provides a stunning vantage point of the entire ranch property and surrounding mountains.

nevada.campingInfo: There is no public camping available at Spring Mountain Ranch State Park; however, nearby Red Rock Canyon offers limited camping options.
nevada.fishingBoating: Fishing and boating are not permitted at this park.

visitorCenter.name: Spring Mountain Ranch Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on the ranch's history, local geology, and guided tour schedules.

nevada.entranceFees: $10.00 per vehicle for Nevada residents, $15.00 per vehicle for non-residents.
nevada.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Fall for mild temperatures and blooming desert flora.
tips: Bring plenty of water as the desert air is very dry.
Check the park website for the schedule of outdoor theater events.
Arrive early on weekends as parking can fill up quickly during peak season.
nearbyAttractions: Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area

nevada.name: Berlin-Ichthyosaur State Park
nevada.shortDescription: Explore the fascinating remains of giant marine reptiles and a well-preserved ghost town in the remote Shoshone Mountains.
nevada.fullDescription: Berlin-Ichthyosaur State Park protects the world's most prolific concentration of Ichthyosaur fossils, massive marine reptiles that swam in a prehistoric ocean 225 million years ago. In addition to the fossil shelter, the park features the historic town of Berlin, a late 19th-century mining camp that remains in a state of 'arrested decay,' offering a unique glimpse into Nevada's silver mining history.

hikingTrails.name: Berlin Town Site Loop
hikingTrails.description: A gentle walk through the historic mining town, passing original structures and mining equipment.

hikingTrails.name: Ichthyosaur Fossil Shelter Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short but steep path leading up to the fossil shelter, providing panoramic views of the surrounding valley.

nevada.campingInfo: The park offers 14 campsites suitable for tents and small RVs, available on a first-come, first-served basis with fire pits and picnic tables.
nevada.fishingBoating: Not applicable; there are no bodies of water suitable for fishing or boating within the park.

visitorCenter.name: Park Ranger Station
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on fossil tours, park history, and safety guidelines for the remote desert environment.

nevada.hours: Open 24 hours daily for day use; camping is permitted in designated sites.
nevada.entranceFees: $5.00 per vehicle for Nevada residents, $10.00 for non-residents.
nevada.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Fall, as summer temperatures can be extreme and winter brings heavy snow.
tips: Bring plenty of water and supplies as the park is very remote.
Check the official website for fossil shelter tour schedules before arriving.
Ensure your vehicle has a full tank of gas before heading into the Shoshone Mountains.

nevada.name: Beaver Dam State Park
nevada.shortDescription: A remote and rugged high-desert oasis featuring dramatic volcanic rock formations and a picturesque reservoir.
nevada.fullDescription: Beaver Dam State Park is located in a deep, narrow canyon in the eastern part of Nevada. The park is known for its unique geology, including dramatic volcanic rock formations and the remnants of a historic dam. Visitors can explore the diverse landscape which transitions from high desert scrub to lush riparian zones along the Beaver Dam Creek.

hikingTrails.name: Beaver Dam Wash Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail follows the creek through the canyon, offering excellent views of the unique rock formations and riparian vegetation.

hikingTrails.name: Overlook Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short path leading to a scenic overlook that provides a panoramic view of the canyon and the reservoir below.

nevada.campingInfo: The park offers two campgrounds, Sagebrush and Mahogany, with primitive sites suitable for tents and small RVs. No hookups are available.
nevada.fishingBoating: Fishing is popular in the reservoir and Beaver Dam Creek; no motorized boats are permitted.

visitorCenter.name: Beaver Dam Ranger Station
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on park history, trail maps, and current conditions.

nevada.address: Beaver Dam State Park, Panaca, NV 89042
tips: The access road is unpaved and can be rough; high-clearance vehicles are recommended.
Bring plenty of water and supplies as the park is very remote.
Check weather conditions before traveling, as flash floods can occur in the canyon.

nevada.name: Kershaw-Ryan State Park
nevada.shortDescription: Nestled in a lush canyon near Caliente, this park features dramatic 700-foot cliffs and a vibrant oasis of gardens and fruit trees.
nevada.fullDescription: Kershaw-Ryan State Park is a unique desert oasis located in Rainbow Canyon. Originally homesteaded by Samuel Kershaw in the 1870s, the park is famous for its dramatic canyon walls that rise 700 feet above the valley floor. The park features a natural spring that feeds a lush landscape of grapevines, fruit trees, and manicured lawns, providing a stark and beautiful contrast to the surrounding arid Nevada desert landscape.
thingsToDo: Picnicking in the shaded garden areas
Bird watching along the canyon walls
Photography of the dramatic rock formations

hikingTrails.name: Kershaw Canyon Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic trail that winds through the canyon, offering spectacular views of the towering cliffs and local flora.

hikingTrails.name: Overlook Trail
hikingTrails.description: A steep climb that rewards hikers with a panoramic view of the entire canyon and the lush park grounds below.

nevada.campingInfo: The park offers 15 campsites suitable for tents and RVs, equipped with fire pits, picnic tables, and access to water and restrooms. No hookups are available.
nevada.fishingBoating: There is no fishing or boating available at this park.

visitorCenter.name: Kershaw-Ryan Park Office
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on park history, trail maps, and local wildlife education.

nevada.hours: Open daily from sunrise to sunset
nevada.entranceFees: $5.00 per vehicle for Nevada residents, $10.00 for non-residents.
nevada.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Fall for mild temperatures and blooming flora.
tips: Bring plenty of water as desert heat can be intense even in the canyon.
Visit during the spring to see the fruit trees in bloom.
Pack a picnic to enjoy in the designated shaded garden areas.

nevada.name: Washoe Lake State Park
nevada.shortDescription: Nestled in the valley between Reno and Carson City, Washoe Lake State Park offers stunning views of the Sierra Nevada mountains and diverse recreational opportunities.
nevada.fullDescription: Washoe Lake State Park is situated in the Washoe Valley, providing a scenic escape with panoramic views of the Carson Range and the Virginia Range. The park is centered around Washoe Lake, a shallow basin that serves as a vital stopover for migratory birds. The area is rich in history, having been a part of the Comstock Lode era, and today it offers a tranquil environment for outdoor enthusiasts to enjoy water sports, hiking, and equestrian activities.

hikingTrails.name: North Beach Trail
hikingTrails.description: A flat, accessible trail that runs along the northern shoreline, perfect for bird watching and sunset views.

hikingTrails.name: Deadman's Creek Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail offers a slight elevation gain and provides excellent vantage points of the surrounding valley and mountain ranges.

nevada.campingInfo: The park features a 49-site campground equipped with tables, grills, and fire pits. Restrooms and showers are available, and some sites can accommodate RVs up to 45 feet.
nevada.fishingBoating: The lake is popular for fishing, primarily for catfish and carp. A boat ramp is available for motorized and non-motorized watercraft.

visitorCenter.name: Washoe Lake State Park Office
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on park history, wildlife, and current trail conditions.

nevada.hours: Open daily from 8:00 AM to sunset
nevada.entranceFees: $5.00 per vehicle for Nevada residents; $10.00 per vehicle for non-residents.
nevada.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Fall for mild temperatures and peak bird migration.
tips: Bring binoculars for excellent bird watching opportunities.
Check wind conditions before heading out for windsurfing or sailing.
Ensure you have plenty of water as the valley can be quite dry and exposed.

new mexico.name: City of Rocks State Park
new mexico.shortDescription: Experience a surreal landscape of massive volcanic rock formations rising from the high desert floor, perfect for hiking and stargazing.
new mexico.fullDescription: City of Rocks State Park features massive volcanic tuff formations that were sculpted by wind and water over millions of years.
