ohio.campingInfo: The park features a large campground with 93 full-service sites offering electric, water, and sewer hookups, as well as primitive sites and cabins available for reservation.
ohio.fishingBoating: The park features a world-class marina with boat slips, launch ramps, and excellent fishing opportunities for walleye, perch, and smallmouth bass.

visitorCenter.name: Geneva State Park Office
visitorCenter.info: The park office provides information on trail conditions, camping reservations, and local area attractions.

ohio.entranceFees: Admission to Geneva State Park is free.
ohio.bestTimeToVisit: Summer for swimming and boating, or autumn for vibrant foliage.
tips: Visit the nearby Geneva-on-the-Lake 'Strip' for classic summer entertainment.
Check the Lake Erie water quality reports online before planning a swim.
Bring binoculars as the park is a great spot for migratory bird watching.
nearbyAttractions: Covered Bridge Tour of Ashtabula County

ohio.name: Salt Fork State Park
ohio.shortDescription: Ohio's largest state park, Salt Fork offers a massive reservoir, rugged hills, and the historic Stone House.
ohio.fullDescription: Salt Fork State Park is Ohio's largest state park, encompassing 17,229 acres of lush forests, open meadows, and the expansive 2,952-acre Salt Fork Lake. The park is renowned for its diverse topography, which includes deep valleys and rolling hills that provide a scenic backdrop for outdoor recreation. Historically, the area is home to the Kennedy Stone House, a structure built in 1837 that stands as a testament to the early settlers of the region. The park's geology is characterized by sandstone formations and rich coal deposits, which have shaped the landscape over millions of years.
thingsToDo: Boating and fishing on Salt Fork Lake
Swimming at the large public beach

hikingTrails.name: Stone House Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic trail that leads hikers to the historic Kennedy Stone House, offering views of the lake and surrounding woodlands.

hikingTrails.name: Morgan Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle path perfect for families, winding through mature hardwood forests and providing excellent opportunities for spotting local wildlife.

ohio.campingInfo: The park features a massive campground with over 600 sites, including full-hookup RV sites, electric-only sites, and primitive camping. Cabins are also available for rent near the lodge.
ohio.fishingBoating: The park features multiple boat launch ramps and a full-service marina. Fishing is popular for largemouth bass, crappie, and walleye.

visitorCenter.name: Salt Fork State Park Office
visitorCenter.info: Provides maps, park information, and assistance with camping reservations and recreational permits.

ohio.hours: Open 24 hours daily for registered campers; day-use areas open from 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM.
ohio.entranceFees: Admission to Salt Fork State Park is free for all visitors.
ohio.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for water activities and fall foliage viewing.
tips: Visit the Kennedy Stone House early in the day to avoid crowds.
Bring binoculars as the park is a prime location for bald eagle sightings.
Check the official website for lake water quality alerts before planning a swimming trip.

ohio.name: Marblehead Lighthouse State Park
ohio.shortDescription: Marblehead Lighthouse is one of the most iconic and photographed landmarks in Ohio, offering stunning views of Lake Erie and the surrounding islands.
ohio.fullDescription: Established in 1821, the Marblehead Lighthouse is the oldest lighthouse in continuous operation on the U.S. side of the Great Lakes. The park features a limestone lighthouse tower, a keeper's house museum, and expansive grounds that provide panoramic views of Sandusky Bay and Kelleys Island. The site is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and serves as a vital piece of maritime history for the region.
thingsToDo: Photography of the lighthouse and lake

hikingTrails.name: Lighthouse Grounds Walk
hikingTrails.description: A scenic paved path that winds around the lighthouse grounds and along the rocky shoreline of Lake Erie.

hikingTrails.name: Marblehead Peninsula Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle trail connecting the park to nearby natural areas, offering great views of the limestone cliffs.

ohio.campingInfo: There is no camping available at Marblehead Lighthouse State Park. Nearby private campgrounds are available in the Marblehead area.
ohio.fishingBoating: Fishing is permitted along the shoreline, but there are no boat ramps or docks located within the state park boundaries.

visitorCenter.name: Marblehead Lighthouse Keeper's House
visitorCenter.info: The museum features exhibits on the history of the lighthouse, the life of the keepers, and the maritime heritage of Lake Erie.

ohio.hours: Grounds open daily from sunrise to sunset.
ohio.entranceFees: Admission to the park grounds is free. A small fee is charged for lighthouse tower tours.
ohio.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for the best weather and lighthouse tour availability.
tips: Visit during sunset for the most spectacular photography opportunities.
Check the official website for lighthouse tower tour schedules as they are seasonal.
Wear comfortable walking shoes to navigate the rocky shoreline areas.

ohio.name: Kelleys Island State Park
ohio.shortDescription: Located on the north shore of Kelleys Island in Lake Erie, this park offers stunning glacial grooves and beautiful limestone beaches.
ohio.fullDescription: Kelleys Island State Park is a 677-acre park that showcases the unique geological history of the Lake Erie islands. The park is most famous for the Glacial Grooves, which are the largest and most accessible examples of glacial scouring in the world. Visitors can explore the rugged limestone shoreline, enjoy expansive views of the lake, and learn about the island's rich history of quarrying and winemaking.
thingsToDo: View the National Natural Landmark Glacial Grooves
Kayaking and canoeing along the shoreline
Fishing for smallmouth bass and walleye

hikingTrails.name: North Shore Loop
hikingTrails.description: A scenic trail that winds along the northern coastline, offering excellent views of the lake and access to rocky beaches.

hikingTrails.name: Glacial Grooves Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short, accessible path that leads directly to the massive, ancient glacial grooves carved into the limestone bedrock.

ohio.campingInfo: The park features a large campground with 127 electric sites and 40 non-electric sites, including amenities like showers, flush toilets, and a dump station.
ohio.fishingBoating: The park offers a boat launch ramp and excellent fishing access along the northern shoreline of Lake Erie.

visitorCenter.name: Kelleys Island State Park Office
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on park programs, maps, and educational displays regarding the island's geology.

ohio.entranceFees: Free admission to the park; camping fees vary by site type and season.
ohio.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for optimal weather and ferry accessibility.
tips: Check the Kelleys Island Ferry Boat schedule in advance as it is the primary way to reach the island.
Bring a bicycle or rent one on the island to easily navigate between the park and the village.
Visit the Glacial Grooves early in the morning to avoid crowds during peak summer weekends.

south dakota.name: Custer State Park
south dakota.shortDescription: Spanning 71,000 acres in the Black Hills, Custer State Park is world-renowned for its free-roaming bison herd and stunning granite spires.
south dakota.fullDescription: Established in 1919, Custer State Park is South Dakota's first and largest state park. It features a diverse landscape ranging from rolling prairie grasslands to rugged mountain terrain. The park is famous for its 'Begging Burros' and the annual Buffalo Roundup, where thousands of bison are gathered. Visitors can explore the Needles Highway, a scenic drive through towering granite formations, and Iron Mountain Road, known for its unique pigtail bridges and tunnels framing Mount Rushmore.
thingsToDo: Wildlife viewing along the Wildlife Loop Road
Hiking the Black Elk Peak trail
Swimming and kayaking at Sylvan Lake
Fishing in mountain streams and lakes

hikingTrails.name: Black Elk Peak Trail
hikingTrails.description: The highest point in South Dakota, offering panoramic views of the Black Hills and a historic fire tower at the summit.

hikingTrails.name: Sunday Gulch Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic loop that winds through narrow granite canyons and lush forest near Sylvan Lake.

south dakota.campingInfo: The park offers 13 campgrounds with over 350 sites, including tent sites, RV hookups, and several historic lodges and cabins available for rent.
south dakota.fishingBoating: Fishing is permitted in several lakes including Sylvan, Stockade, and Center Lake. Boat rentals are available seasonally at Sylvan Lake.

visitorCenter.name: Peter Norbeck Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Features interactive exhibits on the park's history, geology, and the legacy of Peter Norbeck, along with ranger-led programs.

south dakota.entranceFees: $20.00 per vehicle for a 7-day temporary entrance license.
south dakota.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn, specifically September for the Buffalo Roundup.
tips: Stay inside your vehicle when bison are near the road.
Purchase your park entrance license online in advance to save time at the gate.
Visit Sylvan Lake early in the morning to secure parking during peak summer months.

south dakota.name: Bear Butte State Park
south dakota.shortDescription: Bear Butte is a geological marvel and a sacred site to many Native American tribes, offering a unique blend of spiritual significance and rugged hiking.
south dakota.fullDescription: Bear Butte is an intrusive igneous laccolith that rises 1,250 feet above the surrounding plains. Formed millions of years ago, this geological landmark is a place of deep spiritual importance for many Plains Indian tribes, who visit to conduct prayer ceremonies and leave offerings. The park provides a unique opportunity to experience the high plains ecosystem while respecting the cultural heritage of the site.

hikingTrails.name: Summit Trail
hikingTrails.description: A steep, challenging climb that rewards hikers with panoramic views of the Black Hills and the surrounding prairie.

hikingTrails.name: Centennial Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic trail that winds around the base of the butte, offering excellent opportunities to spot local wildlife and wildflowers.

south dakota.campingInfo: The park features a campground with 15 sites, including some with electrical hookups, suitable for tents and small RVs. Reservations are highly recommended during peak season.
south dakota.fishingBoating: There is no fishing or boating available at Bear Butte State Park.

visitorCenter.name: Bear Butte Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: The visitor center provides information on the geological history of the butte and the cultural significance of the site to Native American tribes.

south dakota.entranceFees: $8.00 daily vehicle entrance fee or valid South Dakota State Park annual pass.
south dakota.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for the best weather and trail conditions.
tips: Respect the prayer cloths and offerings left by Native American visitors; do not touch or remove them.
Bring plenty of water, as the Summit Trail is exposed and can get very hot in the summer.
Check the weather forecast before hiking, as high winds are common at the summit.

south dakota.name: Palisades State Park
south dakota.shortDescription: Palisades State Park is famous for its dramatic Sioux Quartzite rock formations that tower above the rushing waters of Split Rock Creek.
south dakota.fullDescription: Located near Garretson, South Dakota, Palisades State Park features unique geological formations known as Sioux Quartzite. These pink-hued rock spires rise up to 50 feet above the creek, creating a stunning landscape that has been carved over millions of years. The park is a popular destination for rock climbers, photographers, and nature enthusiasts looking to explore the rugged beauty of the Big Sioux River valley.

hikingTrails.name: Split Rock Creek Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic trail that follows the edge of the creek, offering excellent views of the quartzite cliffs.

hikingTrails.name: King and Queen Rock Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short but rugged path that leads to the park's most iconic rock formations.

south dakota.campingInfo: The park offers 37 campsites, including several with electrical hookups, as well as six camping cabins available for reservation.
south dakota.fishingBoating: Fishing is permitted along the banks of Split Rock Creek, which is known for smallmouth bass and channel catfish.

visitorCenter.name: Palisades State Park Office
visitorCenter.info: The park office provides information on trail conditions, climbing permits, and local history.

south dakota.hours: Open daily, 24 hours for registered campers; day-use areas open from 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM.
south dakota.entranceFees: A daily park entrance license is $8.00 per vehicle or $36.00 for an annual pass.
south dakota.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for optimal hiking and climbing conditions.
tips: Bring sturdy hiking boots as the terrain near the cliffs can be uneven and rocky.
Check the official website for rock climbing regulations and safety requirements before arrival.
Visit during the golden hour to capture the best light on the pink quartzite rock formations.

south dakota.name: Newton Hills State Park
south dakota.shortDescription: Nestled in a lush, wooded valley, Newton Hills State Park offers a unique escape with its dense forests, rolling hills, and abundant wildlife in southeastern South Dakota.
south dakota.fullDescription: Newton Hills State Park is a geological and ecological gem located in the Coteau des Prairies. The park is characterized by its deep, wooded ravines and diverse hardwood forests, which stand in stark contrast to the surrounding prairie landscape. Historically, the area served as a refuge for early settlers and was a significant site for local indigenous tribes. Today, it provides a sanctuary for hikers, birdwatchers, and campers looking to explore the unique flora and fauna of the Big Sioux River valley.

hikingTrails.name: Woodland Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle loop that winds through the dense hardwood forest, offering excellent opportunities to spot deer and songbirds.

hikingTrails.name: Ridge Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail climbs to the higher elevations of the park, providing panoramic views of the surrounding valley and the Big Sioux River basin.

south dakota.campingInfo: The park features modern campgrounds with electrical hookups, as well as primitive tent sites and several camping cabins available for reservation.
south dakota.fishingBoating: While the park does not have a large lake, there is access to small ponds for fishing, and the nearby Big Sioux River offers opportunities for canoeing and kayaking.

visitorCenter.name: Newton Hills Park Office
visitorCenter.info: The park office provides information on trail conditions, local history, and educational programs for visitors.

south dakota.entranceFees: A South Dakota State Park entrance license is required for all vehicles, costing $8.00 per day or $36.00 for an annual pass.
south dakota.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring for wildflowers or autumn for the vibrant fall foliage.
tips: Bring insect repellent, as the wooded areas can have mosquitoes during summer months.
Visit during the fall to witness the spectacular change of colors in the hardwood forest.
Check the official website for seasonal hunting regulations, as some areas may be restricted.

south dakota.name: Sica Hollow State Park
south dakota.shortDescription: Sica Hollow State Park is a unique, geologically significant area known for its lush, wooded ravines and rich Native American history.
south dakota.fullDescription: Sica Hollow State Park, located in the Coteau des Prairies, is a National Natural Landmark. The park features a deep, wooded ravine carved by glacial activity, offering a stark contrast to the surrounding prairie landscape. The area is steeped in Dakota Sioux history and folklore, with the name 'Sica' meaning 'bad' in the Dakota language, referring to the challenging terrain and mysterious atmosphere of the hollow.

hikingTrails.name: Trail of the Spirits
hikingTrails.description: A scenic loop trail that winds through the dense forest and crosses small streams, offering a glimpse into the park's unique ecosystem.

hikingTrails.name: Sica Hollow Trail
hikingTrails.description: A longer, more rugged trail that traverses the length of the hollow, providing extensive views of the diverse flora and fauna.

south dakota.campingInfo: There are no developed campgrounds within Sica Hollow State Park; however, primitive camping is allowed in designated areas with a permit.
south dakota.fishingBoating: Fishing is not a primary activity at Sica Hollow; however, nearby lakes like Pickerel Lake offer excellent fishing and boating opportunities.

visitorCenter.name: Sica Hollow Information Kiosk
visitorCenter.info: Provides maps, trail information, and historical context about the park's significance.

south dakota.entranceFees: A valid South Dakota State Park entrance license is required for all vehicles.
south dakota.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring for wildflowers or autumn for vibrant fall foliage.
tips: Wear sturdy hiking boots as the trails can be muddy and uneven.
Bring insect repellent, especially during the summer months.
Check the official website for any seasonal trail closures due to weather.

south dakota.name: Angostura Recreation Area
south dakota.shortDescription: Angostura Recreation Area features 36 miles of shoreline and sandy beaches, making it a premier destination for water sports and camping in the Black Hills region.
south dakota.fullDescription: Located in the southern Black Hills, Angostura Recreation Area surrounds a massive reservoir created by the Angostura Dam on the Cheyenne River. The park is renowned for its clear, clean water and sandy beaches, which are rare in the region. The area offers a diverse landscape ranging from open prairie to rugged hills, providing a habitat for a variety of wildlife and excellent opportunities for outdoor recreation including boating, fishing, and hiking.
thingsToDo: Fishing for walleye and smallmouth bass

hikingTrails.name: Cheyenne River Trail
hikingTrails.description: A relatively flat trail that follows the shoreline, offering excellent views of the reservoir and local birdlife.

hikingTrails.name: Angostura Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail winds through the hills surrounding the lake, providing elevated vantage points and a more rugged hiking experience.

south dakota.campingInfo: The park offers several campgrounds including modern sites with electrical hookups, tent-only sites, and camping cabins available for reservation.
south dakota.fishingBoating: The reservoir is a popular fishing spot for walleye, smallmouth bass, and northern pike. Multiple boat ramps are available throughout the recreation area.

visitorCenter.name: Angostura Park Office
visitorCenter.info: The park office provides information on park regulations, fishing licenses, and local trail maps.

south dakota.hours: Open 24 hours daily for camping; day use areas open sunrise to sunset.
south dakota.entranceFees: A daily park entrance license is required for all vehicles, currently $8.00 per vehicle or $36.00 for an annual park entrance license.
south dakota.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for optimal water activities.
tips: Book campsites well in advance during summer months as they fill up quickly.
Bring plenty of sunscreen and water, as shade is limited on the beaches.
Check the South Dakota GFP website for current water levels and boat ramp conditions.

south dakota.name: Lewis and Clark Recreation Area
south dakota.shortDescription: Located on the shores of Lewis and Clark Lake, this expansive recreation area offers premier water sports, camping, and scenic views along the Missouri River.
south dakota.fullDescription: Lewis and Clark Recreation Area is one of South Dakota's most popular outdoor destinations, situated along the massive Lewis and Clark Lake created by Gavins Point Dam. The park features diverse landscapes ranging from sandy beaches to wooded bluffs, providing a rich habitat for wildlife and a variety of recreational opportunities. It serves as a hub for boating, fishing, and camping, with a history deeply tied to the Lewis and Clark Expedition that passed through this region in the early 19th century.

hikingTrails.name: Gavins Point Nature Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle path winding through wooded areas with excellent opportunities for bird watching.

hikingTrails.name: Lewis and Clark Lake Shoreline Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic trail following the lakefront, offering panoramic views of the water and surrounding bluffs.

south dakota.campingInfo: The park features multiple modern campgrounds with electrical hookups, showers, flush toilets, and reservable sites for both tents and RVs.
south dakota.fishingBoating: The park offers multiple boat ramps and extensive shoreline access for fishing, with the lake being a renowned destination for walleye and smallmouth bass.

visitorCenter.name: Lewis and Clark Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Features interactive exhibits on the history of the Lewis and Clark Expedition and the construction of Gavins Point Dam.

south dakota.hours: Open 24 hours for registered campers; day-use areas open sunrise to sunset.
south dakota.entranceFees: A daily park entrance license is required, typically $8.00 per vehicle or $36.00 for an annual pass.
south dakota.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for optimal water activities and camping.
tips: Book campsites well in advance during summer months as they fill up quickly.
Bring insect repellent if visiting during the peak of summer.
Check the official website for current water safety alerts and beach conditions.

south dakota.name: Hartford Beach State Park
south dakota.shortDescription: Nestled on the shores of Big Stone Lake, this park offers a serene escape with lush woodlands, historic sites, and excellent water recreation.
south dakota.fullDescription: Hartford Beach State Park is located on the shores of Big Stone Lake in northeastern South Dakota. The park is known for its beautiful wooded areas, which provide a stark contrast to the surrounding prairie landscape. Historically, the area was a site for Native American encampments and later served as a steamboat landing. Today, visitors can explore the unique geology of the glacial lake valley, enjoy birdwatching, or relax on the sandy beaches.

hikingTrails.name: Woodland Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle path winding through the park's dense hardwood forest, perfect for spotting local wildlife.

hikingTrails.name: Lakeview Trail
hikingTrails.description: Offers stunning panoramic views of Big Stone Lake and the surrounding glacial valley.

south dakota.campingInfo: The park features modern campsites with electrical hookups, as well as tent-only sites and a camping cabin available for reservation.
south dakota.fishingBoating: The park features a boat ramp providing access to Big Stone Lake, which is renowned for walleye, northern pike, and perch fishing.

visitorCenter.name: Hartford Beach Park Office
visitorCenter.info: Provides park information, maps, and assistance with camping reservations and local area inquiries.

south dakota.hours: Open year-round, 24 hours a day for camping; day use areas open from sunrise to sunset.
south dakota.entranceFees: A South Dakota State Park entrance license is required for all vehicles, costing $8.00 per day or $36.00 for an annual pass.
south dakota.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for optimal water activities and foliage.
tips: Bring insect repellent during the summer months as the wooded areas can be buggy.
Book campsites well in advance during peak summer weekends as they fill up quickly.
Check the water conditions at the boat ramp before heading out for a day on Big Stone Lake.
nearbyAttractions: Big Stone Lake State Park (Minnesota side)

wisconsin.name: Devil's Lake State Park
wisconsin.shortDescription: Wisconsin's largest state park, known for 500-foot quartzite bluffs around glacier-formed Devil's Lake.
wisconsin.fullDescription: Devil's Lake State Park covers 9,217 acres in the Baraboo Range just south of Baraboo, about 35 miles northwest of Madison. It is known for 500-foot quartzite bluffs around the 360-acre Devil's Lake, formed about 12,000 years ago when glacial moraines plugged both ends of a gap in the bluffs. The Ice Age Trail passes through.

hikingTrails.name: Devil's Lake via West Bluff Trail
hikingTrails.description: This loop near Baraboo, which AllTrails rates moderately challenging, takes an average of about 2 hours 27 minutes to complete.

hikingTrails.name: Ice Age National Scenic Trail
hikingTrails.description: Devil's Lake State Park is situated along the Ice Age National Scenic Trail.

wisconsin.campingInfo: Camping is available at Devil's Lake State Park, and the official DNR page links to a 'Camping at Devil's Lake' information page.
wisconsin.fishingBoating: The park's 360-acre lake offers paddling opportunities and a North Shore boat launch, which will be unavailable at times during the 2026-2027 construction projects.

visitorCenter.name: Devil's Lake State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

wisconsin.entranceFees: Vehicle admission sticker required; daily pass $13 (Wisconsin plates) / $16 (out-of-state)
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through fall is prime time for bluff hikes, swimming and paddling, but weekdays or early mornings are best because parking lots often fill before 9 a.m. on May–October weekends and holidays.
tips: From May through October, parking lots often fill before 9 a.m. on weekends and holidays, and park access may be temporarily restricted until congestion lessens, so arrive early or visit on a weekday.
Facility improvement projects began in 2026, and North Shore parking lots and the boat launch will be unavailable at times. South Shore facilities remain open.
The park is upgrading its wayfinding maps and signs, so maps on the property may not match. Check the current map before hiking.

wisconsin.name: Peninsula State Park
wisconsin.shortDescription: Door County park with eight miles of Green Bay shoreline, limestone bluffs and the Eagle Bluff Lighthouse.
wisconsin.fullDescription: Peninsula State Park covers 3,776 acres in Door County near Fish Creek, with eight miles of Green Bay shoreline, and draws about a million visitors a year. Established in 1909, it is Wisconsin's third-largest state park. It includes the Eagle Bluff Lighthouse, a golf course, Nicolet Bay beach and the outdoor Northern Sky Theater.

hikingTrails.name: Eagle Trail
hikingTrails.description: A 2-mile loop that can be challenging because of seasonal ice and rocky, uneven conditions.

hikingTrails.name: Hemlock Trail
hikingTrails.description: A 1.8-mile one-way trail that the Wisconsin DNR rates as moderate.

hikingTrails.name: Sunset Bike Trail
hikingTrails.description: A paved and gravel trail through the park's hardwoods and marshes that gives bikers and hikers a safe, scenic alternative to Shore Road.

wisconsin.campingInfo: The park offers over 460 campsites and three group camps.
wisconsin.fishingBoating: The DNR lists boating, canoeing, kayaking and winter ice fishing among the park's recreation, and visitors note a boat landing and a canoe/kayak launch.

visitorCenter.name: Peninsula State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

wisconsin.entranceFees: A vehicle admission sticker is required
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: Summer is ideal for the sand beach, the evening Northern Sky Theater musicals and full facilities; the park is open year-round, but some features may not be accessible outside peak season.
tips: Buy a vehicle admission sticker before entering, because Wisconsin charges an extra $5 fee to anyone who fails to pay admission before using the park.
Wear sturdy footwear on Eagle Trail, which has rocky, uneven footing year-round and can be icy in season.
Touring Eagle Bluff Lighthouse requires park admission plus a donation.

wisconsin.name: Copper Falls State Park
wisconsin.shortDescription: Northern Wisconsin park where the Bad River and Tylers Forks drop over waterfalls in a rocky gorge.
wisconsin.fullDescription: Copper Falls State Park in Ashland County protects a stretch of the Bad River and its tributary Tylers Forks, which run through a gorge and over several waterfalls. Created in 1929, it was developed by the Civilian Conservation Corps. Its 17 miles of trails include part of the North Country National Scenic Trail, and Loon Lake allows swimming and paddling.
thingsToDo: Swimming and paddling on Loon Lake

hikingTrails.name: Doughboy's Nature Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail runs along the Bad River, and the official park page calls it one of the best hikes in Wisconsin.

hikingTrails.name: North Country National Scenic Trail
hikingTrails.description: A portion of this national scenic trail is part of the park's 17-mile trail network.

wisconsin.campingInfo: The park offers camping, including a campground with 24 electric sites and a camper cabin accessible to persons with disabilities.
wisconsin.fishingBoating: Loon Lake offers fishing, kayaking, canoeing and boating with electric motors only, and trout fishing is found on the Bad River and Tylers Forks.

visitorCenter.name: Copper Falls State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

wisconsin.entranceFees: A vehicle admission sticker is required
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through fall is ideal for viewing the waterfalls, hiking the gorge trails and swimming at Loon Lake, while winter brings cross-country skiing and snowshoeing on the park's trails.
tips: A Wisconsin DNR vehicle admission sticker is required to enter the park.
For an easy option, the 0.5-mile universal trail leads to an overlook of Copper Falls and crosses a historic CCC bridge over the Tyler Fork Cascades.
Campsites can be registered and paid for at the park office, or reserved online or by phone at 1-888-947-2757.

wisconsin.name: Wyalusing State Park
wisconsin.shortDescription: Perched high above the confluence of the Wisconsin and Mississippi Rivers, Wyalusing State Park offers some of the most spectacular blufftop views in the Midwest.
wisconsin.fullDescription: Wyalusing State Park is one of Wisconsin's oldest state parks, located at the junction of the Wisconsin and Mississippi Rivers. The park features 500-foot bluffs, ancient Native American burial mounds, and a diverse landscape of hardwood forests and prairies. Its unique geography provides a sanctuary for wildlife and a historic window into the region's geological past.

hikingTrails.name: Old Wagon Road Trail
hikingTrails.description: A historic trail that winds through the forest, offering glimpses of the river valley below.

hikingTrails.name: Bluff Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail follows the edge of the bluffs, providing breathtaking panoramic views of the river confluence.

wisconsin.campingInfo: The park features two main campgrounds, Wisconsin Ridge and Homestead, offering over 100 campsites with some electrical hookups and modern shower facilities.
wisconsin.fishingBoating: Boat launch access is available at the base of the bluffs on the Mississippi River, with excellent fishing for walleye, bass, and panfish.

visitorCenter.name: Wyalusing State Park Nature Center
visitorCenter.info: Features educational exhibits on the park's geology, history, and local flora and fauna.

wisconsin.entranceFees: A Wisconsin State Park vehicle admission sticker is required for all vehicles.
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring for wildflowers or autumn for vibrant fall foliage.
tips: Bring binoculars for excellent bird watching, especially during eagle migration.
Visit the Sentinel Ridge area to see the ancient Native American burial mounds.
Book campsites well in advance as they fill up quickly during summer weekends.

wisconsin.name: High Cliff State Park
wisconsin.shortDescription: Perched atop the Niagara Escarpment, High Cliff State Park offers breathtaking panoramic views of Lake Winnebago and rich historical significance.
wisconsin.fullDescription: High Cliff State Park is the only state-owned recreational area on the shores of Lake Winnebago. The park is named for the limestone cliffs of the Niagara Escarpment, which run through the property. Visitors can explore ancient effigy mounds built by Native Americans, hike through diverse hardwood forests, and enjoy the expansive marina facilities. The park's geology is unique, featuring exposed Silurian dolomite cliffs that provide a dramatic backdrop for outdoor recreation.
thingsToDo: Boating and fishing on Lake Winnebago

hikingTrails.name: Red Bird Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail winds along the top of the Niagara Escarpment, offering spectacular views of Lake Winnebago and passing by several historical effigy mounds.

hikingTrails.name: Forest Management Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle loop through the park's wooded areas, perfect for birdwatching and observing local flora.

wisconsin.campingInfo: The park features a family campground with 112 sites, including some with electrical hookups, as well as a group camping area and a remote hike-in site.
wisconsin.fishingBoating: The park features a large marina on Lake Winnebago with multiple boat slips and a public boat launch for easy access to one of Wisconsin's largest inland lakes.

visitorCenter.name: High Cliff State Park Office
visitorCenter.info: Provides park information, trail maps, and educational displays regarding the Niagara Escarpment and local history.

wisconsin.entranceFees: A Wisconsin State Park vehicle admission sticker is required for all vehicles.
wisconsin.address: N7630 State Park Rd, Sherwood, WI 54169
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for hiking and boating, or winter for snowshoeing.
tips: Visit the observation tower for the best panoramic views of the lake.
Bring binoculars to spot eagles and other raptors along the cliff edge.
Make camping reservations well in advance as sites fill up quickly during summer weekends.

wisconsin.name: Interstate State Park
wisconsin.shortDescription: Established in 1900, this is Wisconsin's oldest state park, featuring dramatic basalt cliffs along the St. Croix National Scenic Riverway.
wisconsin.fullDescription: Interstate State Park is located in St. Croix Falls and offers a unique look at the geological history of the region. The park is situated on the Dalles of the St. Croix, a deep gorge carved by glacial meltwater. Visitors can explore the unique rock formations, including glacial potholes, and enjoy the scenic beauty of the St. Croix River, which serves as a border between Wisconsin and Minnesota.

hikingTrails.name: Pothole Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short but rugged trail that takes you past several unique glacial potholes formed thousands of years ago.

hikingTrails.name: Skyline Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail offers elevated views of the St. Croix River valley and the surrounding basalt cliffs.

wisconsin.campingInfo: The park features 37 family campsites, including some with electrical hookups, and a group campsite. Reservations are highly recommended during the summer season.
wisconsin.fishingBoating: The St. Croix River offers excellent fishing for smallmouth bass and walleye. There is a boat landing available for public use.

visitorCenter.name: Ice Age Interpretive Center
visitorCenter.info: Features exhibits on the glacial history of the area and the formation of the St. Croix River gorge.

wisconsin.entranceFees: A Wisconsin State Park vehicle admission sticker is required for all vehicles.
wisconsin.address: 1271 State Rd 35, St Croix Falls, WI 54024
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for hiking and river activities.
tips: Visit the Ice Age Interpretive Center first to understand the unique geology of the park.
Bring sturdy hiking boots as the terrain near the river can be rocky and uneven.
Check the river conditions before planning any kayaking or canoeing trips.

wisconsin.name: Willow River State Park
wisconsin.shortDescription: Famous for its stunning 45-foot waterfall and scenic river valley, Willow River State Park offers a rugged escape just minutes from the Twin Cities.
wisconsin.fullDescription: Willow River State Park encompasses 2,891 acres of rolling countryside, prairie, and forest. The park is defined by the Willow River, which carved a deep, dramatic gorge through the landscape, culminating in the iconic Willow Falls. The area has a rich history, having served as a site for early milling operations in the 19th century, and today provides a diverse habitat for wildlife and a premier destination for outdoor recreation.

hikingTrails.name: Willow Falls Trail
hikingTrails.description: A popular path that leads visitors down into the gorge for a spectacular view of the multi-tiered waterfall.

hikingTrails.name: Burkhardt Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail winds through wooded areas and offers elevated views of the river valley and surrounding prairie.

wisconsin.campingInfo: The park features a large campground with 124 sites, including 42 sites with electrical hookups, modern restrooms, and showers.
wisconsin.fishingBoating: The Willow River is a designated trout stream, and Willow River Flowage offers opportunities for canoeing and kayaking.

visitorCenter.name: Willow River State Park Nature Center
visitorCenter.info: Features interactive exhibits on the park's geology, local history, and native wildlife, along with educational programming.

wisconsin.entranceFees: Wisconsin resident vehicle admission is $8.00 daily; non-resident vehicle admission is $11.00 daily.
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring for waterfall flow or autumn for vibrant foliage.
tips: Arrive early on summer weekends as the parking lots fill up quickly.
Wear sturdy footwear as the trails leading to the waterfall can be steep and rocky.
Check the DNR website for current water quality reports before planning a swim.

wisconsin.name: Governor Dodge State Park
wisconsin.shortDescription: Spanning over 5,000 acres of steep hills, sandstone bluffs, and deep valleys, Governor Dodge is one of Wisconsin's largest and most diverse state parks.
wisconsin.fullDescription: Located in the heart of the Driftless Area, Governor Dodge State Park features two man-made lakes, Cox Hollow and Twin Valley, surrounded by rolling hills and dramatic rock formations. The park's unique geology, untouched by the last glaciers, provides a rugged landscape perfect for outdoor recreation. Historically, the area was once home to lead miners in the 1800s, and remnants of this era can still be explored throughout the park's extensive trail system.
thingsToDo: Swimming at Cox Hollow and Twin Valley beaches
Horseback riding on designated equestrian trails
Fishing for panfish, bass, and trout
Mountain biking on the Mill Creek Trail

hikingTrails.name: Stephens Falls Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short but scenic trail that leads visitors down into a lush, shaded gorge to view the picturesque Stephens Falls.

hikingTrails.name: Lost Canyon Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail winds through a beautiful wooded valley with impressive sandstone rock outcroppings and diverse forest flora.

wisconsin.campingInfo: The park offers two large campgrounds, Cox Hollow and Twin Valley, featuring over 260 campsites, including electric sites, group sites, and accessible facilities.
wisconsin.fishingBoating: The park features two lakes, Cox Hollow and Twin Valley, both offering boat launches for non-motorized or electric-motor boats and excellent fishing opportunities.

visitorCenter.name: Governor Dodge State Park Office
visitorCenter.info: The park office provides maps, trail information, firewood sales, and assistance from park rangers.

wisconsin.entranceFees: A Wisconsin State Park vehicle admission sticker is required for all vehicles.
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring for wildflowers or autumn for spectacular fall foliage.
tips: Visit the Stephens Falls area early in the morning to avoid crowds.
Bring insect repellent during the summer months, especially near the lakes.
Check the official website for seasonal trail closures due to wet conditions.

alabama.name: Gulf State Park
alabama.shortDescription: A scenic beachside park featuring white sand beaches, freshwater lakes, and miles of hiking and biking trails on the Gulf of Mexico.
alabama.fullDescription: Gulf State Park, located in Gulf Shores, Alabama, is a pristine coastal sanctuary spanning over 6,500 acres of diverse ecosystems. Boasting two miles of sugar-white sand beaches along the Gulf of Mexico, the park transitions into pine forests, freshwater dunes, and three spring-fed lakes, most notably Lake Shelby. It is famous for its massive fishing pier, the Lodge at Gulf State Park, and its commitment to eco-friendly, sustainable tourism. Visitors can swim, fish, kayak, or cycle through a labyrinth of paved multi-use trails that connect different coastal habitats.
thingsToDo: Pier fishing at the Gulf State Park Pier
Kayaking, canoeing, and paddleboarding on Lake Shelby
Biking or jogging on the Hugh S. Branyon Backcountry Trail
Taking a guided Segway or nature tour
Visiting the butterfly garden and interpretive nature exhibits

hikingTrails.name: Hugh S. Branyon Backcountry Trail
hikingTrails.description: A paved, multi-use trail system winding through nine distinct ecosystems, featuring alligator lookouts, butterfly gardens, swamp boardwalks, and ancient coastal dunes.

hikingTrails.name: Gopher Tortoise Trail
hikingTrails.description: A quiet, sandy path showcasing native scrub oak and rosemary habitats, with frequent sightings of the endangered gopher tortoise.

hikingTrails.name: Lake Shelby Overlook Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic boardwalk trail offering breathtaking, unobstructed views of Lake Shelby and opportunities to spot osprey and nesting bald eagles.

alabama.campingInfo: The park offers a massive, modern campground with 496 full-hookup campsites (water, sewer, 20/30/50 amp electricity) and 11 primitive sites. Additionally, there are 20 rustic lakeside cabins, 3 premium lakeside glamping safari tents, and the upscale eco-lodge.
alabama.fishingBoating: Lake Shelby offers excellent freshwater fishing, kayaking, and boating with onsite rentals. The Gulf State Park Pier extends 1,542 feet into the Gulf of Mexico, providing outstanding saltwater fishing, complete with a bait shop, rod rentals, and fish cleaning stations.
wildlife: Alligators (frequently spotted in swamps and lakes)
Bottlenose dolphins (visible from the Gulf Pier)
Great blue herons and Snowy egrets

visitorCenter.name: Gulf State Park Nature Center
visitorCenter.info: A living museum of native plants and animals, offering daily educational programs, guided nature walks, and hands-on interactive exhibits.

alabama.hours: Sunrise to Sunset daily (Beach access and pier have extended hours)
alabama.entranceFees: Vehicles: $10.00 daily parking fee. Gulf State Park Pier access: $3.00 for sightseers, $9.00 for fishing.
alabama.address: 20115 State Park Rd, Gulf Shores, AL 36542
alabama.bestTimeToVisit: March to May and September to November for comfortable temperatures and active bird migrations.
tips: Rent a bicycle at the park headquarters or utilize the park's free bike sharing program to explore the Backcountry Trail.
Bring insect repellent for the interior wooded trails and boardwalks.
Visit the Pier at sunrise or sunset for incredible photo opportunities and dolphin sightings.

alabama.name: Cheaha State Park
alabama.shortDescription: Perched atop Alabamas highest peak, Cheaha offers dramatic mountain vistas, serene waterfalls, and direct access to the Talladega National Forest.
alabama.fullDescription: Cheaha State Park is Alabamas oldest continuously operating state park, established in 1933. Located in the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains, it encompasses Mount Cheaha, the highest point in Alabama at 2,407 feet above sea level. This "island-in-the-sky" park is surrounded by the 392,567-acre Talladega National Forest. It is a haven for hikers, rock climbers, and nature lovers, offering magnificent rock outcroppings, deep granite gorges, and rushing mountain streams that cascade into scenic waterfalls. The historic stone Bunker Tower at the summit provides panoramic 360-degree views of the surrounding valleys.
thingsToDo: Rock climbing and rappelling at Pulpit Rock
Gem panning and searching for gold at the stream beds
Watching magnificent sunrises from Bald Rock

hikingTrails.name: Bald Rock Boardwalk & Trail
hikingTrails.description: A fully wheelchair-accessible wooden boardwalk that leads directly to a spectacular cliffside overlook with panoramic valley views.

hikingTrails.name: Pulpit Rock Trail
hikingTrails.description: A rocky, uneven descent leading to a popular sandstone ledge favored by rock climbers and sunset photographers.

hikingTrails.name: Lake Chinnabee Silent Trail
hikingTrails.description: Winds along a cold mountain stream, passing by pristine waterfalls and ending at a gorgeous alpine lake.

alabama.campingInfo: Features 73 modern campsites (semi-primitive and full hookups), a dedicated group camp, primitive trail-side backpacking sites, 17 historic stone cabins built by the CCC, and the Cheaha Lodge containing 30 hotel-style rooms.
alabama.fishingBoating: A quiet 6-acre lake (Cheaha Lake) is located at the base of the mountain, offering hand-launched paddling, swimming, and peaceful bank fishing for bass, bluegill, and catfish.

visitorCenter.name: Cheaha State Park Interpretive Center & Museum
visitorCenter.info: Features historical exhibits documenting the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) construction, Native American history, and native mountain wildlife.

alabama.hours: 7:00 AM to 10:00 PM daily for day-use visitors.
alabama.entranceFees: Adults: $5.00, Children (4-11): $2.00, Seniors (62+): $2.00, Children under 3: Free.
alabama.bestTimeToVisit: October to November for breathtaking fall foliage, and April to May for blooming mountain laurel.
tips: The Bald Rock Boardwalk is fully lit at dusk, making it a perfect spot for sunset and star viewing.
Temperatures at the summit are typically 10 degrees cooler than the surrounding valleys; bring a light jacket even in summer.
Check the weather forecast for fog, as low cloud cover can completely block mountain views.

alabama.name: Oak Mountain State Park
alabama.shortDescription: Alabamas largest state park, offering over 9,900 acres of outdoor adventure including world-class mountain biking, lakes, and a wildlife center.
alabama.fullDescription: Oak Mountain State Park is the crown jewel of Alabamas state park system and its largest. Spanning nearly 10,000 acres, it lies just 20 miles south of Birmingham. The park is characterized by the rugged ridges of Double Oak Mountain, lush hardwood valleys, and pristine pine forests. It features over 50 miles of award-winning multi-use trails, three scenic lakes, an 18-hole championship golf course, a cable-wakeboarding park, and the Alabama Wildlife Center, which rehabilitates injured native birds. Oak Mountain is a premier destination for both adrenaline-seekers and families seeking a natural retreat.
thingsToDo: Mountain biking on world-class singletrack trails
Cable wakeboarding and waterskiing on Double Oak Lake
Swimming and paddleboarding at the beach area
Visiting the Alabama Wildlife Center and demonstration farm
Horseback riding (rentals and guided tours available)

hikingTrails.name: Peavine Falls Trail
hikingTrails.description: A rocky trail descending into a steep ravine to reach a stunning, 65-foot spring-fed waterfall that cascades into a clear pool.

hikingTrails.name: Double Oak Trail (BUMP Mountain Bike Trail)
hikingTrails.description: An internationally acclaimed singletrack trail loop featuring technical rock gardens, flow sections, and steep climbs, built by the Birmingham Urban Mountain Pedalers.

hikingTrails.name: King's Chair Loop Trail
hikingTrails.description: Leads hikers to a breathtaking rock outcrop called King's Chair, offering panoramic views of the Shelby County valleys.

alabama.campingInfo: The campground features 85 full-hookup sites, 60 water/electric sites, and a primitive camping area. There are also 10 fully equipped modern lakeside cabins available for rent year-round.
alabama.fishingBoating: Three lakes (Double Oak Lake, Beaver Lake, and Lunker Lake) are stocked with bass, bream, and catfish. Motorized boats are not allowed, making them peaceful for canoeing, kayaking, and paddleboarding. Rowboats and canoes are available for rent.
wildlife: Rehabilitated raptors (at the Alabama Wildlife Center)

visitorCenter.name: Oak Mountain Park Headquarters & Wildlife Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides trail maps, park passes, and information on the park's history. The adjacent Alabama Wildlife Center features a boardwalk overlooking raptor cages and a rehabilitation clinic.

alabama.entranceFees: Adults: $5.00, Seniors (62+): $2.00, Children (6-11): $2.00, Children under 6: Free.
alabama.bestTimeToVisit: September to November for pleasant hiking temperatures and autumn colors, and June to August for lake activities.
tips: If hiking to Peavine Falls, wear sturdy shoes with good traction as the descent into the gorge is steep and can be slippery.
Rent a kayak or paddleboard on Double Oak Lake during the summer weekends for a relaxing water excursion.
Check out the Alabama Wildlife Center's treetop nature trail—it's a free, elevated boardwalk that lets you see owls and hawks up close.

alabama.name: DeSoto State Park
alabama.shortDescription: Nestled on Lookout Mountain, DeSoto features rushing mountain streams, waterfalls, and stunning spring blooms of wild azaleas.
alabama.fullDescription: DeSoto State Park is situated on the scenic Lookout Mountain in Northeast Alabama. Spanning over 3,500 acres, the park is famed for its rugged beauty, mountain streams, and roaring waterfalls. Developed in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps, the park preserves a rustic, historic charm with stone structures and bridges. In the spring, the park erupts with the vibrant pink and white blooms of native wild azaleas and rhododendrons. DeSoto is located just minutes from the deep and awe-inspiring Little River Canyon National Preserve.
thingsToDo: Viewing spectacular waterfalls including DeSoto Falls
Kayaking and canoeing on the West Fork of the Little River
Biking and hiking on historic CCC-built trails
Participating in guided wildflower and ecology walks
Swimming in the Olympic-sized seasonal pool
Dining at the historic Mountain Inn Restaurant

hikingTrails.name: Talmadge Butler Boardwalk Trail
hikingTrails.description: A fully accessible wooden boardwalk winding through a peaceful forest canopy, ending at a scenic overlook of the rapid Azalea Cascade.

hikingTrails.name: DeSoto Falls Trail
hikingTrails.description: A rocky path that leads down to the base of the majestic, 104-foot DeSoto Falls, one of the tallest and most photographed waterfalls in the state.

hikingTrails.name: Silver Shingle Trail
hikingTrails.description: Follows a rocky mountain stream bed with picturesque rock formations and excellent opportunities for children to search for fossils.

alabama.campingInfo: Offers 94 full-hookup campsites, 18 primitive tent camping sites, and a modern group camp. Lodging includes 22 historic CCC-built rustic stone cabins, 14 modern chalets, and the historic DeSoto Lodge containing hotel rooms.
alabama.fishingBoating: The West Fork of the Little River is popular for peaceful flat-water kayaking and canoeing. Fishing is excellent for spotted bass, bluegill, and rainbow trout (stocked seasonally). Paddlecraft can be rented nearby.

visitorCenter.name: DeSoto State Park Lodge & Nature Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides historical displays about the CCC, trail maps, and wildlife guides. The park naturalist hosts regular weekend programs and educational hikes here.

alabama.hours: Sunrise to Sunset daily for day-use areas.
alabama.entranceFees: No general park entrance fee! (Some specific areas or trailheads have a $4.00 parking fee).
alabama.address: 7104 DeSoto Parkway NE, Fort Payne, AL 35967
alabama.bestTimeToVisit: April to May for roaring waterfalls and blooming wild azaleas, and October for peak mountain fall foliage.
tips: DeSoto Falls is located in a separate, non-contiguous parcel of the park about 7 miles from the main park area; make sure to get directions from the lodge.
Visit the Little River Canyon overlook, just a short drive down the Parkway, to see one of the deepest canyon gorges east of the Mississippi.
Book the stone cabins months in advance, especially for the autumn foliage season, as they are highly coveted.

alabama.name: Monte Sano State Park
alabama.shortDescription: Famed for its Mountain of Health, Monte Sano offers fresh mountain air, historical CCC stone cabins, and a serene Japanese garden.
alabama.fullDescription: Monte Sano State Park is located in Huntsville, Alabama, sitting high atop the plateau of Monte Sano Mountain (Spanish for "Mountain of Health"). Spanning over 2,100 acres, the park is known for its cool mountain breezes and fresh spring waters, which made it a popular health resort in the late 19th century. Built by the CCC during the Great Depression, the park features stunning hand-carved stone cabins and extensive hiking and mountain biking trails that wind past scenic limestone sinks, waterfalls, and lookouts. The park is also home to a beautiful public Japanese Garden, featuring a tea house and cherry blossom trees.
thingsToDo: Hiking and trail running through limestone valleys
Mountain biking on singletrack plateau trails
Exploring the scenic Monte Sano Japanese Garden
Picnicking at the CCC-built stone pavilions
Stargazing at the on-site Von Braun Astronomical Society Planetarium
Discovering seasonal waterfalls and limestone sinkholes

hikingTrails.name: Stone Cuts Trail
hikingTrails.description: A fascinating trail that takes hikers through deep, narrow rock fissures and natural stone arches carved out of the mountain's limestone.

hikingTrails.name: Mackay Hollow Trail
hikingTrails.description: A rugged descent into a deep forest hollow, passing seasonal waterfalls, streams, and offering a challenging climb back up to the plateau.

hikingTrails.name: North Plateau Loop Trail
hikingTrails.description: A flat trail tracing the rim of the mountain, offering panoramic overlooks of the city of Huntsville below.

alabama.campingInfo: Features 89 campsites (both full-hookup and water/electric), a primitive campground, and 14 historic CCC-built stone cabins with fireplaces and fully equipped kitchens.
alabama.fishingBoating: No fishing or boating is available in this high-altitude mountain park, but scenic streams and small ponds dot the hiking routes.

visitorCenter.name: Monte Sano State Park Office & Planetarium
visitorCenter.info: Provides maps and cabin check-ins. The Von Braun Planetarium, located within the park, offers public astronomy shows and telescope viewings on Saturday nights.

alabama.entranceFees: Adults: $5.00, Children (4-11): $2.00, Seniors (62+): $2.00, Active Military: Free.
alabama.bestTimeToVisit: April for blooming azaleas and cherry blossoms in the Japanese Garden, and late October for vibrant fall forest colors.
tips: Attend a Saturday night planetarium show at the Von Braun Astronomical Society inside the park—it's a wonderful, family-friendly educational experience.
Bring robust hiking boots if you plan to tackle the Stone Cuts Trail, as the rocky crevasses require stable footing.
Watch for deer near the cabin loop in the early morning and late evening—they are very accustomed to visitors.

alabama.name: Cathedral Caverns State Park
alabama.shortDescription: Home to a massive cave entrance, spectacular stalagmites, and "Goliath"—one of the largest stalagmites in the world.
alabama.fullDescription: Cathedral Caverns State Park, located in Woodville, Alabama, is home to one of the most spectacular cave formations in North America. Originally called "Kennamer Cave," the cavern was renamed by its developer due to its cathedral-like chambers. The cave entrance is a record-breaking 126 feet wide and 25 feet high. Inside, the cave maintains a cool 60 degrees Fahrenheit year-round. Guided tours lead visitors along a concrete pathway to marvel at "Goliath," a colossal stalagmite measuring 45 feet tall and 243 feet in circumference, a stalagmite forest, a frozen waterfall of stone, and an ancient, mysterious underground river.
thingsToDo: Taking a 90-minute guided underground cavern tour
Gemstone panning at the custom mining sluice
Hiking on the scenic forest trails of Kennamer Cove
Exploring cave history at the visitor center
Backcountry camping in the hardwood forest

hikingTrails.name: Cathedral Caverns Mountain Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic, uphill hike winding through a dense hardwood forest and limestone outcroppings, offering beautiful views of the cove below.

hikingTrails.name: Kennamer Cove Loop
hikingTrails.description: A peaceful, flat loop trail tracing the edge of the mountain and featuring interpretive markers explaining the unique geology of the valley.

alabama.campingInfo: The park has a primitive campground with tent sites, 15 back-in RV campsites with water and electric hookups, and a climate-controlled bathhouse.
alabama.fishingBoating: No fishing or boating is available within the cave system or park, though nearby Guntersville Lake offers extensive water sports.
wildlife: Little brown bats (visible in the cave)
Cave crickets and Blind cave fish

visitorCenter.name: Cathedral Caverns Welcome Center & Gift Shop
visitorCenter.info: The hub for booking cave tours, purchasing gemstone panning bags, and exploring geologic displays of cave development.

alabama.hours: 9:00 AM to 5:30 PM daily. Cavern tours are scheduled throughout the day.
alabama.entranceFees: Park entry is free! Cave tours are: Adults: $20.05, Children (5-12): $9.00, Children under 5: Free.
alabama.bestTimeToVisit: Year-round! Since the cave is a constant 60 degrees, it is an excellent escape from the summer heat or winter cold.
tips: Book your cave tour tickets online in advance, as tour sizes are strictly limited and popular weekend times sell out quickly.
Wear a light sweater or jacket during the cave tour, even in the dead of summer, as 60 degrees can feel chilly after 90 minutes.
Cavern walkways are fully wheelchair and stroller accessible, making this one of the most accessible cave tours in the country.
nearbyAttractions: Sauta Cave National Wildlife Refuge (famous for summer bat flights)

alabama.name: Lake Guntersville State Park
alabama.shortDescription: A premier lakeside resort park featuring bald eagle watching, championship golf, zip-line canopy tours, and expansive water sports.
alabama.fullDescription: Lake Guntersville State Park spans 6,000 acres along the banks of Alabamas largest lake, the 69,000-acre Lake Guntersville. Nestled in the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains, this resort-style park is a nature-lovers dream. It is internationally renowned for its Bald Eagle Awareness programs, which draw visitors every winter to see nesting eagles. The park features an 18-hole championship golf course, a massive beach complex, a full-service marina, the Screaming Eagle Zip Line Canopy Tour, over 36 miles of hiking trails, and a premier Lodge perched high on a ridge overlooking the water.
thingsToDo: Boating, jet skiing, and pontoon rentals at the marina
Lakeside swimming and volleyball at the beach complex
Gliding through the forest on the Screaming Eagle Zip Line
Playing 18 holes at the Eagle's Nest Golf Course
Attending winter Eagle Awareness weekend seminars
Hiking and mountain biking on extensive ridge trails
Dining at the Pine Ledge Restaurant in the Lodge

hikingTrails.name: Tom Bevill Trail
hikingTrails.description: A beautiful ridge trail climbing through dense pine forests and offering scenic overlooking spots of the massive lake below.

hikingTrails.name: Cutchenmine Trail
hikingTrails.description: Follows an old coal mine tramroad along the banks of Town Creek, flat and peaceful, with frequent sightings of waterfowl and beaver dams.

hikingTrails.name: Cave Trail
hikingTrails.description: A rocky trail leading to a small, scenic cave opening that was historically mined for saltpeter during the Civil War.

alabama.campingInfo: The campground offers 322 improved campsites (most with full water/sewer/electric hookups) and 10 primitive tent sites. Lodging includes the Lake Guntersville Lodge (112 resort-style rooms), 20 mountain chalets, and 20 lakeside cabins.
alabama.fishingBoating: Lake Guntersville is internationally recognized as one of the premier largemouth bass fishing lakes in the world. The full-service marina offers pontoon, bass boat, kayak, and paddleboard rentals, as well as boat slips and fuel.
wildlife: Bald eagles (especially active November through February)
Great blue herons and Canada geese

visitorCenter.name: Lake Guntersville Lodge & Nature Center
visitorCenter.info: Perched on a 150-foot bluff, the Lodge serves as the park's command center. The Nature Center offers wildlife exhibits, snake demonstrations, and guided weekend hikes.

alabama.hours: Sunrise to Sunset daily for day-use areas (Campground and Lodge open 24/7).
alabama.entranceFees: No general park entrance fee! (Some specific trailheads or beach areas have a nominal $3.00 parking fee).
alabama.bestTimeToVisit: January to February for nesting bald eagles, and May to September for summer lake and boating activities.
tips: Rent a pontoon boat for a half-day at the marina—it's the best way to see the massive scale of Lake Guntersville and its secluded mountain inlets.
Make reservations for Eagle Awareness weekends (January/February) months in advance, as these seminars draw visitors from all over the country.
Have a meal at the Pine Ledge restaurant in the Lodge around sunset; the floor-to-ceiling windows offer the most spectacular mountain lake views in Alabama.

alabama.name: Wind Creek State Park
alabama.shortDescription: One of the largest state-owned campgrounds in the nation, offering pristine lakeside camping, swimming, and hiking on beautiful Lake Martin.
alabama.fullDescription: Wind Creek State Park spans 1,445 acres along the shores of the massive, crystal-clear Lake Martin, a 41,000-acre reservoir in East-Central Alabama. Wind Creek is famous for hosting one of the largest state-operated campgrounds in the United States, containing over 500 spacious campsites, many of which sit directly on the shoreline. This park is a premier destination for water sports lovers, offering an extensive beach area, a modern marina with double-slip boat ramps, and canoe and kayak rentals. The park also features scenic hiking trails through rolling hills and pine forests, and a beautiful miniature golf course.
thingsToDo: Lakeside camping with direct water access
Swimming and building sandcastles at the sandy beach
Boating, sailing, and jet skiing on Lake Martin
Fishing for striped bass, crappie, and bluegill
Hiking through pine forests and climbing the forest fire tower
Playing miniature golf and archery at the park range

hikingTrails.name: Campfire Trail
hikingTrails.description: A pleasant forest loop that climbs gently through tall longleaf pines and hardwood hills, offering beautiful views of small creek beds.

hikingTrails.name: Wind Creek Fire Tower Trail
hikingTrails.description: Leads hikers to a historic, 100-foot forest fire tower. Visitors can climb up the stairs to get an unparalleled bird's-eye view of Lake Martin.

hikingTrails.name: Reunion Trail
hikingTrails.description: Meanders through mature pine stands and along small, quiet inlets of Lake Martin, perfect for birdwatching and photography.

alabama.campingInfo: Boasts an incredible 586 campsites. Out of these, 187 are full-hookup sites, and 399 are water and electric sites. Over 150 campsites are situated directly on the lake edge. There are also 7 lakeside camping cabins available for rent.
alabama.fishingBoating: Lake Martin is renowned for clean, clear water and active fishing. The park marina offers double-slip launching, wet slips, marine fueling, and pontoon, canoe, and kayak rentals. Excellent for catching striped bass, large largemouth bass, and crappie.

visitorCenter.name: Wind Creek Welcome Center & Marina
visitorCenter.info: The central hub for registering campsites, purchasing marine gas, rent-a-boats, and grabbing fishing tackle or bait at the camp store.

alabama.hours: Sunrise to Sunset daily for day-use areas (Campground check-in is 24/7).
alabama.entranceFees: Adults: $5.00, Children (6-11): $2.00, Seniors (62+): $2.00, Children under 6: Free.
alabama.bestTimeToVisit: May to September for summer boating and swimming, and October for comfortable camping under autumn foliage.
tips: If you are camping, try to book one of the waterfront sites in loops A, B, or C—there is nothing like waking up and walking straight into Lake Martin.
Don't miss climbing the historic fire tower; the panoramic vistas of Lake Martin are the absolute best in the region.
Bring your own fishing gear and purchase a local freshwater license; the shoreline fishing at Wind Creek is highly productive.
nearbyAttractions: Children's Harbor with its iconic lighthouse

arkansas.name: Petit Jean State Park
arkansas.shortDescription: Arkansas mountaintop park known for 95-foot Cedar Falls and the 1930s CCC-built Mather Lodge.
arkansas.fullDescription: Petit Jean State Park covers 3,471 acres atop Petit Jean Mountain above the Arkansas River, between the Ouachita Mountains and the Ozarks. The Civilian Conservation Corps built Mather Lodge and the Cedar Falls Trail, which drops into the canyon to the 95-foot falls. Other trails lead to Bear Cave and the Rock House cave.

hikingTrails.name: Cedar Falls Trail
hikingTrails.description: This CCC-built trail runs from Mather Lodge down into the canyon and crosses Cedar Creek on a bridge, in the canyon where Cedar Creek drops in a 95-foot waterfall.

hikingTrails.name: Seven Hollows Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail passes through the Seven Hollows area, where climbing, rappelling and bouldering are also offered.

hikingTrails.name: CCC Hike & Bike Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail is open to both hiking and biking, and its name honors the Civilian Conservation Corps, which built much of the park.

arkansas.campingInfo: Wikipedia lists 127 campsites, 32 cabins and the 24-room Mather Lodge, and camping and lodging reservations are taken through the Arkansas State Parks reservation site.
arkansas.fishingBoating: The 100-acre Lake Bailey is used for fishing, kayaking and pedal boating, and its boathouse is open in the summer months with boat rentals, supplies and a snack bar.

visitorCenter.name: Petit Jean State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

arkansas.address: 1285 Petit Jean Mountain Rd, Morrilton, AR 72110
arkansas.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and fall offer mild weather for hiking to Cedar Falls and the canyon overlooks, while summer is the time for the pools and the Lake Bailey boathouse, which is open in the summer months.
tips: Self-guided climbing, rappelling and bouldering in the Seven Hollows area requires a permit, which you can get at the Visitor Center or Mather Lodge.
The Petit Jean Via Ferrata is open only by guided reservation through the park's partner, Frontier Climbing Company, so book ahead.
If you plan to hike the full 12-mile trail loop, register at the visitor center first.
nearbyAttractions: Petit Jean Mountain Museum of Automobiles

arkansas.name: Mount Nebo State Park
arkansas.shortDescription: Arkansas mountaintop park 1,350 feet above the valley, with views of Lake Dardanelle and the Arkansas River.
arkansas.fullDescription: Mount Nebo State Park sits on a plateau about 1,755 feet above sea level near Dardanelle, looking over Lake Dardanelle and the Arkansas River. A resort area in the late 1800s, it became a state park in 1928 and was developed by the Civilian Conservation Corps. It has cabins, campsites, a swimming pool and 25 miles of hiking and mountain biking trails.

hikingTrails.name: Rim Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail goes around the top of the mountain and offers panoramic views of the Arkansas River.

hikingTrails.name: Bench Trail
hikingTrails.description: This level trail follows the mountain's bench, a terrace below the summit where numerous springs are found.

hikingTrails.name: Nebo Springs/Nebo Steps Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail is listed among the park's trails on the official page and shares its name with Nebo Springs on the mountain's bench.

arkansas.campingInfo: The park has 34 campsites (24 Class B and 10 hike-in tent sites), most with river valley views, plus 15 cabins, but there is no dump station.
arkansas.fishingBoating: Check the official park website for current boating and fishing details.

visitorCenter.name: Mount Nebo State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

arkansas.hours: Visitor Center open daily 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. (closed New Year's Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day); campground/picnic area open year-round
arkansas.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and fall offer comfortable weather for hiking the CCC-built trails and taking in the bluff-top views of the Arkansas River Valley, while summer adds access to the seasonal pool.
tips: There is no dump station at the park, so RV campers should plan to dump tanks elsewhere.

The swimming pool requires a fee and is open only seasonally, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. weather permitting: Wednesday to Sunday from Memorial Day weekend to August 9, then weekends only from August 15 through Labor Day.
The Visitor Center is closed on New Year's Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day.
nearbyAttractions: Old Post Park Mountain Bike Trail

arkansas.name: Crater of Diamonds State Park
arkansas.shortDescription: Arkansas park where visitors can search a plowed field for real diamonds and keep what they find.
arkansas.fullDescription: Crater of Diamonds State Park covers 911 acres near Murfreesboro and has a 37.5-acre plowed field, one of the few diamond-bearing sites open to the public. Visitors find about two diamonds a day on average and keep what they find. The Uncle Sam, found here in 1924 at over 40 carats, is the largest diamond ever found in the United States.

hikingTrails.name: Prospector Trail
hikingTrails.description: A self-guided loop trail in Crater of Diamonds State Park.

hikingTrails.name: Little Missouri River Trail
hikingTrails.description: A loop trail with interpretive features that AllTrails users rate as the best hike in the park.

arkansas.campingInfo: The park has 47 Class AAA campsites with 50-, 30- and 20-amp electric, water and sewer hookups, plus walk-in tent sites, and the campground is open all year.
arkansas.fishingBoating: A boat launch onto the Little Missouri River, known for trout fishing, sits across from the park's entrance and is a common starting point for fishing trips.

visitorCenter.name: Crater of Diamonds State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Check the official park website for visitor center details.

arkansas.hours: Diamond Search Area: daily 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.; Visitor Center/Gift Shop/Diamond Discovery Center: daily 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.; closed New Year's Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. Campground/picnic area open all year.
arkansas.entranceFees: Diamond search area admission: $15 per person (ages 13+), $7 per person (ages 6-12), free under 6
arkansas.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and fall offer the most comfortable weather for digging in the open diamond field, while summer visitors can cool off at the seasonal Diamond Springs Water Park (Memorial Day to Labor Day).
tips: You may bring your own mining equipment or rent tools from the park, but ladders and battery-operated or motor-driven mining tools are not allowed. Admission does not include tool rental.
The Diamond Search Area closes at 4 p.m., an hour before the visitor center, so arrive early for a full day of digging. Park staff identify your finds for free.
Diamond Springs Water Park is closed Mondays and Tuesdays and may open on weekends only starting mid-August.

arkansas.name: Devil's Den State Park
arkansas.shortDescription: Nestled in the Lee Creek Valley, Devil's Den State Park is one of the most iconic parks in Arkansas, featuring unique rock formations and historic CCC-built structures.
arkansas.fullDescription: Established in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps, Devil's Den State Park showcases rustic stone and timber architecture that blends seamlessly into the rugged Ozark landscape. The park is renowned for its dramatic rock crevices, caves, and the scenic Lee Creek, which winds through the valley. Visitors can explore the unique geology of the area, including the famous Devil's Den cave, while enjoying the lush hardwood forests that provide stunning displays of color during the autumn months.

hikingTrails.name: Yellow Rock Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail leads to a stunning overlook providing a panoramic view of the Lee Creek Valley.

hikingTrails.name: Devil's Den Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic loop that takes hikers past the park's namesake cave and through impressive rock formations.

arkansas.campingInfo: The park offers 135 campsites, including full hookup sites, as well as 17 historic cabins with kitchens and fireplaces available for rent.
arkansas.fishingBoating: Fishing is permitted in Lee Creek; the park also features a small lake where pedal boats can be rented seasonally.

visitorCenter.name: Devil's Den Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Features exhibits on the history of the Civilian Conservation Corps, local geology, and park wildlife.

arkansas.hours: Open 24 hours for registered campers; day-use areas open sunrise to sunset.
arkansas.address: 11333 W. Arkansas Hwy. 74, West Fork, AR 72774
arkansas.bestTimeToVisit: Spring for wildflowers and autumn for fall foliage.
tips: Bring a flashlight if you plan to explore the caves.
The park is a popular destination for mountain bikers; check trail status before heading out.
Book cabins well in advance as they are highly sought after during peak seasons.

arkansas.name: Lake Ouachita State Park
arkansas.shortDescription: Nestled in the Ouachita Mountains, this park offers access to Arkansas's largest and cleanest lake, perfect for water sports and nature lovers.
arkansas.fullDescription: Lake Ouachita State Park is located on the shores of Lake Ouachita, a 40,000-acre reservoir surrounded by the Ouachita National Forest. The lake is renowned for its crystal-clear water and is a premier destination for scuba diving, fishing, and boating. The park features a rich history of Civilian Conservation Corps development and offers visitors a chance to explore the unique geology of the Ouachita Mountains.
thingsToDo: Scuba diving in crystal clear waters
Fishing for striped bass and bream
Bird watching in the national forest

hikingTrails.name: Caddo Bend Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic loop that offers stunning panoramic views of Lake Ouachita and the surrounding mountain ridges.

hikingTrails.name: Dogwood Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short, interpretive nature trail perfect for families and those looking to identify local flora.

arkansas.campingInfo: The park offers 92 campsites with water and electric hookups, as well as several fully equipped cabins overlooking the lake.
arkansas.fishingBoating: The park features a full-service marina with boat rentals, fuel, and bait, plus multiple boat ramps for easy lake access.

visitorCenter.name: Lake Ouachita State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Features exhibits on the lake's history, geology, and local wildlife, along with a gift shop and park information.

arkansas.entranceFees: Free entrance to the park; fees apply for camping and cabin rentals.
arkansas.address: 5451 Mountain Pine Rd, Mountain Pine, AR 71956
arkansas.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Fall for mild temperatures and beautiful foliage.
tips: Bring polarized sunglasses to better see the fish and underwater structures in the clear lake water.
Book your campsite or cabin well in advance, especially during summer weekends.
Check the park website for current lake levels and water safety alerts before heading out on a boat.
nearbyAttractions: Magic Springs Theme and Water Park

arkansas.name: Pinnacle Mountain State Park
arkansas.shortDescription: A day-use park featuring the iconic Pinnacle Mountain, offering diverse trails and scenic views of the Big Maumelle and Little Maumelle Rivers.
arkansas.fullDescription: Pinnacle Mountain State Park is a 2,356-acre park located in Little Rock, Arkansas. It is known for its namesake mountain, a prominent peak that rises 1,011 feet above the surrounding landscape. The park is a geological treasure, featuring unique rock formations and diverse ecosystems ranging from bottomland hardwoods to rocky mountain slopes. It serves as a vital outdoor recreation hub for the central Arkansas region, preserving natural beauty while providing educational opportunities about the local environment.

hikingTrails.name: East Summit Trail
hikingTrails.description: A steep, rocky climb that rewards hikers with panoramic views of the Arkansas River Valley.

hikingTrails.name: Kingfisher Trail
hikingTrails.description: A flat, accessible trail that winds through the bottomland forest along the Little Maumelle River.

arkansas.campingInfo: Pinnacle Mountain State Park is a day-use park and does not offer overnight camping or cabin rentals.
arkansas.fishingBoating: Fishing is permitted in the Big and Little Maumelle Rivers. Boat ramps are available for access to the rivers for kayaking and canoeing.

visitorCenter.name: Pinnacle Mountain State Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Features interactive exhibits on the park's geology, history, and wildlife, along with a gift shop and helpful park rangers.

arkansas.address: 11901 Pinnacle Valley Road, Little Rock, AR 72223
arkansas.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Fall for mild temperatures and vibrant foliage.
tips: Wear sturdy hiking boots as the summit trails are very rocky.
Bring plenty of water, especially during the summer months.
Check the park website for trail closures due to weather conditions.
nearbyAttractions: Little Rock Central High School National Historic Site

arkansas.name: Queen Wilhelmina State Park
