south carolina.shortDescription: Preserves the largest intact tract of old-growth bottomland hardwood forest remaining in the southeastern United States.
south carolina.fullDescription: Congaree National Park in South Carolina protects the largest intact expanse of old-growth bottomland hardwood forest in the southeastern United States. Fed by the waters of the Congaree and Wateree rivers, the park features towering bald cypress, loblolly pines, and massive water tupelos, some of which form one of the highest temperate deciduous forest canopies in the world. Visitors can explore the lush floodplain forest via the 2.4-mile Boardwalk Loop, paddle the Cedar Creek Canoe Trail, and witness spectacular seasonal synchronous firefly displays.

south carolina.shortDescription: Preserves the historic Charleston sea forts where the Civil War began and 171 years of coastal defense.
south carolina.fullDescription: Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie National Historical Park in Charleston Harbor preserves the historic sea forts that defined American coastal defense for nearly two centuries. On April 12, 1861, Confederate batteries opened fire on Union-occupied Fort Sumter, marking the official beginning of the American Civil War. Nearby, Fort Moultrie on Sullivan's Island represents 171 years of military engineering, famously repelling British forces during the Revolutionary War in 1776 and serving actively through World War II.

south carolina.shortDescription: Preserves the monumental history, community sites, and stories of the Reconstruction Era following the American Civil War.
south carolina.fullDescription: Reconstruction Era National Historical Park, located in Beaufort County, South Carolina, preserves key sites associated with the transformative post-Civil War Reconstruction Era. Centering on the historic Beaufort region, the park documents the struggles and triumphs of newly freed African Americans during this period of monumental social and political change. Notable sites include the Penn School, established in 1862 as one of the first schools for freed slaves, the historic Brick Baptist Church, and the Emancipation Oak site where the Emancipation Proclamation was read to local citizens.

south carolina.fullDescription: Charles Pinckney National Historic Site in Mount Pleasant, South Carolina, protects 28 acres of Snee Farm, a remnant of the coastal plantation owned by Charles Pinckney. Pinckney was a prominent early American statesman, South Carolina governor, and a key contributor to the drafting of the United States Constitution. The site features an 1828 lowcountry cottage housing exhibits on Pinckney's life, the framing of the Constitution, the history of Snee Farm, and the experiences of the enslaved Gullah-Geechee people who lived and worked on the land.

south carolina.fullDescription: Ninety Six National Historic Site protects the historic frontier trading post of Ninety Six, South Carolina, which played a strategic role in early colonial history and the Revolutionary War. The site witnessed the first land battle of the war south of New England in 1775 and the dramatic 1781 siege led by General Nathanael Greene against loyalist defenders. Today, visitors can hike beautiful, peaceful trails to see the extraordinarily well-preserved Star Fort, historic road traces, the colonial town site, and the historic Kosciuszko mine.

south carolina.name: Kings Mountain National Military Park
south carolina.shortDescription: Commemorates the pivotal Battle of Kings Mountain, a decisive Patriot victory that turned the tide of the Revolutionary War.
south carolina.fullDescription: Kings Mountain National Military Park protects the forested ridge in South Carolina where the Battle of Kings Mountain was fought on October 7, 1780. In this critical Revolutionary War encounter, American Patriots (including the legendary Overmountain Men) decisively defeated Loyalist forces led by British Major Patrick Ferguson. The crushing victory was celebrated as a major turning point in the southern campaign, described by Thomas Jefferson as the "turn of the tide of success" for the American independence movement.

south carolina.shortDescription: Commemorates Brigadier General Daniel Morgan's brilliant 1781 tactical victory over the British army.
south carolina.fullDescription: Cowpens National Battlefield preserves the site of the Battle of Cowpens, a masterpiece of military tactics fought on January 17, 1781. Under the masterly leadership of Brigadier General Daniel Morgan, a diverse force of American Continentals and militia achieved a stunning double-envelopment victory over Lieutenant Colonel Banastre Tarleton's elite British forces. This decisive battle crippled British troops in the South, boosting Patriot morale and ultimately paving the way for the British surrender at Yorktown.

It traces the historic trail taken by the frontier "Overmountain Men" Patriots who marched over the Blue Ridge Mountains in the autumn of 1780 to confront and defeat Loyalist forces at the Battle of Kings Mountain. Today, the trail connects modern hikers and travelers to the courage and perseverance of early American settlers who helped shape the outcome of the Revolutionary War.

south carolina.fullDescription: Eutaw Springs Battlefield, located near Eutawville, South Carolina, preserves the site of the Battle of Eutaw Springs, fought on September 8, 1781. This brutal encounter was the last major Revolutionary War battle in South Carolina. Although tactically inconclusive, the heavy losses suffered by British forces under Colonel Alexander Stewart forced their retreat to Charleston, effectively breaking British military control over the southern backcountry. The site is managed as an affiliated area of the National Park Service in cooperation with local historical trusts.

The site features reconstructed historic houses, colonial farm structures, archaeological remains, and the nearby battlefields of Camden and Hobkirk's Hill, telling the stories of early southern settlement and the struggles of the Revolutionary War.

south dakota.shortDescription: Features striking geologic formations, rugged canyons, and the largest undisturbed mixed-grass prairie in the United States.
south dakota.fullDescription: Badlands National Park in southwestern South Dakota protects 244,000 acres of sharply eroded sedimentary buttes, pinnacles, and spires, layered in striking shades of gold and rose. This rugged, beautiful landscape is surrounded by the largest undisturbed mixed-grass prairie in the United States, home to bison, bighorn sheep, swift foxes, and endangered black-footed ferrets. The park's incredibly rich fossil beds contain ancient layers that document the evolution of mammal species like camels, horses, and saber-toothed cats from millions of years ago.

south dakota.fullDescription: Mount Rushmore National Memorial in South Dakota's Black Hills features colossal 60-foot granite portraits of Presidents George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln. Sculpted by Gutzon Borglum and over 400 workers between 1927 and 1941, the massive monument represents the birth, growth, development, and preservation of the United States. Today, the memorial attracts millions of visitors annually, offering museum exhibits, a scenic Presidential Trail, and evening lighting ceremonies.

tennessee.fullDescription: Cumberland Gap National Historical Park preserves the legendary mountain pass through the Appalachian Mountains where Tennessee, Kentucky, and Virginia meet. Known as the gateway to the West, the gap was carved by wind and water, serving as a vital pathway for Native Americans, early pioneers like Daniel Boone, and Civil War forces. tennessee.fullDescription: Shiloh National Military Park protects the sacred ground where the Battle of Shiloh was fought on April 6-7, 1862. The park preserves the beautifully forested battlefield, the Shiloh Indian Mounds National Historic Landmark, and the Shiloh National Cemetery, offering visitors a deep, solemn look at the war's immense human cost.

The Union victory here, commanded by General Ulysses S. Grant, was a major strategic breakthrough, capturing a key Confederate fort, forcing the surrender of over 12,000 Confederate soldiers, and opening the Cumberland River for Union advances. The park preserves the earthen fort, river batteries, the historic Dover Hotel, and the Fort Donelson National Cemetery.

Today, the park features a peaceful battlefield trail winding through Cedar Glades, the historic Hazen Brigade Monument (the oldest intact Civil War monument), and the Stones River National Cemetery.

Today, the trail preserves historic landmarks and tells the story of the westward expansion, communication, and transportation in pre-Civil War America.

tennessee.name: Great Smoky Mountains National Park
tennessee.shortDescription: America's most visited national park, famous for its mist-covered peaks, rich biodiversity, and historic Appalachian log cabins.
tennessee.fullDescription: Great Smoky Mountains National Park, spanning the border of Tennessee and North Carolina, is renowned for its sweeping mountain vistas, mist-covered ridges, rich biodiversity, and well-preserved Southern Appalachian historic structures. As a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the park protects a vast, pristine forest ecosystem containing over 19,000 documented species of plants and animals. Visitors can hike over 800 miles of trails—including the Appalachian Trail—climb to the high vista of Clingmans Dome, explore historic Cades Cove, and enjoy spectacular year-round scenery.

texas.name: Big Bend National Park
texas.shortDescription: Protects a vast expanse of the Chihuahuan Desert, offering dramatic river canyons, rugged mountains, and abundant wildlife.
texas.fullDescription: Big Bend National Park in southwestern Texas preserves over 800,000 acres of Chihuahuan Desert landscape, spectacular limestone canyons, and the rugged Chisos Mountains. Named after the prominent bend in the Rio Grande, the park showcases a dramatic contrast of desert expanses, mountain forests, and riparian environments. Visitors can explore popular trails like the Lost Mine Trail, hike the breathtaking Santa Elena Canyon, and relax in natural hot springs, all under some of the darkest night skies in North America.

texas.name: Guadalupe Mountains National Park
texas.shortDescription: Features the highest peak in Texas, pristine desert ecosystems, and the world's premier fossilized Permian reef.
texas.fullDescription: Guadalupe Mountains National Park in West Texas protects the extraordinary, fossilized Permian Capitan Reef rising high above the Chihuahuan Desert. The park is home to Guadalupe Peak, the highest point in Texas at 8,751 feet, as well as the stunning fall colors of McKittrick Canyon and the pristine white sands of the Salt Basin Dunes. Hiking and backpacking are premier activities, offering access to beautiful pine-oak forests, dramatic canyons, and rich wildlife habitats.

texas.name: Alibates Flint Quarries National Monument
texas.shortDescription: Preserves ancient quarries where Native Americans harvested colorful Alibates flint for thousands of years.
texas.fullDescription: Alibates Flint Quarries National Monument, located in the Texas Panhandle, preserves historic quarries that were vital to prehistoric human survival for over 13,000 years. Native Americans and early cultures excavated the beautiful, highly durable, and colorful Alibates flint to fabricate essential tools and weapons. Ranger-guided tours take visitors up to the quarry hills to view ancient excavation pits and learn about the geologic processes and rich cultural history of the Southern Plains.

texas.name: Waco Mammoth National Monument
texas.shortDescription: Preserves the nation's only recorded discovery of a nursery herd of Pleistocene Columbian mammoths.
texas.fullDescription: Waco Mammoth National Monument is a paleontological site in Waco, Texas, protecting the fossil remains of Columbian mammoths and other ice age animals. Discovered in 1978, the site represents the only known nursery herd of Columbian mammoths in the world, who perished in a sudden mudslide or flood approximately 65,000 years ago. A climate-controlled dig shelter features a suspended walkway, allowing visitors to look down at the beautifully preserved, in-situ fossils of these giant prehistoric creatures.

texas.name: Big Thicket National Preserve
texas.shortDescription: A highly diverse biological crossroads, protecting dense forests, cypress swamps, and winding bayous.
texas.fullDescription: Big Thicket National Preserve in southeastern Texas is recognized as a biological crossroads where multiple ecosystems converge, creating an incredibly biodiverse sanctuary of piney woods, hardwood forests, cypress-tupelo swamps, and coastal prairies. The preserve supports a wide range of flora and fauna, including rare orchids, carnivorous pitcher plants, and numerous migratory bird species. Visitors can explore this unique wilderness through paddling trails, hiking paths, and ranger-led tours.

texas.name: Lyndon B. Johnson National Historical Park
texas.shortDescription: Preserves the birthplace, home, ranch, and final resting place of the 36th President of the United States.
texas.fullDescription: Lyndon B. Johnson National Historical Park in the Texas Hill Country tells the comprehensive story of the 36th U.S. President. The park spans two districts: the Johnson City District, featuring his boyhood home, and the LBJ Ranch District in Stonewall, containing the famous "Texas White House" where LBJ spent a quarter of his presidency. Visitors can tour the active cattle ranch, see his restored birthplace, and learn about the major Great Society legislations that reshaped American society.

texas.name: Palo Alto Battlefield National Historical Park
texas.shortDescription: Commemorates the site of the first major battle of the U.S.-Mexican War in 1846.
texas.fullDescription: Palo Alto Battlefield National Historical Park in Brownsville, Texas, preserves the site of the Battle of Palo Alto, fought on May 8, 1846. This clash was the first major battle of the U.S.-Mexican War, a conflict that dramatically reshaped the map of North America. The park is the only NPS unit dedicated primarily to documenting the war, offering peaceful walking trails across the historic coastal prairie, interpretive exhibits, and a film detailing the perspectives and legacies of both nations.

texas.name: Blackwell School National Historic Site
texas.shortDescription: Preserves the historic schoolhouse commemorating the era of de facto segregation of Mexican American students in Texas.
texas.fullDescription: The Blackwell School National Historic Site in Marfa, Texas, preserves the 1909 schoolhouse that served as the primary educational facility for the town's Mexican and Mexican American students during the era of de facto segregation. Operating until 1965, the school is a powerful national symbol of cultural identity, resilience, and the struggles for equality in the American public education system. The site features photographs, memories, and personal objects donated by former students.

texas.name: Fort Davis National Historic Site
texas.shortDescription: One of the best-preserved western frontier military posts, active during the Indian Wars from 1854 to 1891.
texas.fullDescription: Fort Davis National Historic Site, nestled in a scenic canyon of the Davis Mountains in West Texas, is one of the nation's most outstanding examples of a southwestern frontier military post. Serving from 1854 to 1891, the fort protected emigrants, mail coaches, and freight wagons on the Trans-Pecos trail, and was home to the legendary Buffalo Soldiers. Today, visitors can tour meticulously restored historic buildings, hike scenic mountain trails, and experience vivid history demonstrations.

texas.name: Chamizal National Memorial
texas.shortDescription: Commemorates the peaceful settlement of a century-long border dispute between the United States and Mexico.
texas.fullDescription: Chamizal National Memorial in El Paso, Texas, celebrates the peaceful resolution of the Chamizal boundary dispute, a 100-year border conflict caused by the shifting course of the Rio Grande. Established as a symbol of mutual respect, cooperation, and goodwill between the U.S. and Mexico, the memorial serves as an active cultural center. It features an art gallery, a theater hosting diverse bilingual programs, and a spacious park area connecting local communities across international borders.

texas.name: Amistad National Recreation Area
texas.shortDescription: A premier water recreation oasis in Southwest Texas, famous for boating, fishing, and ancient rock art.
texas.fullDescription: Amistad National Recreation Area preserves the US portion of the international Amistad Reservoir, formed by the damming of the Rio Grande, Devils, and Pecos rivers. Located near Del Rio, Texas, the park is a spectacular desert oasis renowned for outstanding boating, houseboating, water skiing, and world-class bass fishing. The steep limestone cliffs surrounding the reservoir also protect exceptionally rare and ancient Native American rock art panels dating back thousands of years.

Formed by Sanford Dam on the Canadian River, the lake is framed by striking red-mesa canyons and dramatic cliffs. The park is a popular local destination for motorized boating, jet skiing, fishing, swimming, and camping, offering an unexpected aquatic escape in a semi-arid landscape rich in geological and pioneer history.

texas.shortDescription: The longest stretch of undeveloped barrier island in the world, protecting pristine beaches and nesting sea turtles.
texas.fullDescription: Padre Island National Seashore protects 70 miles of pristine coastline, dunes, and salt flats along the Gulf of Mexico, representing the longest undeveloped barrier island in the world. The park separating the Gulf from the Laguna Madre is a critical sanctuary for over 380 bird species and serves as a vital nesting ground for the endangered Kemp's ridley sea turtle. Visitors can enjoy primitive beach camping, beachcombing, outstanding windsurfing, and public turtle hatchling releases.

texas.shortDescription: Protects a free-flowing, remote segment of the Rio Grande winding through spectacular desert canyons.
texas.fullDescription: The Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River protects a remote 196-mile stretch of the legendary border river, winding through towering limestone canyons, rugged desert rapids, and lush riparian corridors in West Texas. Accessible primarily by multi-day raft or canoe trips, this pristine river wilderness offers deep isolation, spectacular geological formations, and exceptional birdwatching, showcasing the true wild character of the American Southwest.

texas.shortDescription: Traces the historic 2,500-mile Spanish colonial road network that connected Mexico City to East Texas and Louisiana.
texas.fullDescription: El Camino Real de los Tejas National Historic Trail preserves the historic Spanish colonial route network that connected Mexico City and early Texas missions to Natchitoches, Louisiana. Spanning over 2,500 miles, this royal road was crucial for Spanish exploration, settlement, trade, and military movements from 1690 through the early 19th century. Today, the trail connects modern travelers to historic sites, old river crossings, and beautiful trails across Texas and Louisiana.

texas.name: Butterfield Overland National Historic Trail
texas.shortDescription: Traces the historic mid-19th-century stagecoach mail route that connected the eastern United States to San Francisco.
texas.fullDescription: The Butterfield Overland National Historic Trail commemorates the historic stagecoach and mail route operated by the Butterfield Overland Mail Company from 1858 to 1861. Spanning over 3,200 miles across eight states, including Texas, this trail was the nation's first transcontinental postal route, connecting St. Louis and Memphis to San Francisco. Today, the trail preserves historic landmarks and tells the story of the westward expansion, communication, and transportation in pre-Civil War America.

texas.name: El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro National Historic Trail
texas.shortDescription: Traces the historic 1,600-mile trade route connecting Mexico City to Santa Fe, New Mexico.
texas.fullDescription: El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro National Historic Trail, or the Royal Road of the Interior Lands, traces the historic 1,600-mile trade route that connected Mexico City with Santa Fe, New Mexico, from 1598 to 1881. It was the oldest and longest Spanish colonial trail in North America, facilitating trade, cultural exchange, and migration across the American Southwest. Today, the trail protects historic river crossings, old plazas, and natural landmarks along the Rio Grande corridor.

Sculpted by water and ice over millions of years, the landscape features massive balanced rocks, soaring pinnacles, and deep canyons. Visitors can explore scenic drives, hike the Devils Garden trail, and stargaze under spectacularly desert night skies.

The park is a series of massive amphitheaters carved into the eastern edge of the Paunsaugunt Plateau, offering breathtaking, high-contrast vistas of orange, pink, and white rock. Popular trails like the Queens Garden and Navajo Loop descend into the canyon, offering an immersive hike among towering spires.

utah.shortDescription: Preserves a massive, rugged wilderness of deep canyons, mesas, and arches carved by the Colorado and Green rivers.
utah.fullDescription: Canyonlands National Park in southeastern Utah protects a vast, primitive wilderness of canyons, mesas, arches, and river gorges carved by the Colorado and Green rivers. The park is divided into four distinct districts: the accessible Island in the Sky mesa, the rugged needles of The Needles, the remote canyons of The Maze, and the rivers themselves. It is a premier destination for backcountry hiking, four-wheel driving, white-water rafting, and exploring ancient rock art.

utah.name: Capitol Reef National Park
utah.shortDescription: Protects the Waterpocket Fold, a massive 100-mile warp in the Earth's crust, and historic pioneer orchards.
utah.fullDescription: Capitol Reef National Park in south-central Utah protects the Waterpocket Fold, a giant 100-mile-long wrinkle in the Earth's crust known as a monocline. The park features dramatic sandstone cliffs, deep canyons, white domes resembling the US Capitol, and historic pioneer orchards in the valley of Fruita. Visitors can hike scenic trails, explore historic petroglyphs carved by early indigenous people, and harvest fresh fruit from heritage orchards.

utah.name: Zion National Park
utah.shortDescription: A spectacular canyon of towering cream, pink, and red sandstone cliffs, famous for world-class slot canyon hikes.
utah.fullDescription: Zion National Park in southwestern Utah is defined by the massive, steep-walled Zion Canyon, carved by the Virgin River. The canyon features soaring sandstone cliffs of Navajo sandstone, hanging gardens, and world-renowned trails. Hikers from around the globe come to challenge the dizzying heights of Angels Landing or wade through the cold waters of the Virgin River in the towering narrows of The Narrows, experiencing some of the most dramatic canyon scenery in the world.

utah.name: Cedar Breaks National Monument
utah.shortDescription: A breathtaking, high-elevation natural amphitheater filled with colorful hoodoos, spires, and ancient bristlecone pines.
utah.fullDescription: Cedar Breaks National Monument, situated over 10,000 feet high on the Markagunt Plateau in Utah, features a colossal half-mile-deep natural amphitheater. Carved from the same geologic formation as Bryce Canyon, its limestone walls display brilliant shades of red, yellow, and purple. The park is famous for spectacular summer wildflower meadows, groves of ancient bristlecone pine trees, outstanding stargazing, and scenic overlooks peering down into the majestic badlands.

utah.name: Dinosaur National Monument
utah.shortDescription: Features an extraordinary quarry wall containing over 1,500 dinosaur fossils, and rugged river canyons.
utah.fullDescription: Dinosaur National Monument, spanning the border of Utah and Colorado, preserves an incredibly rich paleontological deposit. The world-famous Quarry Exhibit Hall protects an exposed rock face embedded with over 1,500 fossilized bones of Jurassic dinosaurs like Allosaurus, Diplodocus, and Stegosaurus. Beyond fossils, the monument offers scenic wild river canyons carved by the Green and Yampa rivers, ancient petroglyphs, and pristine wilderness backcountry.

utah.name: Hovenweep National Monument
utah.shortDescription: Preserves six prehistoric ancestral Puebloan villages famous for their highly advanced, multi-story masonry towers.
utah.fullDescription: Hovenweep National Monument, spanning the Utah-Colorado border, protects six prehistoric, ancestral Puebloan agricultural villages built between 1200 and 1300 CE. The site is highly celebrated for its remarkably well-preserved stone masonry, featuring multi-story square, circular, and D-shaped towers perched on canyon rims. Visitors can hike scenic loop trails through the high desert to view these ancient architectural marvels, which reflect a highly sophisticated civilization.

hikingTrails.name: Hike the Holly Trail

utah.name: Natural Bridges National Monument
utah.shortDescription: Showcases three massive natural sandstone bridges carved by water and the world's first International Dark Sky Park.
utah.fullDescription: Natural Bridges National Monument in southeastern Utah preserves three extraordinarily large and beautiful stream-carved natural bridges: Sipapu, Kachina, and Owachomo. Formed over thousands of years as water cut through sandstone canyons, the bridges can be viewed from scenic loops or hiked to directly. The park was designated as the world's very first International Dark Sky Park in 2007, offering unparalleled night-sky clarity and brilliant views of the Milky Way.

hikingTrails.name: Hike to Sipapu Bridge

utah.name: Golden Spike National Historical Park
utah.shortDescription: Commemorating the completion of the First Transcontinental Railroad in 1869, this park preserves the site where the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines met.
utah.fullDescription: Golden Spike National Historical Park marks the location of Promontory Summit, where the 'Last Spike' was driven on May 10, 1869, forever changing American travel and commerce. The site features reconstructed locomotives, the Jupiter and No. 119, which operate during the summer months to demonstrate the technology of the era. Visitors explore the historic railroad grade, tunnels, and cuts that highlight the immense labor and engineering prowess of the nineteenth century.

utah.name: Timpanogos Cave National Monument
utah.shortDescription: A spectacular cave system carved into the sheer cliffs of American Fork Canyon, famous for its delicate helictites and colorful flowstone.
utah.fullDescription: Timpanogos Cave National Monument features a three-cave system—Chimes, Hansen, and Timpanogos—accessible via a steep 1.5-mile hike. The monument preserves unique geological formations shaped by subterranean waters and ancient seismic activity. Due to the high altitude and narrow cave passages, tours are strictly regulated and require advance reservations during the operating season.

hikingTrails.name: Timpanogos Cave Trail

utah.name: Glen Canyon National Recreation Area
utah.shortDescription: A vast playground spanning over 1.25 million acres, centered around the massive Lake Powell and the Colorado River.
utah.fullDescription: Glen Canyon National Recreation Area offers world-class boating, fishing, and swimming opportunities against a backdrop of dramatic red rock canyons. The area was created by the construction of the Glen Canyon Dam, which formed Lake Powell, one of the largest man-made reservoirs in the United States. Beyond the water, visitors can explore slot canyons, hike desert plateaus, and witness the architectural marvel of the Glen Canyon Dam.

utah.name: Rainbow Bridge National Monument
utah.shortDescription: One of the world's largest known natural bridges, considered sacred by local Native American tribes.
utah.fullDescription: Rainbow Bridge National Monument is a remote and stunning geological feature carved by water flowing down Bridge Creek. Standing 290 feet tall and spanning 275 feet across, the bridge is accessible primarily by boat via Lake Powell or by a strenuous long-distance trek across the Navajo Nation land. It is a place of profound significance to the Navajo, Hopi, San Juan Southern Paiute, and other indigenous peoples.

vermont.name: Marsh-Billings-Rockefeller National Historical Park
vermont.shortDescription: This park serves as a monument to land stewardship and forest conservation, featuring a working dairy farm and the historic Billings Farm.
vermont.fullDescription: Established in 1992, this park preserves the boyhood home of George Perkins Marsh, one of America's first conservationists, and the subsequent home of Frederick Billings. It is the only national park unit in Vermont and highlights the evolution of land management, sustainable forestry, and scientific agriculture in the United States.
thingsToDo: Tour the historic Billings Farm & Museum
Explore the historic mansion and formal gardens
Participate in guided forest health walks
Enjoy snowshoeing or cross-country skiing in winter

vermont.bestTimeToVisit: Late September to mid-October for peak fall foliage.
vermont.accessibilityInfo: The visitor center and certain sections of the carriage roads are accessible. Steep terrain limits access in forested areas.
travelTips: Visit in mid-October to see the vibrant Vermont autumn leaves.
Bring comfortable walking shoes for the gravel carriage roads.
Check the website for mansion tour reservation requirements.

vermont.name: Appalachian National Scenic Trail
vermont.shortDescription: A world-renowned footpath spanning over 2,100 miles, with approximately 105 miles passing through the scenic Green Mountains of Vermont.
vermont.fullDescription: The Appalachian Trail (A.T.) is one of the longest hiking-only footpaths in the world. In Vermont, the trail follows the ridgeline of the southern Green Mountains, overlapping for a significant portion with the Long Trail. Hikers experience deep forests, mountain bogs, and challenging terrain that defines the rugged character of the New England wilderness.
thingsToDo: Thru-hike or section-hike the Vermont segment

hikingTrails.name: Thundering Falls Trail
hikingTrails.description: A boardwalk path leading to a spectacular view of one of Vermont’s tallest waterfalls.

vermont.bestTimeToVisit: June through September for optimal weather conditions.
vermont.accessibilityInfo: Most of the trail is rugged and unpaved, with the exception of the Thundering Falls boardwalk.
travelTips: Avoid hiking during mud season (April-May) to protect the fragile trail surface.

vermont.name: North Country National Scenic Trail
vermont.shortDescription: The longest National Scenic Trail in the U.S., connecting the diverse landscapes of the northern United States, with a dedicated segment in Vermont.
vermont.fullDescription: The North Country Trail stretches 4,800 miles from Vermont to North Dakota. In Vermont, it traverses the rugged terrain near the border of the Green Mountain National Forest, offering hikers a unique opportunity to traverse through iconic New England hardwood forests and rolling hills before heading westward toward the Adirondacks.

virgin islands.name: Virgin Islands National Park
virgin islands.shortDescription: Covers two-thirds of the island of St. John, offering pristine white-sand beaches, crystal-clear snorkeling waters, and lush tropical forests. The park preserves significant Taino archeological sites and historic sugar plantation ruins.
virgin islands.fullDescription: Established in 1956, Virgin Islands National Park protects a diverse landscape that includes dry tropical forests, mangrove shorelines, and extensive coral reefs. The terrain is characterized by steep, rugged topography carved by geological uplift and historical agriculture. Beyond the natural beauty, the park preserves the cultural heritage of the island, including the 18th-century Danish sugar plantation remnants such as Annaberg and the prehistoric petroglyphs at Reef Bay, providing a window into thousands of years of human habitation.

hikingTrails.name: Reef Bay Trail

virgin islands.bestTimeToVisit: December through April for the driest weather and mild temperatures.
virgin islands.accessibilityInfo: Limited accessibility; Trunk Bay has a paved walkway to the beach, but many trails are steep and unpaved.

Carry plenty of water as there are no natural springs

virgin islands.name: Buck Island Reef National Monument
virgin islands.shortDescription: One of the first marine protected areas in the US, featuring a spectacular barrier coral reef and an underwater snorkeling trail.
virgin islands.fullDescription: Buck Island is a small, uninhabited island located 1.5 miles north of St. Croix. The monument is globally significant for its massive Elkhorn coral barrier reef that creates a vibrant, protected lagoon. The park provides critical nesting grounds for hawksbill sea turtles and green turtles. Historically, the island has served as a place of refuge and military importance, but today it is primarily focused on marine ecosystem conservation and research.

Do not touch the coral
Bring snorkeling gear if your tour doesn't provide it

virgin islands.name: Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument
virgin islands.shortDescription: A vast marine protected area surrounding St. John, established to protect and preserve the delicate coral reef ecosystems.
virgin islands.fullDescription: This monument encompasses 12,708 acres of submerged lands under federal jurisdiction. It was created to provide a buffer for the coral reefs and marine environments surrounding St. John, ensuring protection for spawning areas and habitat for migratory species. The area is closed to most types of fishing and anchoring to protect the fragile biodiversity from anthropogenic damage.

visitorCenter.name: Cruz Bay Visitor Center

Respect all 'no-anchoring' buoys
Contact the visitor center regarding research permits

virgin islands.name: Salt River Bay National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve
virgin islands.shortDescription: The site of the only known location where Columbus landed on what is now US territory, featuring bioluminescent bays and mangroves.
virgin islands.fullDescription: Salt River Bay is a rich, complex ecosystem containing mangrove forests, coral reefs, and an estuary that serves as a nursery for marine life. Historically, it is the site of the 1493 encounter between Christopher Columbus's crew and the indigenous Carib people. The park also contains the ruins of Fort Salé and remains of a prehistoric Taino ceremonial ball court, marking its importance as a place of major cultural collision and ecological significance.

hikingTrails.name: Salt River Trail
hikingTrails.description: A flat trail leading to views of the estuary and historical markers near the fort site.

visitorCenter.name: Salt River Visitor Contact Station

virgin islands.accessibilityInfo: Some flat dirt paths, but accessibility is limited.

Respect the sensitive mangrove roots

virgin islands.name: Christiansted National Historic Site
virgin islands.shortDescription: Preserves the historic Danish architecture of Christiansted, including Fort Christiansvaern and the Custom House.
virgin islands.fullDescription: Situated on the waterfront of Christiansted, this site showcases the 18th and 19th-century colonial history of the Danish West Indies. The park preserves well-maintained yellow-brick structures and fortifications that reflect the influence of trade, sugar production, and the history of enslaved labor in the Caribbean. The buildings now serve as a living museum for the town's complex colonial past.

visitorCenter.name: Fort Christiansvaern
visitorCenter.info: Central site office and museum.

virgin islands.hours: The Park is open every day from 8:30 am to 4:30 pm. The park is closed on Thanksgiving Day and Christmas Day.
virgin islands.address: 2100 Church St, Christiansted, St. Croix, VI 00820
virgin islands.bestTimeToVisit: Cooler mornings for walking the town.
virgin islands.accessibilityInfo: Grounds are paved and generally accessible; some interior fort areas have stairs.
travelTips: Wear comfortable walking shoes for the historic streets
Bring a hat for the sun at the harbor
Visit the nearby local marketplace

virginia.name: Shenandoah National Park
virginia.shortDescription: Stretching along the crest of the Blue Ridge Mountains, Shenandoah offers stunning vistas and serene woodlands just 75 miles from Washington, D.C.
virginia.fullDescription: Established in 1935, Shenandoah National Park protects the northern portion of the Blue Ridge Mountains in Virginia. Its unique geology is defined by Precambrian-age igneous and metamorphic rocks, sculpted over millions of years by erosion to create the rolling topography visitors see today. The park is a critical sanctuary for biodiversity, featuring massive hardwood forests that serve as a vibrant habitat for diverse flora and fauna, alongside the world-famous Skyline Drive which winds through its heart.

hikingTrails.name: Old Rag Mountain Loop
hikingTrails.description: Features a famous rock scramble and panoramic 360-degree views of the Blue Ridge.

hikingTrails.name: Stony Man Trail
hikingTrails.description: Provides a relatively short ascent to one of the most iconic viewpoints in the park.

scenicDrives.name: Skyline Drive
scenicDrives.description: The only public road through the park, running the length of the Blue Ridge Mountains.

visitorCenter.name: Dickey Ridge Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Located at Mile 4.6, offering orientation and park information.

washington.name: Manhattan Project National Historical Park
washington.shortDescription: Preserves the sites associated with the development of the first atomic bomb at Hanford.
washington.fullDescription: The Hanford unit focuses on the B Reactor, the world's first full-scale plutonium production reactor. It tells the complex story of the scientific, social, and geopolitical impacts of the Manhattan Project.

hikingTrails.name: Hanford: Hike the White Bluffs North Trail
hikingTrails.description: On this trail you may explore rolling sand dunes, take in vast vistas dotted with relics of plutonium production during the Manhattan Project and Cold War, and observe a variety of wildlife.

hikingTrails.name: Hanford: Hike Candy Mountain
hikingTrails.description: The trail up Candy Mountain is a moderate 3.6 mile (5.8 km) roundtrip hike that offers sweeping views of the Tri-Cities region and a walk through time. Signs along the trail explain the impact of the ice age floods on ar

hikingTrails.name: Hanford: Hike the White Bluffs South Slope Trail
hikingTrails.description: This trail provides one of the best views of the old Hanford town site and location of the Hanford construction camp for the Manhattan Project. This trail will reward you with expansive views of the Hanford site and oppo

visitorCenter.name: Manhattan Project Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Information on tours.

washington.campingInfo: No camping.
washington.hours: The Hanford Visitor Center is open Monday - Friday 9:00 AM-4:00 PM. Access to the Hanford B Reactor is suspended due to major construction projects.
washington.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Fall.
travelTips: Tours require advance reservation
Bring photo ID for site entry
Dress for field conditions

washington.name: Lewis and Clark National Historical Park
washington.shortDescription: Commemorating the Corps of Discovery's arrival at the Pacific Ocean and winter stay at Fort Clatsop.
washington.fullDescription: This park encompasses sites in Oregon and Washington, honoring the expedition's winter at Fort Clatsop (1805-1806). It interprets the cultural encounter with the Chinookan people and the scientific achievements of the expedition.

hikingTrails.name: Fort to Sea Trail
hikingTrails.description: Follows the trail once used by the explorers to reach the Pacific.

visitorCenter.name: Fort Clatsop Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Extensive museum and replica fort.

washington.campingInfo: No camping at the fort; nearby state parks exist.
washington.hours:
Winter Hours:
Begin the day after Labor Day
Open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
washington.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Summer.
travelTips: Allow 2-3 hours
Visit the salt works site
Check for seasonal events

washington.name: Nez Perce National Historical Park
washington.shortDescription: Explores the history and culture of the Nimiipuu people and their relationship with the landscape.
washington.fullDescription: This park spans across four states, commemorating the Nez Perce people. The Washington sites highlight key locations in the 1877 flight of the Nez Perce and traditional village sites. It emphasizes tribal perspectives and survival.

hikingTrails.name: Dayton Site trail
hikingTrails.description: Short interpretive walking loop.

visitorCenter.name: Nez Perce National Historical Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Main interpretive hub.

washington.campingInfo: No camping.
washington.hours: Summer visitor center operating hours are 8:30 am - 4:00 pm daily. In the winter, the visitor center is open 5-days a week from Tuesday - Saturday from 8:30 am - 4:00 pm.
washington.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Fall.
travelTips: Visit multiple park units
Respect cultural sites
Check the website for specific WA locations

west virginia.name: New River Gorge National Park and Preserve
west virginia.shortDescription: Home to one of the oldest rivers in the world, this park features a massive steel arch bridge and rugged canyon terrain perfect for rock climbing and whitewater rafting.
west virginia.fullDescription: New River Gorge National Park and Preserve protects over 70,000 acres of the New River, one of the oldest rivers on the planet. The park is characterized by its deep canyon, diverse forests, and the iconic New River Gorge Bridge, which rises 876 feet above the river. Geologically, the area is rich in sandstone cliffs and coal-bearing rock formations that fueled the regional industrial revolution, leaving behind a fascinating cultural history of boom-town coal camps.
thingsToDo: Whitewater rafting on the New River
Rock climbing on world-class sandstone cliffs
Mountain biking on the Arrowhead Trails
Walking the catwalk under the New River Gorge Bridge

hikingTrails.name: Long Point Trail
hikingTrails.description: A forest trek leading to a dramatic rocky outcrop offering an unparalleled view of the New River Gorge Bridge.

hikingTrails.name: Endless Wall Trail
hikingTrails.description: Follows the cliff edge through hemlock forests and rhododendron thickets with stunning overlooks of the gorge.

scenicDrives.name: Fayette Station Road
scenicDrives.description: A winding, narrow road that takes you down into the heart of the gorge, crossing the river near the historic town of Fayette.

visitorCenter.name: Canyon Rim Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Located near the New River Gorge Bridge, offering exhibits and information.

west virginia.campingInfo: The park offers several primitive campgrounds such as Grandview Sandbar, Stone Cliff, and Army Camp, available on a first-come, first-served basis.
west virginia.hours: Open 24 hours a day (per nps.gov; visitor center hours vary)
west virginia.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring for rhododendron blooms or October for peak fall foliage.
west virginia.accessibilityInfo: The Canyon Rim Visitor Center and associated boardwalks are fully ADA accessible.
travelTips: Check water levels before planning a whitewater rafting trip.
Bring sturdy hiking boots for rocky terrain.
Pack rain gear as weather in the gorge can change rapidly.

west virginia.name: Harpers Ferry National Historical Park
west virginia.shortDescription: A historic town located at the confluence of the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers, famous for John Brown's 1859 abolitionist raid.
west virginia.fullDescription: Harpers Ferry is a place of profound American history, serving as a key site for industrialization, the Civil War, and the struggle for civil rights. The town was the site of John Brown's raid on the federal arsenal in 1859, a pivotal event leading to the Civil War. Visitors can explore preserved 19th-century buildings, hike through the Water Gap, and trace the steps of diverse historical figures.

hikingTrails.name: Maryland Heights Trail
hikingTrails.description: A challenging hike that ascends the mountain to provide a panoramic view of the historic town and river confluence.

hikingTrails.name: Loudoun Heights Trail
hikingTrails.description: Rugged forest trail that offers quiet solitude and overlooks of the Shenandoah River.

visitorCenter.name: Harpers Ferry National Historical Park Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Shuttle access to historic town and main museum.

west virginia.campingInfo: No camping is permitted within the park boundaries; private campgrounds are available in the surrounding Harpers Ferry area.
west virginia.hours: Harpers Ferry National Historical Park is open year-round with the exception of Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, and New Year's Day. Park museums/exhibits, the Visitor Center, and restroom facilities are open from 9 a.m.
west virginia.bestTimeToVisit: Autumn for mild temperatures and historical reenactment events.
west virginia.accessibilityInfo: Shuttle buses are wheelchair accessible; some historic cobblestone streets in Lower Town may be challenging.
travelTips: Use the park shuttle to reach the historic town.
Wear comfortable walking shoes.
Bring water as there are limited facilities on the mountain trails.

west virginia.name: Bluestone National Scenic River
west virginia.shortDescription: A protected, rugged river corridor offering remote fishing, hiking, and primitive scenic beauty.
west virginia.fullDescription: The Bluestone National Scenic River flows through a deep, rugged gorge in southern West Virginia. This park unit preserves the natural, cultural, and historic integrity of the river, which remains largely undeveloped. The area is a sanctuary for flora and fauna and serves as a quiet retreat for those seeking wilderness-style experiences, accessible primarily by trail or river craft.
thingsToDo: Canoeing and kayaking in Class I and II waters
Hiking along the Bluestone Turnpike Trail

hikingTrails.name: Bluestone Turnpike Trail
hikingTrails.description: An old historic roadbed that follows the river, perfect for long-distance hiking or trail running.

hikingTrails.name: Little Bluestone Trail
hikingTrails.description: A trail that winds through historic farmsteads and connects to the river corridor.

visitorCenter.name: Sandstone Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Serves as the information hub for the New River Gorge and Bluestone area.

west virginia.campingInfo: Primitive backcountry camping is allowed along the river by permit only; there are no developed campgrounds.
west virginia.hours: Open 24 hours a day (per nps.gov; visitor center hours vary)
west virginia.bestTimeToVisit: Summer for river recreation or autumn for migration views.
west virginia.accessibilityInfo: Limited; most of the park is rugged terrain intended for experienced hikers and boaters.
travelTips: Ensure you have a map, as cell service is non-existent in the canyon.
Practice Leave No Trace principles.
Wear life jackets when on the water.

west virginia.name: Gauley River National Recreation Area
west virginia.shortDescription: Famous for high-adrenaline whitewater rafting, this park features a wild, free-flowing river with intense rapids.
west virginia.fullDescription: The Gauley River is world-renowned for its intense whitewater, challenging rafters and kayakers with over 100 rapids in a 25-mile stretch. When the Summersville Dam releases water in the fall, this river provides some of the most technical and exhilarating rafting in North America. Beyond the water, the recreation area preserves a deep, scenic canyon and lush, temperate rainforest environments.
thingsToDo: Rock climbing on the upper gorge

hikingTrails.name: Woods Ferry Trail
hikingTrails.description: Leads to the river and provides access to historic swimming and fishing spots.

hikingTrails.name: Confluence Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short but beautiful walk to the spot where the Gauley and Meadow Rivers meet.

visitorCenter.name: Canyon Rim Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Information shared with New River Gorge facilities.

west virginia.campingInfo: Primitive camping is available at the Gauley Tailwaters; reservations required for high-demand season.
west virginia.hours: Open 24 hours a day (per nps.gov; visitor center hours vary)
west virginia.bestTimeToVisit: September-October during the scheduled 'Gauley Season' dam releases.
west virginia.accessibilityInfo: Minimal accessibility; designed for active, mobile visitors.
travelTips: Only experienced rafters should attempt the Upper Gauley.
Stay clear of dam release warning sirens.
Always wear a helmet and PFD.

wisconsin.name: Apostle Islands National Lakeshore
wisconsin.shortDescription: Located on the shores of Lake Superior, this park encompasses 21 islands and 12 miles of mainland coast known for historic lighthouses and sea caves.
wisconsin.fullDescription: Apostle Islands National Lakeshore protects a unique landscape of red sandstone sea caves, old-growth forests, and the largest collection of historic lighthouses in the National Park System. Formed by glacial activity, these islands represent a fragile ecosystem where Lake Superior's harsh environment meets rich, diverse terrestrial habitats. The islands have served as homes to indigenous Ojibwe people, commercial fishermen, and brownstone quarrymen, leaving behind a complex cultural landscape layered over ancient geological formations.
thingsToDo: Sea kayaking through the mainland sea caves
Sailing or motorboating between the archipelago

hikingTrails.name: Lakeshore Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic path along the mainland cliff tops providing access to the famous sea caves.

hikingTrails.name: Sand Island Lighthouse Trail
hikingTrails.description: A trail leading through a historic forest setting to the 1881 Sand Island Lighthouse.

visitorCenter.name: Bayfield Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Located in the historic Old Bayfield County Courthouse.

wisconsin.campingInfo: Camping is available on 18 of the 21 islands and at one mainland site; reservations are required via recreation.gov.
wisconsin.hours: Open 24 hours a day (per nps.gov; visitor center hours vary)
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: July through September for warmer water and island boat accessibility.
wisconsin.accessibilityInfo: Limited; visitor center is ADA accessible, but island trails are generally rugged and not paved.
travelTips: Check the marine forecast daily as Lake Superior weather changes rapidly.
Bring extra layers as temperatures on the water are significantly cooler than inland.
Pack out all trash as there are no trash facilities on the islands.

wisconsin.name: Saint Croix National Scenic Riverway
wisconsin.shortDescription: Spanning 252 miles of pristine water, the St. Croix and Namekagon Rivers offer world-class paddling, fishing, and boating experiences.
wisconsin.fullDescription: The Saint Croix National Scenic Riverway protects two of the cleanest and most scenic rivers in the upper Midwest. Designated as part of the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System, this park provides critical habitat for endangered species and a recreational corridor for millions. The riverway follows the border between Wisconsin and Minnesota, winding through diverse landscapes ranging from deep pine forests and dramatic rock formations to lush wetland floodplains.
thingsToDo: Canoeing and kayaking the river corridors
Fishing for smallmouth bass and walleye

hikingTrails.name: Sandstone Bluff Trail
hikingTrails.description: Short trail providing views of the St. Croix River valley.

hikingTrails.name: Namekagon Fen Trail
hikingTrails.description: Boardwalk trail through a unique peatland wetland habitat.

scenicDrives.name: River Road Drive
scenicDrives.description: Follows the river valley north of St. Croix Falls, offering river views and autumn foliage.

visitorCenter.name: St. Croix River Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Located in St. Croix Falls, Wisconsin.

wisconsin.campingInfo: Primitive riverside camping is available on a first-come, first-served basis; some islands require permits.
wisconsin.hours: Open 24 hours a day (per nps.gov; visitor center hours vary)
wisconsin.address: 401 N. Hamilton Street, St. Croix Falls, WI 54024
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: Late spring through early autumn for optimal water levels and warm weather.
wisconsin.accessibilityInfo: Select landings and the visitor center are wheelchair accessible.
travelTips: Always wear a PFD when on the water.
Check water levels via the NPS website before planning your paddle.
Use bug spray during the peak summer months.

wisconsin.name: Ice Age National Scenic Trail
wisconsin.shortDescription: A 1,200-mile footpath located entirely within Wisconsin, tracing the terminal moraine of the last continental glacier.
wisconsin.fullDescription: The Ice Age National Scenic Trail is one of the premier long-distance trails in America, specifically designed to highlight the glacial landscape left behind 15,000 years ago. The trail wanders through massive end moraines, glacial lakes, drumlins, and eskers, showcasing how ice shaped the state's geography. Managed in partnership with the Ice Age Trail Alliance, the trail connects various state parks, forests, and public lands across Wisconsin.

hikingTrails.name: Holy Hill Segment
hikingTrails.description: Features high ridges and panoramic views near the famous Holy Hill basilica.

hikingTrails.name: Kettle Moraine State Forest Segment
hikingTrails.description: Rugged terrain through steep glacial hills and deep kettle depressions.

visitorCenter.name: Ice Age Trail Alliance Office/Visitor Info
visitorCenter.info: Located in Cross Plains, WI; provides maps and planning assistance.

wisconsin.campingInfo: Camping varies by segment; many sections utilize designated campgrounds in State Parks or private lands.
wisconsin.hours: Open 24 hours a day (per nps.gov; visitor center hours vary)
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: Autumn for fall colors or spring for wildflower displays.
wisconsin.accessibilityInfo: Accessibility varies; some segments near visitor hubs are surfaced, but much of the trail is rugged.
travelTips: Use the 'Ice Age Trail Guidebook' for detailed section information.
Stay hydrated as many segments do not have reliable water sources.
Wear blaze orange during Wisconsin's hunting seasons.

wisconsin.name: North Country National Scenic Trail
wisconsin.shortDescription: The longest National Scenic Trail in the U.S., traversing over 4,800 miles across eight states, including a significant stretch through northern Wisconsin.
wisconsin.fullDescription: The North Country National Scenic Trail (NCT) is a monumental effort to link the Appalachian Trail to the Lewis and Clark Trail through the heart of the northern United States. In Wisconsin, the trail winds through the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest, passing through some of the most remote and pristine landscapes in the state. The trail offers hikers a deep-woods experience characterized by vast wetlands, dense pine and hardwood forests, and glacial landforms.

hikingTrails.name: Copper Falls Segment
hikingTrails.description: Winds through beautiful river gorges and hemlock-hardwood forests.

hikingTrails.name: Chequamegon Forest Segment
hikingTrails.description: Remote wilderness trail through rolling hills and around small woodland lakes.

visitorCenter.name: NCT Headquarters (Lowell, MI)
visitorCenter.info: National administrative office; for Wisconsin, check local US Forest Service offices.

wisconsin.campingInfo: Dispersed camping is allowed in many National Forest sections along the trail; verify local regulations.
wisconsin.hours: Open 24 hours a day (per nps.gov; visitor center hours vary)
wisconsin.bestTimeToVisit: June through August for warmer temperatures; late September for foliage.
wisconsin.accessibilityInfo: Minimal; primarily a primitive wilderness trail.
travelTips: Carry a physical map as cell service is unreliable in the northern forest.
Be bear-aware and use proper food storage techniques.
Check for local logging activity which may impact trail accessibility.

wyoming.name: Grand Teton National Park
wyoming.shortDescription: Home to the jagged Teton Range, this park offers world-class alpine scenery, pristine glacial lakes, and abundant wildlife.
wyoming.fullDescription: Grand Teton National Park protects the major peaks of the Teton Range, a young mountain range formed by active faulting. The park encompasses a landscape shaped by glaciers, rivers, and the historic settlement of Jackson Hole, providing a dramatic backdrop for ecological diversity and human history.

hikingTrails.name: Cascade Canyon Trail
hikingTrails.description: An iconic trail starting with a boat ride across Jenny Lake, leading into a U-shaped glacial canyon.

hikingTrails.name: Taggart Lake Loop
hikingTrails.description: A relatively flat hike offering spectacular views of the Cathedral Group peaks reflecting in the lake.

scenicDrives.name: Teton Park Road
scenicDrives.description: The main artery of the park running parallel to the Teton Range, offering numerous pullouts and trailheads.

visitorCenter.name: Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: The primary visitor center featuring exhibits on local culture and geology.

wyoming.campingInfo: Several campgrounds including Jenny Lake, Signal Mountain, and Colter Bay; reservations highly recommended via Recreation.gov.
wyoming.hours: Open 24 hours a day (per nps.gov; visitor center hours vary)
wyoming.bestTimeToVisit: June through September for hiking; winter for skiing.
wyoming.accessibilityInfo: Accessible boardwalks at Colter Bay and various viewing platforms.
travelTips: Carry bear spray
Pack layers for rapid weather changes
Visit early morning to avoid crowds

wyoming.name: Yellowstone National Park
wyoming.shortDescription: The world's first national park, featuring massive geothermal wonders and iconic megafauna.
wyoming.fullDescription: Yellowstone sits atop a massive volcanic caldera and is renowned for its geothermal activity, including more than half of the world's geysers. The park serves as a massive ecological laboratory, supporting a vast array of wildlife including grizzly bears, gray wolves, and bison.
thingsToDo: Exploring the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone

hikingTrails.name: Uncle Tom's Trail
hikingTrails.description: Explore local highlights.

hikingTrails.name: Mount Washburn Trail
hikingTrails.description: Provides expansive panoramic views of the entire park from the summit.

scenicDrives.name: Grand Loop Road
scenicDrives.description: The main road forming a figure-eight that connects all major attractions in the park.

visitorCenter.name: Albright Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Located at Mammoth Hot Springs, focusing on park history and wildlife.

wyoming.campingInfo: Twelve campgrounds; many require reservations well in advance via Yellowstone National Park Lodges.
wyoming.hours: Open 24 hours a day (per nps.gov; visitor center hours vary)
wyoming.accessibilityInfo: Many boardwalks are ADA compliant; wheelchair-accessible shuttles available.
travelTips: Stay 100 yards from bears/wolves
Expect traffic delays due to animal sightings
Download offline maps

wyoming.name: Devils Tower National Monument
wyoming.shortDescription: A stunning igneous intrusion rising 1,267 feet above the Belle Fourche River.
wyoming.fullDescription: Known to many Northern Plains tribes as Bear Lodge, Devils Tower is a sacred site and a geologic marvel. The tower is a laccolith, formed by magma cooling and cracking into hexagonal columns, resulting in the unique vertical striations seen today.

hikingTrails.name: Tower Trail
hikingTrails.description: A paved path that circles the base of the tower, providing diverse perspectives of the monolith.

hikingTrails.name: Red Beds Trail
hikingTrails.description: A loop that takes visitors through the red sandstone formations around the monument.

visitorCenter.name: Devils Tower Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides information on the geology and tribal significance of the site.

wyoming.campingInfo: Belle Fourche River Campground offers first-come, first-served sites.
wyoming.hours: Open 24 hours a day (per nps.gov; visitor center hours vary)
wyoming.accessibilityInfo: The Tower Trail is mostly paved and accessible for visitors with limited mobility.
travelTips: Bring a jacket for windy summit winds
Respect tribal prayer cloths
Bring binoculars for climbing sightings

wyoming.name: Fossil Butte National Monument
wyoming.shortDescription: Contains some of the world's best-preserved fossils from the Eocene Epoch.
wyoming.fullDescription: Fossil Butte showcases the remains of an ancient lake system that existed 50 million years ago. The high desert landscape preserves incredible detail of fish, plants, insects, and mammals that lived in a subtropical environment.

hikingTrails.name: Historic Quarry Trail
hikingTrails.description: Leads to a historic fossil quarry where visitors can see where scientists excavated fossils.

hikingTrails.name: Nature Trail
hikingTrails.description: An interpretive loop explaining the desert flora and fauna.

visitorCenter.name: Fossil Butte Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Houses extensive fossil collections and rotating exhibits.

wyoming.campingInfo: No camping inside the monument; nearby camping available in Kemmerer.
wyoming.hours: Visitors may enter the park any day sunrise to sunset, but visitor services and motor vehicle access vary throughout the year. Camping is not available.
travelTips: Bring plenty of water
Sun protection is essential
Check the forecast for high winds

wyoming.name: Fort Laramie National Historic Site
wyoming.shortDescription: A former fur trading post and military installation critical to the history of the Oregon Trail.
wyoming.fullDescription: Fort Laramie served as a vital hub for pioneers, the Pony Express, and the US military. It remains a physical testament to the expansion westward and the complex interactions between settlers, the US government, and Native American tribes.

hikingTrails.name: Laramie River Trail
hikingTrails.description: A riverside trail providing views of the confluence and local bird habitat.

hikingTrails.name: Confluence Trail
hikingTrails.description: A short walk through the site's history and natural landscape.

visitorCenter.name: Fort Laramie Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Located in the former Commissary Storehouse.

wyoming.campingInfo: No on-site camping; nearby facilities in Guernsey, WY.
wyoming.hours: The park grounds are open from dawn until dusk every day of the year. Some historic buildings may be closed in winter.
wyoming.address: 965 Gray Rocks Rd, Fort Laramie, WY 82212
wyoming.accessibilityInfo: Several restored buildings have ramps; grounds are mostly flat.
travelTips: Wear comfortable shoes
Bring a hat for sun protection
Plan for a half-day visit

wyoming.name: Bighorn Canyon National Recreation Area
wyoming.shortDescription: A dramatic landscape featuring a 55-mile long reservoir and deep canyon scenery.
wyoming.fullDescription: Straddling the Wyoming-Montana border, Bighorn Canyon offers a diverse ecosystem from alpine forests to desert scrub. The Bighorn Lake is a centerpiece for boating, while the surrounding Pryor Mountains are famous for wild horses.

hikingTrails.name: Mustang Flat Trail
hikingTrails.description: Excellent trail for spotting wild horses in the Pryor Mountain area.

hikingTrails.name: Sullivan's Knob Trail
hikingTrails.description: Short trail leading to spectacular views over the canyon.

scenicDrives.name: Devil Canyon Overlook Road
scenicDrives.description: A short drive ending in one of the most stunning views in the American West.

visitorCenter.name: Yellowtail Dam Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Information on the dam and canyon history.

wyoming.campingInfo: Several developed campgrounds available along the reservoir.
wyoming.hours: Open 24 hours a day (per nps.gov; visitor center hours vary)
wyoming.accessibilityInfo: Most overlooks are paved and accessible.
travelTips: Check water conditions before boating
Carry extra water
Watch for wildlife on roads

wyoming.name: John D. Rockefeller, Jr. Memorial Parkway
wyoming.shortDescription: The scenic link connecting Grand Teton and Yellowstone National Parks.
wyoming.fullDescription: Dedicated to the man who contributed immensely to American national parks, this parkway preserves the corridor between the two giant parks. It is characterized by the rushing Snake River, lodgepole pine forests, and mountain views.

hikingTrails.name: Flagg Canyon Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic path overlooking the Snake River and surrounding hills.

hikingTrails.name: Arizona Creek Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle trail through marshy meadows ideal for bird watching.

scenicDrives.name: John D. Rockefeller, Jr. Memorial Parkway
scenicDrives.description: The scenic drive along US 191 connecting Grand Teton and Yellowstone.

visitorCenter.name: Flagg Ranch Information Station
visitorCenter.info: A small visitor center providing road info.

wyoming.campingInfo: Headwaters Campground provides tent and RV sites.
wyoming.entranceFees: Free to drive; entrance to adjacent parks requires fees
wyoming.accessibilityInfo: Standard road accessibility; limited facility access.
travelTips: Keep speed limits to protect wildlife
Have a full tank of gas
Use pullouts for views

arizona.name: Monument Valley Navajo Tribal Park
arizona.shortDescription: World-famous red sandstone buttes and sacred Navajo landscapes immortalized in classic cinema.
arizona.fullDescription: Monument Valley Navajo Tribal Park straddles the Arizona-Utah border on the sacred ancestral lands of the Navajo Nation (Diné). Towering sandstone monoliths, buttes, and spires rise between 400 and 1,000 feet above the vibrant desert floor. Visitors can drive the legendary 17-mile unpaved Valley Drive or hire licensed Navajo guides to access sacred backcountry areas like Mystery Valley, Hunts Mesa, and Ear of the Wind.
thingsToDo: Take a Certified Navajo Guided 4x4 Tour
Hike the Wildcat Trail around West Mitten Butte
Photograph Sunset and Sunrise at the View Hotel Overlook
Visit Navajo Hogan Demonstrations and Artisan Stands

hikingTrails.name: Wildcat Trail
hikingTrails.description: The only self-guided hiking trail in the park, circling around the iconic West Mitten Butte with spectacular ground-level views of the Mittens and Merrick Butte.

hikingTrails.name: Mystery Valley Backcountry Tour (Guided Only)
hikingTrails.description: Accessible only with licensed Navajo guides, leading to ancient Anasazi cliff dwellings, pictographs, petroglyphs, and secluded natural arches.

scenicDrives.name: 17-Mile Valley Drive
scenicDrives.description: A graded dirt road passing the East and West Mitten Buttes, Merrick Butte, Three Sisters, John Ford Point, Totem Pole, and Artist Point.

scenicDrives.name: US-163 Scenic Byway (Forrest Gump Point)
scenicDrives.description: The iconic highway straightaway with panoramic head-on views of Monument Valley buttes made famous in the film Forrest Gump.

visitorCenter.name: Monument Valley Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Features an observation deck, Navajo cultural exhibits, restaurant, and gift shop with authentic Navajo silversmithing and rugs.
visitorCenter.hours: Peak Season (May 1 – Sep 30): 6:00 AM – 8:00 PM; Off-Peak (Oct 1 – Apr 30): 8:00 AM – 5:00 PM

arizona.campingInfo: The View Campground offers primitive wilderness campsites and RV sites overlooking the valley. Gouldings Resort & Campground (5 miles west) provides full hookups, cabins, and indoor pool.
bestViewpoints: Forrest Gump Hill (Mile Marker 13 on US-163)
arizona.entranceFees: $8.00 per person entry fee. Children 9 and under are free. (National Park America the Beautiful passes are not accepted on sovereign tribal land).
arizona.hours: Open 7 days a week year-round; Valley Drive closes to entry 2 hours before park gates close.
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: Spring (April to May) and Autumn (September to October) for pleasant daytime temperatures and striking desert sunset lighting.
arizona.accessibilityInfo: The Visitor Center, observation terrace, and The View Hotel are fully ADA accessible. Valley Drive is a rough dirt road; trails are sandy and non-paved.
travelTips: Sovereign Tribal Land: Alcohol is strictly prohibited across the Navajo Nation.
Photography Rules: Commercial filming requires permits. Always request permission before photographing local Navajo artisans and residents.
High Clearance Recommended: Valley Drive is rough washboard dirt with deep ruts; low-clearance sedans may scrape.
Nearest Staging Towns: Kayenta, AZ (23 miles south) and Mexican Hat / Bluff, UT (22–45 miles north).

arizona.name: Antelope Canyon (Upper & Lower)
arizona.shortDescription: Mesmerizing sandstone slot canyons known for glowing sunbeams, flowing wave-like curves, and deep Navajo cultural significance.
arizona.fullDescription: Antelope Canyon (Tsé bighánílíní - "the place where water runs through rocks" in Navajo) is the most famous slot canyon system in the world. Located near Page, Arizona, within the LeChee Chapter of the Navajo Nation, the canyon is split into two distinct sections: Upper Antelope Canyon (famous for vertical midday light shafts in summer) and Lower Antelope Canyon (renowned for metal stairs, dynamic climb-through passages, and swirling sculptured sandstone). Access is strictly restricted to licensed Navajo guided tours.
thingsToDo: Book a Guided Tour of Upper Antelope Canyon for Midday Sunbeams
Climb through the Sculpted Passages of Lower Antelope Canyon
Experience Canyon X and Secret Antelope for Lower Crowds
Capture Iconic Swirling Sandstone Textures and Color Gradients
Learn Navajo Heritage and Geologic History from Native Guides

hikingTrails.name: Upper Antelope Canyon Tour Walk
hikingTrails.description: A flat, sandy walk through narrow 120-foot tall canyon corridors with dramatic overhead light shafts (guided access only).

hikingTrails.name: Lower Antelope Canyon Trek
hikingTrails.description: Navigates multiple flights of steep metal staircases and narrow sandstone crevices, exiting via a flat overland walkway.

scenicDrives.name: AZ-98 Scenic Desert Highway
scenicDrives.description: Connects Page, AZ to Kaibeto, passing Antelope Canyon tour staging areas and panoramic desert sandstone mesas.

visitorCenter.name: Navajo Nation Lake Powell Tribal Parks Office
visitorCenter.info: Manages permits and oversight for Antelope Canyon, Horseshoe Bend overlook lands, and Lake Powell tribal shorelines.

arizona.campingInfo: No camping inside the canyon. Extensive camping and RV resorts are available 10 minutes away at Wahweap Marina (Lake Powell) and Page, AZ.
bestViewpoints: The Sunbeam Chambers (Upper Antelope, 10:30 AM - 1:00 PM May-Sep)
The Lady in the Wind (Lower Antelope)
arizona.entranceFees: $8.00 Navajo Nation Park Entry Permit + Tour Operator Ticket ($70 - $120+ per person depending on operator and season).
arizona.hours: Guided tours depart daily between 7:30 AM and 4:30 PM (weather permitting).
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: May through September for the famous overhead light shafts; October through April for cooler weather and fewer crowds.
arizona.accessibilityInfo: Upper Antelope Canyon is level on sand but bumpy 4x4 ride is required; Lower Antelope Canyon features steep metal stairs and is not wheelchair accessible.
travelTips: Advance Booking Required: Tours sell out weeks to months in advance, especially during peak spring/summer months.
Strict Bag Policy: Bags, backpacks, and tripods are strictly prohibited by tour operators for safety and space constraints inside the slots.
Flash Flood Closures: Slot canyons can close immediately with zero warning if rainfall occurs anywhere upstream in the watershed.
Time Zone Note: Page and Navajo Nation time zones can differ depending on Daylight Saving Time—verify tour check-in time with operator.

arizona.name: Havasu Falls & Mooney Falls
arizona.shortDescription: World-renowned turquoise waterfalls plunging into travertine pools on the sovereign sovereign Havasupai Indian Reservation.
arizona.fullDescription: Havasu Falls is the crown jewel of Havasu Canyon on the Havasupai Indian Reservation, located within a remote tributary of the Grand Canyon. Fed by underground mineral springs that deposit calcium carbonate, the crystal-clear waters shine in vivid shades of turquoise and aquamarine contrasting sharply against red sandstone amphitheaters. The area includes Navajo Falls, Fifty Foot Falls, Havasu Falls, Mooney Falls (200 ft), and Beaver Falls.
thingsToDo: Backpack the 10-Mile Canyon Trail from Hualapai Hilltop to Supai Village
Swim in the Brilliant Travertine Pools beneath Havasu Falls
Descend the Thrilling Rock Tunnel and Chains to the Base of Mooney Falls
Trek Down-Canyon to Beaver Falls through Cottonwood Groves
Sample Fresh Traditional Frybread in Supai Village

hikingTrails.name: Hualapai Hilltop to Supai Village & Campground
hikingTrails.description: A desert hike through switchbacks into canyon beds leading to Supai Village (mile 8) and Havasu Falls Campground (mile 10).

hikingTrails.name: Mooney Falls to Beaver Falls Hike
hikingTrails.description: Includes descending Mooney chains and ladders, multiple waist-deep river crossings, and lush canyon paths to Beaver Falls cascade.

scenicDrives.name: Indian Road 18 to Hualapai Hilltop
scenicDrives.description: Remote paved highway branching north from Route 66 across the high desert plateau to the trailhead overlook at Hualapai Hilltop.

visitorCenter.name: Havasupai Tourism & Check-in Office
visitorCenter.info: All visitors must check in at the Tourism Office in Supai Village with valid reservation confirmation, photo ID, and permit tags.

arizona.campingInfo: Campground permit includes a 3-night / 4-day reservation alongside Havasu Creek between Havasu Falls and Mooney Falls. Spring water and composting toilets provided.
arizona.entranceFees: Multi-night campground reservations are mandatory (approximately $395 – $455 per person for the mandatory 3-night package). No day hiking allowed.
arizona.hours: Open to confirmed permit holders only; trailhead open 24 hours for registered permit holders.
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: Spring (April to May) and Fall (September to October) for warm swimming weather without dangerous mid-summer triple-digit heat.
arizona.accessibilityInfo: Not wheelchair accessible. Strenuous 10-mile hike or pre-booked tribal helicopter transport (space-available basis for visitors).
travelTips: Strict Multi-Day Commitment: Mandatory 3 nights / 4 days. Absolutely no day hiking allowed.
Extreme Remoteness & Zero Connectivity: There is zero cell service at Hualapai Hilltop, throughout the canyon, and in Supai village.
Permit Release: Annual permits open every February 1 at 8:00 AM MST and sell out within minutes on the official website.
No Services on Road 18: Fill gas tanks in Peach Springs, Seligman, or Kingman before turning onto Indian Road 18 (no gas for 65+ miles).

arizona.name: The Wave (Coyote Buttes North)
arizona.shortDescription: One of Earth’s most surreal geological wonders featuring undulating Navajo sandstone troughs sculpted by Jurassic winds and water.
arizona.fullDescription: The Wave is a world-famous Jurassic-age sandstone rock formation located in the Paria Canyon-Vermilion Cliffs Wilderness on the Arizona-Utah border. Delicate intersecting troughs with swirling stripes of red, orange, pink, and yellow create an optical illusion resembling ocean waves frozen in stone. Due to the fragile nature of the sandstone and extreme desert environment, the Bureau of Land Management strictly limits entry to 64 people per day through a competitive lottery.
thingsToDo: Navigate the Untracked 6.4-Mile Wilderness Route to The Wave
Photograph the Swirling Sandstone Curves and Reflections in Rain Pools
Explore The Second Wave, Sand Cove, and The Alcove Formations
Visit Dinosaur Tracks Pressed in Jurassic Sandstone Layers
Scramble to Top Rock and The Melody Arch Natural Window

hikingTrails.name: Wire Pass Trailhead to The Wave
hikingTrails.description: No marked trail; requires navigating via GPS coordinates and photo-guide landmarks across open desert, wash beds, and slickrock ridges.

scenicDrives.name: House Rock Valley Road
scenicDrives.description: Unpaved dirt road passing along the base of the Vermilion Cliffs, connecting US-89 in Utah to US-89A in Arizona.

visitorCenter.name: Kanab BLM Visitor Center / Paria Contact Station
visitorCenter.info: Provides daily wilderness briefings, topographic route maps, daily lotteries, and road conditions for Vermilion Cliffs.

arizona.campingInfo: No camping allowed within Coyote Buttes North. Dispersed BLM camping is permitted along House Rock Valley Road at Stateline Campground (primitive, free).
bestViewpoints: The Second Wave (Best at Late Afternoon)
arizona.entranceFees: Strict Lottery Permit Required ($9.00 per person permit fee + $9.00 application fee via Recreation.gov). No non-permit access allowed.
arizona.hours: Open 24 hours for confirmed permit holders with day-use privileges.
arizona.address: House Rock Valley Rd, Marble Canyon, AZ 86036
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: Spring (April to May) and Autumn (September to October). Summer temperatures routinely exceed 100°F with zero shade.
arizona.accessibilityInfo: Strictly wilderness terrain with deep sand, steep slickrock, and zero trail markers. Not accessible.
travelTips: Lottery Requirements: Two lotteries exist: the Advanced Lottery (4 months in advance) and Daily Geofence Lottery (2 days prior via Recreation.gov mobile app).
Navigation Hazard: There is NO established trail. Every year hikers get lost in extreme heat; bring GPS device and power bank.
Water Requirements: Carry a minimum of 4 to 5 liters of water per person (no natural water sources exist).
Road Hazard: House Rock Valley Road turns into impassable slick mud during rain storms; high-clearance 4WD recommended.
nearbyAttractions: Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park

arizona.name: White Pocket & Coyote Buttes South
arizona.shortDescription: A mind-bending wonderland of twisted, brain-like white and candy-red slickrock formations deep in the Vermilion Cliffs.
arizona.fullDescription: White Pocket is an isolated, otherworldly expanse of contorted, brain-textured Navajo sandstone located in the remote depths of Vermilion Cliffs National Monument in northern Arizona. Unlike The Wave, White Pocket currently requires no advance lottery permit. The swirling layers of white calcium-rich rock overlaying fiery red, orange, and purple sandstone create one of the most visually stunning and photogenic natural landscapes on the continent.
thingsToDo: Explore the Mind-Blowing Brain Rocks and Twisted White Formations
