Photograph Sunrise and Sunset over Cauliflower Formations and Desert Water Pockets
Experience True Deep Wilderness Solitude Far from Paved Roads
Stargaze under Class 1 Bortle Dark Sky Sanctuary
Scramble Across Multi-Colored Slickrock Domes and Natural Potholes

hikingTrails.name: White Pocket Exploration Loop
hikingTrails.description: No defined trail; visitors wander freely across approximately 1 square mile of surreal slickrock domes, swirling channels, and solitary hoodoos.

scenicDrives.name: Pine Tree Road / BLM Road 1087 Deep Sand Trail
scenicDrives.description: Extremely rugged deep-sand 4WD backcountry route traversing the Paria Plateau to the White Pocket trailhead.

visitorCenter.name: Paria Contact Station / BLM Kanab Office
visitorCenter.info: Provides road condition updates, deep-sand advisories, and maps for the Paria Plateau.

arizona.campingInfo: Dispersed wilderness dry-camping allowed at the White Pocket trailhead and across BLM public lands. No water, no trash cans; pack out all waste.
arizona.entranceFees: Free entry for White Pocket (no permit currently required). Coyote Buttes South requires a BLM Day-Use Permit ($5.00/person).
arizona.hours: Open 24 hours daily year-round.
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: October through May. Summer temperatures are dangerously scorching with high risk of vehicle overheating in deep sand.
arizona.accessibilityInfo: Remote backcountry desert with deep sand and slickrock; not wheelchair accessible.
travelTips: Mandatory True 4WD: A high-clearance 4WD vehicle with low-range transfer case is mandatory. All-wheel-drive (AWD) crossovers get stuck regularly in deep sand ruts.
Tire Deflation: Air down tires to 15–18 PSI for deep sand navigation; bring a portable 12V air compressor to reinflate.
Towing Cost: Backcountry vehicle recovery from White Pocket costs upwards of $1,500–$2,500 due to extreme isolation.
Zero Connectivity: Zero cellular service across the entire Paria Plateau; carry satellite communicator (Garmin inReach).

arizona.name: Horseshoe Bend Scenic Overlook
arizona.shortDescription: A breathtaking 270-degree horseshoe-shaped meander of the Colorado River carved 1,000 feet below sandstone canyon rims.
arizona.fullDescription: Horseshoe Bend is a dramatic incised river meander located 5 miles downstream from Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell, just outside Page, Arizona. Standing on the sheer 1,000-foot sandstone rim, visitors look directly down at the emerald-green Colorado River making a sweeping 270-degree turn around a massive sandstone promontory.
thingsToDo: Walk the Wide ADA Accessible Pathway to the Canyon Edge
Photograph the Emerald Colorado River 1,000 Feet Below
Watch Kayakers and Rafts Navigating the Deep Canyon Meander
Witness Spectacular Sunset Glow illuminating the Curved Walls
Relax at the Shaded Viewing Pavilions along the Trail

hikingTrails.name: Horseshoe Bend Trail
hikingTrails.description: A smooth, graded, ADA-accessible gravel/paved pathway with two shade structures leading from the parking lot to the viewing rim.

scenicDrives.name: US-89 South Scenic Corridor
scenicDrives.description: Connects Page to the Grand Canyon South Rim and Flagstaff, passing the Echo Cliffs and high desert plateau.

visitorCenter.name: Horseshoe Bend Information Center & Plaza
visitorCenter.info: Features staffed parking kiosks, restrooms, shade structures, and safety information run by the City of Page.

arizona.campingInfo: No camping at Horseshoe Bend overlook. Extensive camping is available 15 minutes away at Wahweap Marina Campground on Lake Powell.
bestViewpoints: East and West Unfenced Natural Rim Outcrops
arizona.entranceFees: $10.00 per standard passenger vehicle parking fee (City of Page managed facility; NPS America the Beautiful pass does not cover parking).
arizona.hours: Open daily from sunrise to sunset (gates open 30 minutes before sunrise and close 30 minutes after sunset).
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: Early morning for calm viewing and mid-day for direct sunlight penetrating the river floor, or sunset for vibrant sky colors.
arizona.accessibilityInfo: Fully ADA-compliant path and fenced overlook platform suitable for wheelchairs and strollers.
travelTips: Extreme Heat Warning: Temperatures routinely reach 105°F+ in summer; bring water and sun protection despite the short walk.
Rim Safety: Beyond the central fenced railing, the cliffs are 1,000-foot sheer vertical drops with friable sandstone edges; watch children carefully.
Drone Prohibition: Operating drones at Horseshoe Bend is illegal under Glen Canyon National Recreation Area regulations.
Staging Town: Page, Arizona is 5 minutes away with full hotels, restaurants, gas, and groceries.

arizona.name: Four Corners Monument Navajo Tribal Park
arizona.shortDescription: The only geographic point in the United States where four sovereign states (AZ, UT, CO, NM) meet at a single marker.
arizona.fullDescription: Four Corners Monument Navajo Tribal Park marks the unique intersection where the boundaries of Arizona, Utah, Colorado, and New Mexico converge at a single bronze disc. Situated on sovereign land shared by the Navajo Nation and the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, visitors can stand in four states simultaneously while browsing open-air artisan booths featuring authentic Native American jewelry, pottery, rugs, and traditional foods like Navajo tacos and frybread.
thingsToDo: Stand in Four US States Simultaneously at the Center Bronze Marker
Shop Handcrafted Silver & Turquoise Jewelry from Navajo and Ute Artisans
Taste Fresh Warm Navajo Frybread and Green Chile Tacos
Learn about Navajo Nation and Ute Tribal Cultural Boundaries
Photograph the State Boundary Lines and Flags

hikingTrails.name: Monument Plaza Perimeter Walk
hikingTrails.description: A level concrete walkway around the central monument disc and surrounding vendor booths and state flag displays.

scenicDrives.name: US-160 Four Corners Highway
scenicDrives.description: Traverses scenic red-rock and open desert badlands connecting Kayenta, AZ to Cortez, CO.

visitorCenter.name: Four Corners Visitor Pavilion
visitorCenter.info: Open-air demonstration plaza with Native American craft vendor booths, picnic tables, and restroom facilities.
visitorCenter.hours: Peak Season (May 27 – Aug 19): 8:00 AM – 6:45 PM; Fall/Winter: 8:00 AM – 4:45 PM

arizona.campingInfo: No camping inside the monument plaza. RV and tent camping available in nearby Cortez, CO (40 miles) or Bluff, UT (50 miles).
arizona.entranceFees: $8.00 per person entry fee. Children 6 and under are free. (Cash and credit cards accepted; NPS passes not valid).
arizona.hours: Open 7 days a week year-round (hours adjust seasonally; last entry 15 minutes before gate closing).
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Autumn for mild temperatures; visit early in the morning to avoid midday photo lines.
arizona.accessibilityInfo: Fully paved and ramp-accessible plaza with level walkways around the marker and vendor booths.
travelTips: Cash Recommended: While the entry gate accepts credit cards, many independent artisan craft booths are cash-only.
Remote Isolation: No running water or gas station at the monument; fill gas in Teec Nos Pos, AZ (6 miles) or Shiprock, NM (33 miles).
No Cell Service: Connectivity is very weak or nonexistent at the monument plaza.
Visit Duration: Most visitors spend 45–60 minutes to take photos, browse artisan crafts, and enjoy frybread.

arizona.name: Buckskin Gulch & Paria Canyon
arizona.shortDescription: The longest and deepest continuous slot canyon in the world, spanning over 15 miles of towering sandstone narrows.
arizona.fullDescription: Buckskin Gulch is recognized as the longest and deepest slot canyon on Earth. Located within the Paria Canyon-Vermilion Cliffs Wilderness on the Utah-Arizona border, the canyon narrows into a dark, serpentine sandstone corridor reaching up to 500 feet deep and often just a few feet wide.
thingsToDo: Hike the Wire Pass Shortcut into the Deep Narrows of Buckskin Gulch
Photograph the Ancient Native American Petroglyph Panel at the Confluence
Wade Through Mysterious Water Cesspools and Sandstone Chambers
Backpack the Epic 21-Mile Multi-Day Wilderness Trek to Lee's Ferry
Experience Towering 500-Foot Vertical Sandstone Canyon Walls

hikingTrails.name: Wire Pass to Buckskin Gulch Confluence
hikingTrails.description: The most popular day hike entering via Wire Pass slot (with a short 8-foot wooden ladder) reaching the petroglyphs and confluence with main Buckskin Gulch.

scenicDrives.name: House Rock Valley Road
scenicDrives.description: Unpaved dirt access road leading to Wire Pass, Buckskin, and Stateline trailheads along the Vermilion Cliffs.

visitorCenter.name: Kanab BLM Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides mandatory flash flood risk reports, weather alerts, day-use permits, and Paria Canyon wilderness permits.

arizona.campingInfo: No camping in the narrow slot sections. Wilderness backpackers with BLM overnight permits camp along designated elevated benches in Paria Canyon.
arizona.entranceFees: $6.00 per person and $6.00 per dog for day-use permits (payable at trailhead self-pay kiosk or online via Recreation.gov).
arizona.hours: Open 24 hours daily for day-use and permit holders.
arizona.address: House Rock Valley Rd, Kanab, UT 84741
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: Spring (April–May) and Autumn (September–October). Avoid during summer monsoon season (July–August).
arizona.accessibilityInfo: Rugged wilderness slot canyon. Not wheelchair accessible.
travelTips: Extreme Flash Flood Hazard: Never enter Buckskin Gulch if rain is forecasted anywhere in the region.
Water & Mud Gear: Expect to wade through cold mud and water pools; bring neoprene socks and trekking poles.
Zero Cell Service: No reception at the trailhead or inside the canyon.
Nearby Towns: Kanab, UT (42 miles) and Page, AZ (45 miles).
nearbyAttractions: Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park

arizona.name: Little Colorado River Gorge Navajo Tribal Park
arizona.shortDescription: A sheer, 3,000-foot vertical limestone abyss carved by the turquoise waters of the Little Colorado River before entering Grand Canyon.
arizona.fullDescription: Little Colorado River Gorge Navajo Tribal Park protects an astonishing, narrow canyon chasm along AZ-64 on the Navajo Nation. Formed by the Little Colorado River slicing through layers of Kaibab limestone, the gorge plunges thousands of vertical feet with near-vertical walls. Two scenic rim overlooks provide staggering, unobstructed views into the deep abyss, while authentic Navajo artisans sell handmade jewelry and crafts along the boardwalks.
thingsToDo: Gaze 3,000 Feet Down into the Sheer Vertical Gorge Overlook
Shop Authentic Handmade Navajo Jewelry and Pottery at the Rimside Stands
View the Vivid Turquoise River Waters (Spring and Early Summer)
Photograph Dramatic Light and Shadow across the Narrow Canyon Chasm
Enjoy a Scenic Picnic on the High Rim Overlooking the Painted Desert

hikingTrails.name: Gorge Rim Boardwalk & Overlook Walk
hikingTrails.description: A level, paved/gravel rim pathway leading from the artisan parking plaza to the metal observation deck perched directly over the canyon edge.

scenicDrives.name: AZ-64 Desert View Scenic Byway
scenicDrives.description: Connects Cameron, AZ on US-89 to Desert View and the East Entrance of Grand Canyon National Park.

visitorCenter.name: Little Colorado River Tribal Park Overlook Kiosks
visitorCenter.info: Staffed Navajo Nation Parks & Recreation kiosks with local park guides, artisan booths, and portable restrooms.

arizona.campingInfo: No camping at the overlooks. Camping available in Cameron, AZ (Cameron Trading Post RV Park, 10 miles) or inside Grand Canyon Desert View Campground (22 miles).
bestViewpoints: Little Colorado River Gorge Overlook 1 (Main Observation Deck)
arizona.entranceFees: $8.00 per vehicle / per person entry fee supporting Navajo Nation Parks (NPS passes not accepted).
arizona.hours: Open 7 days a week from 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM (weather permitting).
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Autumn for clear skies and pleasant weather; visit during spring for turquoise mineral-rich river flow.
arizona.accessibilityInfo: The main parking area and viewing deck walkway at Overlook 1 are wheelchair and stroller accessible.
travelTips: Artisan Crafts: The Navajo vendors at the overlook are local artisans offering authentic handcrafted turquoise and silver jewelry at direct prices.
High Winds: The canyon rim can experience strong sudden wind gusts; hold on to hats and camera equipment.
Turquoise Water Condition: The water turns vibrant turquoise during dry periods; heavy rain turns it silt-brown temporarily.
Nearest Staging Towns: Cameron, AZ (10 miles east) and Grand Canyon Village / Tusayan (32 miles west).

arizona.name: Meteor Crater & Barringer Space Museum
arizona.shortDescription: The world’s best-preserved meteorite impact site on Earth, blasted 50,000 years ago by an asteroid traveling 26,000 mph.
arizona.fullDescription: Meteor Crater (Barringer Crater) is the world’s best-preserved meteorite impact crater, located near Winslow, Arizona. Created approximately 50,000 years ago when a 150-foot nickel-iron meteorite struck the Colorado Plateau with the explosive force of 20 million tons of TNT, the crater measures nearly 1 mile across (3,900 feet) and 560 feet deep. The site served as official training grounds for Apollo astronauts preparing for lunar landings and features an interactive science discovery center.
thingsToDo: Stand on the Rim Observation Decks Overlooking the 1-Mile Wide Crater
Join the Expert Guided Rim Walking Tour with Staff Geologists
Touch Genuine Iron-Nickel Meteorite Fragments in the Discovery Center
Explore the Apollo Astronaut Training Test Capsule and Memorial

hikingTrails.name: Guided Rim Trail Walk
hikingTrails.description: A staff-guided walking tour along the paved upper rim path explaining the impact physics, geology, and Apollo training history.

scenicDrives.name: Meteor Crater Road Scenic Approach
scenicDrives.description: Paved spur road heading south from I-40 (Exit 233) climbing through high desert plains directly to the crater rim.

visitorCenter.name: Meteor Crater Discovery Center & Space Museum
visitorCenter.info: State-of-the-art interactive science center, 4D immersive theater, Apollo exhibit hall, gift shop, and Blimpies restaurant.

arizona.campingInfo: Meteor Crater RV Park is located at the I-40 interchange (Exit 233) featuring full hookups, Wi-Fi, private showers, and recreation room.
arizona.entranceFees: $27.00 Adults (13–59), $18.00 Juniors (6–12), $25.00 Seniors (60+). Private National Natural Landmark (NPS passes not valid).
arizona.hours: Open daily 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM (extended summer hours 7:00 AM to 7:00 PM). Closed Christmas Day.
arizona.bestTimeToVisit: Year-round; early morning or late afternoon visits provide dramatic shadow relief across the crater floor and cooler temperatures.
arizona.accessibilityInfo: The Discovery Center, theaters, indoor observation deck, and main outdoor telescope platform are fully ADA accessible.
travelTips: High Elevation & Wind: The crater rim sits at 5,700 feet elevation and experiences intense winds; hold tight to loose items.
Guided Tour Included: The 45-minute guided rim tour is included free with general admission and departs every hour (weather permitting).
Interior Hiking Restricted: Hiking down to the crater floor is strictly prohibited to preserve the fragile impact geology.
Gateway Towns: Winslow, AZ is 18 miles east; Flagstaff, AZ is 35 miles west along I-40 with full lodging and dining.

utah.name: Monument Valley Navajo Tribal Park
utah.shortDescription: World-famous red sandstone buttes and sacred Navajo landscapes immortalized in classic cinema.
utah.fullDescription: Monument Valley Navajo Tribal Park straddles the Arizona-Utah border on the sacred ancestral lands of the Navajo Nation (Diné). Towering sandstone monoliths, buttes, and spires rise between 400 and 1,000 feet above the vibrant desert floor. Visitors can drive the legendary 17-mile unpaved Valley Drive or hire licensed Navajo guides to access sacred backcountry areas like Mystery Valley, Hunts Mesa, and Ear of the Wind.
thingsToDo: Take a Certified Navajo Guided 4x4 Tour
Hike the Wildcat Trail around West Mitten Butte
Photograph Sunset and Sunrise at the View Hotel Overlook
Visit Navajo Hogan Demonstrations and Artisan Stands

hikingTrails.name: Wildcat Trail
hikingTrails.description: The only self-guided hiking trail in the park, circling around the iconic West Mitten Butte with spectacular ground-level views of the Mittens and Merrick Butte.

scenicDrives.name: 17-Mile Valley Drive
scenicDrives.description: A graded dirt road passing the East and West Mitten Buttes, Merrick Butte, Three Sisters, John Ford Point, Totem Pole, and Artist Point.

scenicDrives.name: US-163 Scenic Byway (Forrest Gump Point)
scenicDrives.description: The iconic highway straightaway with panoramic head-on views of Monument Valley buttes made famous in the film Forrest Gump.

visitorCenter.name: Monument Valley Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Features an observation deck, Navajo cultural exhibits, restaurant, and gift shop with authentic Navajo silversmithing and rugs.
visitorCenter.hours: Peak Season: 6:00 AM – 8:00 PM; Off-Peak: 8:00 AM – 5:00 PM

utah.campingInfo: The View Campground offers primitive wilderness campsites and RV sites overlooking the valley. Gouldings Resort & Campground (5 miles west) provides full hookups, cabins, and indoor pool.
bestViewpoints: Forrest Gump Hill (Mile Marker 13 on US-163)
utah.entranceFees: $8.00 per person entry fee. (NPS passes are not accepted on sovereign tribal land).
utah.hours: Open 7 days a week year-round.
utah.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Autumn for mild temperatures and striking desert lighting.
utah.accessibilityInfo: Visitor Center and observation deck are ADA accessible.
travelTips: Sovereign Tribal Land: Alcohol is strictly prohibited across the Navajo Nation.
High Clearance Recommended: Valley Drive is rough washboard dirt with deep ruts.
Nearest Staging Towns: Mexican Hat / Bluff, UT (22–45 miles north) and Kayenta, AZ (23 miles south).

utah.name: Valley of the Gods
utah.shortDescription: A dramatic, peaceful red-sandstone wilderness of solitary buttes, towers, and pinnacles known as a mini-Monument Valley.
utah.fullDescription: Valley of the Gods is a breathtaking 17-mile scenic drive winding through solitary Cedar Mesa sandstone buttes, pinnacles, and towers in southeastern Utah. Managed by the Bureau of Land Management, this uncrowded red-rock basin offers the dramatic geological drama of Monument Valley with complete solitude, zero admission fees, and pristine free dispersed wilderness camping.
thingsToDo: Drive the 17-Mile Scenic Dirt Loop through Sandstone Monoliths
Camp under Pristine Dark Skies among Towering Red Buttes
Photograph Sunrise and Sunset on Rooster Butte and Castle Rock
Scramble around Balanced Rocks and Natural Sandstone Pillars
Combine with Moki Dugway and Muley Point Overlooks

hikingTrails.name: Valley of the Gods Open Wilderness Wandering
hikingTrails.description: No established trails; visitors can wander off-road around the bases of named monoliths like Setting Hen Butte and Battleship Rock.

scenicDrives.name: Valley of the Gods 17-Mile Scenic Backway
scenicDrives.description: Graded dirt road connecting US-163 (near Mexican Hat) to UT-261 (at the base of the Moki Dugway switchbacks).

visitorCenter.name: BLM Monticello Field Office
visitorCenter.info: Provides maps, road condition updates, and dispersed camping regulations for San Juan County public lands.

utah.campingInfo: Free dispersed BLM camping permitted throughout the entire valley in existing pullouts. Strict Leave No Trace rules apply; pack out all trash and waste.
bestViewpoints: Muley Point (1,200 ft directly above on Cedar Mesa)
utah.entranceFees: Free (no entrance fees or permits required).
utah.hours: Open 24 hours daily year-round.
utah.bestTimeToVisit: Spring (March–May) and Autumn (September–November) for ideal desert driving and camping weather.
utah.accessibilityInfo: Scenic loop is an unpaved gravel/dirt road; accessible by standard vehicles during dry conditions but washboarded.
travelTips: Road Conditions: The 17-mile road is typically passable for standard cars when dry, but impassable during and after rain due to muddy wash crossings.
Zero Facilities: No water, no restrooms, and no trash cans in the valley.
Moki Dugway Connection: The west exit connects directly to UT-261 leading up the legendary 1,200-foot unpaved switchbacks of Moki Dugway to Muley Point.
Nearby Towns: Mexican Hat (5 miles) and Bluff (15 miles) offer gas, dining, and lodging.

utah.name: Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument
utah.shortDescription: A vast, rugged 1.87-million-acre wilderness of labyrinth slot canyons, towering monoliths, and ancient fossil beds.
utah.fullDescription: Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument spans nearly 1.87 million acres of pristine canyon wilderness in southern Utah. Spanning three distinct physiographic regions—the Grand Staircase cliffs, the Kaiparowits Plateau, and the Escalante River Canyons—it preserves world-famous slot canyons like Peek-a-boo and Spooky Gulch, majestic waterfalls like Lower Calf Creek Falls, and premier dinosaur fossil deposits.
thingsToDo: Squeeze Through the Narrow Passages of Peek-a-boo and Spooky Slot Canyons
Hike to the 126-Foot Lower Calf Creek Falls and Emerald Plunge Pool
Drive the Spectacular Unpaved Burr Trail Road and Switchbacks
Explore the Otherworldly Hoodoos of Devils Garden off Hole-in-the-Rock Road
Backpack the Pristine Wild Narrows of the Escalante River

hikingTrails.name: Lower Calf Creek Falls Trail
hikingTrails.description: A sandy trail through a lush canyon corridor passing beaver ponds and prehistoric Fremont rock art panels to a 126-foot cascading waterfall.

hikingTrails.name: Peek-a-boo and Spooky Slot Canyons Loop
hikingTrails.description: Thrilling technical slot canyons requiring climbing a 12-foot dryfall into Peek-a-boo and squeezing through 10-inch tight narrows in Spooky Gulch.

scenicDrives.name: Utah Scenic Byway 12 (All-American Road)
scenicDrives.description: One of the most spectacular scenic highways in America, crossing the Hogback ridge and cutting through the heart of Grand Staircase.

scenicDrives.name: Burr Trail Scenic Backway
scenicDrives.description: Scenic backcountry drive from Boulder through Long Canyon and Capitol Reef Waterpocket Fold switchbacks.

visitorCenter.name: Escalante Interagency Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Provides trail conditions, weather forecasts, free backcountry camping permits, and interpretive exhibits on canyon geology.

utah.campingInfo: Developed campgrounds at Calf Creek Campground (13 sites). Free dispersed wilderness camping is permitted across BLM lands with a free self-issued permit.
utah.entranceFees: Free general admission. Calf Creek Recreation Area day-use fee is $5.00/vehicle (or NPS America the Beautiful pass).
utah.hours: Open 24 hours daily year-round.
utah.bestTimeToVisit: Spring (April–May) and Autumn (September–October). Summer flash flood risk is high during July–August monsoons.
utah.accessibilityInfo: Escalante Visitor Center is fully accessible. Calf Creek trail is deep sand; slot canyons are extremely narrow and rugged.
travelTips: Hole-in-the-Rock Road Driving: Unpaved, severe washboard dirt; dry conditions required. Rain makes the clay impassable even for 4WD.
Spooky Slot Tightness: Spooky Gulch narrows to under 10 inches wide in sections; remove backpacks and do not attempt if claustrophobic.
Zero Cell Service: Over 90% of the monument has zero cellular reception.
Gateway Towns: Escalante, Boulder, and Kanab provide lodging, outfitters, fuel, and groceries.

utah.name: Bears Ears National Monument
utah.shortDescription: A sacred 1.36-million-acre ancestral landscape of sandstone canyons, twin mesa buttes, and thousands of ancient cliff dwellings.
utah.fullDescription: Bears Ears National Monument encompasses 1.36 million acres of protected canyonlands in San Juan County, Utah. Named for the iconic pair of winged sandstone buttes rising over Cedar Mesa, this sacred homeland is co-managed between the federal government (BLM & USFS) and the Bears Ears Inter-Tribal Coalition (representing the Navajo Nation, Hopi Tribe, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, Pueblo of Zuni, and Ute Indian Tribe). The region protects more than 100,000 cultural and archaeological sites, including House on Fire, Moon House Ruin, and Grand Gulch.
thingsToDo: Hike to the Glowing Ceiling of House on Fire in Mule Canyon
Photograph the Sacred Twin Bears Ears Buttes from Elk Ridge
Explore the Ancient Ancestral Puebloan Moon House Ruin (Permit Required)
Drive the Daring 1,200-Foot Cliffs of Moki Dugway to Muley Point
Visit the Bears Ears Education Center in Bluff to Learn "Visit with Respect" Ethics

hikingTrails.name: House on Fire (Mule Canyon)
hikingTrails.description: A level walk up South Mule Canyon to a stunning 700-year-old cliff granary where morning sunlight makes the overhead rock look like licking flames.

hikingTrails.name: Moon House Ruin Trail (McLoyd Canyon)
hikingTrails.description: Descent into McLoyd Canyon to an exceptionally preserved Ancestral Puebloan defensive complex with rare interior paintings (BLM permit required).

scenicDrives.name: UT-95 Trail of the Ancients Scenic Byway
scenicDrives.description: Paved scenic highway passing Comb Ridge, Mule Canyon, Natural Bridges, and the northern Bears Ears landscape.

scenicDrives.name: UT-261 & Moki Dugway
scenicDrives.description: Climbs 1,200 vertical feet up Cedar Mesa on unpaved gravel switchbacks with dramatic vistas of Valley of the Gods and Monument Valley.

visitorCenter.name: Bears Ears Education Center / BLM Monticello Office
visitorCenter.info: Non-profit grassroots visitor center in Bluff providing cultural etiquette guides, maps, and Leave No Trace education.

utah.campingInfo: Primitive dispersed camping is permitted on BLM and USFS land outside archaeological sites. Developed camping available at Natural Bridges and Comb Wash.
bestViewpoints: Elk Ridge Bears Ears Buttes Vista
utah.entranceFees: Free general admission. Cedar Mesa day-use hiking permits ($5.00/person) and Moon House permits required for specific canyons.
utah.hours: Open 24 hours daily year-round.
utah.bestTimeToVisit: Spring (April to May) and Autumn (September to October). High summer brings dangerous heat; winter brings snow to Elk Ridge.
utah.accessibilityInfo: Bears Ears Education Center in Bluff is ADA accessible. Backcountry ruins and trails are remote, sandy, and rugged.
travelTips: Visit with Respect Guidelines: Never touch, lean on, or climb into ancient ruin walls. Never touch rock art panels or pick up pottery sherds.
Leave Archaeological Sites Undisturbed: All artifacts and ruins are strictly protected under federal and tribal law.
High Clearance 4WD: Roads to Moon House and Elk Ridge are rough dirt and require high-clearance 4WD vehicles.
Gateway Staging Towns: Blanding, Monticello, and Bluff provide fuel, lodging, groceries, and outfitters.
nearbyAttractions: Edge of the Cedars State Park Museum

utah.name: Bonneville Salt Flats
utah.shortDescription: A 30,000-acre expanse of blindingly white, table-flat salt crust famous worldwide for land speed record racing.
utah.fullDescription: The Bonneville Salt Flats is a 30,000-acre geologic remnant of the ancient Pleistocene Lake Bonneville, located in northwestern Utah near the Nevada border. Composed of pure potassium and sodium chloride crystals, the flats are so intensely level that the curvature of the Earth is visibly noticeable. Famous worldwide as the stage for legendary land speed record runs at the Bonneville Speedway, the flats transform into a massive liquid mirror during winter and spring rains reflecting endless sky.
thingsToDo: Walk onto the Blinding White Table-Flat Salt Crust
Photograph Incredible Sky Mirror Reflections after Winter and Spring Rains
Visit the Legendary Bonneville Speedway Starting Line
Watch High-Speed Racing Runs during Speed Week (August)
Capture Perspective-Bending Illusion Photography across the Horizon

hikingTrails.name: Salt Flats Open Surface Walk
hikingTrails.description: Visitors walk directly out onto the firm, hard-packed salt crust from the end of the paved access road or I-80 Rest Area.

scenicDrives.name: Bonneville Speedway Access Road
scenicDrives.description: Paved road branching north from I-80 (Exit 4) leading directly onto the salt surface at the Bonneville Speedway staging area.

visitorCenter.name: BLM Salt Lake Field Office / I-80 Salt Flats Rest Area
visitorCenter.info: Provides interpretive displays, water wash-off stations, observation walkways, and safety guidelines for driving on the salt.
visitorCenter.hours: Rest Area open 24 hours; BLM office Monday–Friday 8:00 AM – 4:30 PM

utah.campingInfo: No camping allowed directly on the salt flats. Free dispersed BLM camping is permitted on surrounding public lands outside the salt crust (e.g. Silver Island Mountains).
bestViewpoints: I-80 Westbound Salt Flats Rest Area View Deck
utah.entranceFees: Free (no entrance fees or day-use permits required for standard visits).
utah.hours: Open 24 hours daily year-round (subject to seasonal weather and flooding closures).
utah.bestTimeToVisit: Summer and Autumn (July to October) for dry, driveable salt conditions and racing events; Winter/Spring for giant water mirror reflections.
utah.accessibilityInfo: The I-80 Rest Area features paved ADA observation decks, walkways, and restrooms overlooking the salt expanse.
travelTips: Never Drive on Wet Salt: When standing water or moisture is present, the salt is soft mud underneath; vehicles sink to their axles and require $1,000+ specialized tow rescues.
Intense Sun Reflection: The white salt reflects nearly 100% of UV rays; polarized sunglasses, sunscreen, and lip balm are essential.
Vehicle Undercarriage Wash: Driving on salt deposits corrosive sodium; wash your car's undercarriage thoroughly at Wendover car washes immediately after visiting.
Gateway Town: Wendover, UT and West Wendover, NV are 10 miles west with hotels, casinos, gas, and 24-hour amenities.

new-mexico.name: Taos Pueblo
new-mexico.shortDescription: An ancient, multi-storied adobe pueblo continuously inhabited by the Tiwa-speaking people for over 1,000 years.
new-mexico.fullDescription: Taos Pueblo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and National Historic Landmark located at the base of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains in northern New Mexico. Belonging to the sovereign Taos Pueblo nation, its multi-storied adobe apartment complexes (Hlauuma and Hlaukwima) have been continuously inhabited for more than 1,000 years. Preserving ancient Tiwa traditions, no electricity or running water is permitted within the historic adobe village walls, through which the sacred Red Willow Creek flows.
thingsToDo: Take an Informative Guided Walking Tour led by Taos Pueblo Tribal Members
Admire the Multi-Story Adobe Architecture of Hlauuma (North House) and Hlaukwima (South House)
Sample Fresh Pueblo Bread and Sweet Pastries Baked in Traditional Adobe Horno Ovens
Visit San Geronimo Chapel and the Historic Ruins of the Original 1619 Church
Shop Direct for Handcrafted Micaceous Pottery, Silver Jewelry, and Moccasins

hikingTrails.name: Historic Pueblo Village Walking Tour
hikingTrails.description: A level walk through the central village plaza, crossing footbridges over Red Willow Creek and passing artisan hornos and shops.

scenicDrives.name: Enchanted Circle Scenic Byway
scenicDrives.description: Spectacular mountain highway looping around Wheeler Peak, connecting Taos, Questa, Red River, and Angel Fire.

visitorCenter.name: Taos Pueblo Tourism Office & Welcome Center
visitorCenter.info: Coordinates visitor tickets, registered photography permits, native guided tours, and cultural etiquette orientations.
visitorCenter.hours: Thursday – Monday: 9:00 AM – 4:00 PM (Closed Tuesday & Wednesday; seasonal ceremonial closures)

new-mexico.campingInfo: No camping on sovereign Taos Pueblo tribal lands. Extensive campgrounds located nearby in Carson National Forest and Taos RV parks (3 miles away).
new-mexico.entranceFees: $25.00 Adults, $22.00 Seniors & Students, Free for children under 10. Photography fee for personal cameras is included with admission.
new-mexico.hours: Open Thursday through Monday 9:00 AM – 4:00 PM. Closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays and during confidential tribal ceremonies.
new-mexico.bestTimeToVisit: Spring through Autumn for comfortable mountain weather and daily guided tours; winter offers snow-capped adobe photography.
new-mexico.accessibilityInfo: The main plaza and village roads are packed dirt and gravel; wheelchair accessible with assistance in dry conditions.
travelTips: Strict Photography Protocol: Commercial filming and tripods are strictly prohibited without written tribal permission. Never photograph tribal members without asking first.
Respect Restricted Areas: Do not enter residential doors marked private, do not climb on adobe ladders, and do not enter the sacred kivas or cemetery.
Check for Religious Closures: Taos Pueblo closes periodically for sovereign spiritual ceremonies; always check taospueblo.com before traveling.
Gateway Town: The town of Taos is just 3 miles south, offering world-class art galleries, restaurants, and hotels.

new-mexico.name: Shiprock Peak (Tsé Bitʼaʼí)
new-mexico.shortDescription: A sacred volcanic monadnock rising 1,583 feet above the high desert floor, revered as the "Rock with Wings" in Navajo tradition.
new-mexico.fullDescription: Shiprock (Diné: Tsé Bitʼaʼí - "rock with wings") is a towering volcanic neck rising 1,583 feet above the high desert plain of northwestern New Mexico on the Navajo Nation. Formed 27 million years ago, the peak is framed by prominent radiating volcanic dike walls that stretch for miles like dark stone spines across the desert. In Navajo tradition, the formation represents the great bird that carried the ancestral Diné from the north.
thingsToDo: Photograph the Magnificent Volcanic Monolith from Indian Service Route 13
Witness the Long Radiating Volcanic Dike Walls Extending Across the Plain
Capture Dramatic Sunrise and Sunset Golden Hour Lighting on the Pinnacle
Experience the Peaceful High Desert Solitude of the Four Corners Region
Stargaze under Unpolluted Navajo Nation Dark Skies

hikingTrails.name: Dike Wall Observation Walk
hikingTrails.description: A brief roadside walk from the unpaved pullouts to examine the dark igneous volcanic dike walls extending toward the base of the peak.

scenicDrives.name: Indian Service Route 13 (Navajo 13)
scenicDrives.description: Paved and graded highway connecting US-491 to Red Rock, offering panoramic 360-degree views of Shiprock Peak.

visitorCenter.name: Navajo Nation Parks & Recreation Department
visitorCenter.info: Manages tourism oversight and cultural protections across the Navajo Nation.

new-mexico.campingInfo: No camping permitted at Shiprock Peak. Lodging and RV parks available in Shiprock, NM (12 miles) and Farmington, NM (40 miles).
bestViewpoints: Navajo Route 13 Roadside Pullout (Best Direct Perspective)
new-mexico.entranceFees: Free roadside viewing. (Climbing is strictly prohibited under Navajo Nation law).
new-mexico.hours: Open 24 hours for roadside viewing and photography from public rights-of-way.
new-mexico.address: US-491 & Indian Service Route 13, Shiprock, NM 87420
new-mexico.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Autumn for clear, crisp desert air; early morning sunrise provides unmatched golden illumination on the eastern rock faces.
new-mexico.accessibilityInfo: Best viewed directly from roadside paved and gravel pullouts along Indian Service Route 13.
travelTips: Strict Climbing Ban: Climbing on Shiprock Peak or its volcanic dikes is strictly illegal under Navajo Nation law and heavily penalized.
Respect Sacred Ground: Shiprock is deeply sacred in Navajo cosmology; treat the land with quiet reverence and pack out all trash.
Unpaved Dirt Roads: Dirt tracks leading closer to the base can have deep sand and sharp rocks; stay on main gravel corridors.
Nearby Towns: Shiprock, NM is 12 miles northeast with gas and food; Farmington, NM is 40 miles east with full hotels and amenities.

new-mexico.name: Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness
new-mexico.shortDescription: A surreal 45,000-acre badland maze of bizarre stone hoodoos, petrified wood logs, and otherworldly "alien egg" rock formations.
new-mexico.fullDescription: The Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness is a vast 45,000-acre badland expanse in the San Juan Basin of northwestern New Mexico. Preserved in near-lunar isolation, this ancient Cretaceous river delta has eroded into one of the most surreal landscapes on Earth. Visitors wander through a dreamscape of mushroom-capped hoodoos, petrified wood trunks up to 30 feet long, coal seams, and the famous "Alien Throne" and "Cracked Eggs" rock clusters.
thingsToDo: Hunt for the Famous "Alien Throne" and "Cracked Eggs" (Egg Garden) Hoodoos
Navigate the Untracked Labyrinth of Colored Siltstone and Shale Badlands
Stargaze under Pristine Dark Skies among Ghostly Stone Pillars
Photograph Dramatic Sunrise and Sunset Shadows across the Stone Forest

hikingTrails.name: Bisti Main Wash Exploration
hikingTrails.description: Untracked wilderness route navigating east up the broad sandy wash into the North and South hoodoo labyrinths (GPS navigation required).

scenicDrives.name: NM-371 Badlands Highway
scenicDrives.description: Paved highway connecting Farmington to Crownpoint, passing the access turnoff for County Road 7297.

visitorCenter.name: BLM Farmington Field Office
visitorCenter.info: Provides topographic maps, GPS coordinate guides, weather warnings, and wilderness regulations.

new-mexico.campingInfo: Free dispersed wilderness camping permitted throughout the BLM wilderness. No campfires allowed; pack out all trash and waste.
new-mexico.entranceFees: Free (no entrance fees or day-use permits required).
new-mexico.bestTimeToVisit: Spring (March–May) and Autumn (September–November). Summer temperatures exceed 100°F with zero shade; winter brings freezing winds.
new-mexico.accessibilityInfo: Strictly untamed wilderness terrain with deep sand, wash crossings, and badland mounds; not wheelchair accessible.
travelTips: Mandatory GPS Navigation: There are NO marked trails or signs in the badlands. All hoodoos look identical on the return hike; carry a GPS device or offline phone maps.
Bentonite Clay Warning: During or after rain, the badland clay turns into sticky, impassable mud that coats boots and traps vehicles.
Carry Ample Water: Carry at least 1 gallon (4 liters) of water per person; there is zero water anywhere in the wilderness.
Staging Town: Farmington, NM is 36 miles north with hotels, outdoor gear shops, gas, and restaurants.

new-mexico.name: Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wilderness Study Area
new-mexico.shortDescription: An eerie, multi-colored badland basin filled with mushroom-shaped hoodoos, yellow sandstone spires, and rich dinosaur fossil beds.
new-mexico.fullDescription: Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wilderness Study Area is a 6,563-acre badland wonderland located in the San Juan Basin of northwestern New Mexico. Carved into the Cretaceous Fruitland and Kirtland formations, this secluded valley features bizarre yellowish-green sandstone hoodoos, capped pillars, petrified tree stumps, and abundant fossilized dinosaur bones. Far less visited than nearby Bisti, Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah provides an extraordinary wilderness adventure.
thingsToDo: Wander Among Strange Multi-Colored Hoodoos and Balanced Mushroom Rocks
Discover Cretaceous Fossil Beds, Dinosaur Bone Fragments, and Turtle Shells
Photograph Glowing Yellow and Orange Siltstone Spired Amphitheaters
Hike the Quiet Wash Corridors with Complete Backcountry Solitude
Experience World-Class Night Sky Astrophotography among Stone Sculptures

hikingTrails.name: Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wash Cross-Country Loop
hikingTrails.description: An open cross-country exploration navigating from the rim down into the main badland wash and exploring side hoodoo canyons.

scenicDrives.name: San Juan County Road 7870
scenicDrives.description: Unpaved dirt and gravel backcountry road branching west from US-550 toward the wilderness study area boundary.

visitorCenter.name: BLM Farmington Field Office
visitorCenter.info: Provides maps, road condition reports, and paleontological resource protection information.

new-mexico.campingInfo: Free dispersed wilderness camping is permitted. Camp on durable surfaces; do not camp directly beneath fragile hoodoos or on fossil deposits.
new-mexico.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Autumn for mild temperatures and dry road access.
new-mexico.accessibilityInfo: Rugged wilderness badland terrain with no developed paths; not wheelchair accessible.
travelTips: Fossil Protection: All fossils, petrified wood, and cultural artifacts are strictly protected by federal law; collecting or disturbing them is illegal.
Unpaved Road Warning: County Road 7870 is unpaved dirt that becomes slick clay when wet; high-clearance 4WD recommended.
Offline Maps Essential: No cellular service; download offline maps and GPS tracks before leaving paved highways.
Gateway Towns: Bloomfield (45 miles) and Farmington (55 miles) provide fuel, hotels, and supplies.

new-mexico.name: Kasha-Katuwe Tent Rocks National Monument
new-mexico.shortDescription: Towering cone-shaped volcanic tent rocks and a dramatic slot canyon carved on the sacred ancestral lands of Pueblo de Cochiti.
new-mexico.fullDescription: Kasha-Katuwe Tent Rocks National Monument is a remarkable geological landscape located on the Pajarito Plateau of north-central New Mexico. Formed by violent pyroclastic volcanic explosions from the Jemez Volcanic Field 6 to 7 million years ago, the monument features towering cone-shaped tent rock hoodoos up to 90 feet tall capped by resilient boulders. Co-managed between the Bureau of Land Management and the sovereign Pueblo de Cochiti, visitors hike through a soaring slot canyon to a high mesa overlook.
thingsToDo: Hike the Spectacular Slot Canyon Trail through Sheer Volcanic Walls
Climb to the Mesa Top Overlook for 360-Degree Views of the Jemez Mountains
Walk the Level Cave Loop Trail to View Prehistoric Cavate Dwellings
Photograph the Cone-Shaped Volcanic Tent Rock Formations and Banded Pumice
Observe Native Birds along the Riparian Cottonwood Groves

hikingTrails.name: Canyon Trail (Slot Canyon to Mesa Top)
hikingTrails.description: Narrows into a dramatic slot canyon before ascending 630 vertical feet through switchbacks to a panoramic mesa overlook.

hikingTrails.name: Cave Loop Trail
hikingTrails.description: A gentle, level gravel loop past the bases of tent rocks and a historic cliff cave used by ancestral Puebloans.

scenicDrives.name: NM-22 / Cochiti Reservoir Scenic Route
scenicDrives.description: Scenic highway leading from I-25 through Cochiti Pueblo and along Cochiti Lake to the monument entrance.

visitorCenter.name: Tent Rocks Contact Station / BLM Rio Puerco Office
visitorCenter.info: Provides interpretive brochures, trail safety orientation, weather advisories, and timed entry verification.

new-mexico.campingInfo: No camping inside the national monument. Developed camping and boat ramps available nearby at Cochiti Lake Recreation Area (Corps of Engineers, 6 miles).
bestViewpoints: Mesa Top Overlook (Top of Canyon Trail)
new-mexico.entranceFees: $5.00 per vehicle entry fee (or NPS America the Beautiful pass). Timed entry reservations may be required through Recreation.gov.
new-mexico.hours: Open 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM (gates close to incoming entry at 3:00 PM). Check BLM status for current tribal access schedules.
new-mexico.address: 0 Indian Service Route 92, Cochiti Pueblo, NM 87072
new-mexico.bestTimeToVisit: Spring and Autumn for pleasant hiking conditions; avoid midday summer heat due to steep, exposed slickrock climbs.
new-mexico.accessibilityInfo: The first portion of the Cave Loop Trail is flat and accessible; the Slot Canyon Trail is narrow with rock scrambles.
travelTips: Check Operational Status: Co-managed with Pueblo de Cochiti; check the official BLM website for current reopening schedules and reservation requirements.
No Pets Allowed: Domestic pets are strictly prohibited within the monument to protect native wildlife and sensitive cultural resources.
Early Arrival: The parking lot fills quickly on weekends; arrive when gates open at 8:00 AM.
Gateway Cities: Santa Fe (40 miles northeast) and Albuquerque (50 miles southwest) provide full amenities along I-25.
nearbyAttractions: Jemez Mountain Trail National Scenic Byway

nevada.name: Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area
nevada.shortDescription: Towering red Aztec sandstone cliffs, ancient petroglyphs, and a 13-mile scenic drive just 17 miles from the Las Vegas Strip.
nevada.fullDescription: Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area protects 195,819 acres of vibrant Mojave Desert wilderness within the Spring Mountains, located just 17 miles west of the Las Vegas Strip. World-famous for its massive 3,000-foot Aztec Sandstone escarpment, Keystone Thrust Fault geologic marvel, ancient Native American roasting pits, and 13-mile one-way paved Scenic Loop Drive, it is an international destination for rock climbing, hiking, and wildlife viewing.
thingsToDo: Drive the 13-Mile One-Way Paved Scenic Loop Drive
Hike to the Natural Sandstone Pools of Calico Tanks with Las Vegas Skyline Views
Scramble Across the Vibrant Red and Cream Dunes of Calico Hills
World-Class Sport and Traditional Rock Climbing on Aztec Sandstone Cliffs
Discover Ancient Native American Petroglyphs at Petroglyph Wall

hikingTrails.name: Calico Tanks Trail
hikingTrails.description: Hikes up a sandstone canyon with moderate rock scrambling to a hidden natural water pool and stunning panoramic view of the Las Vegas Strip.

hikingTrails.name: Ice Box Canyon Trail
hikingTrails.description: A rugged boulder-strewn hike up a shaded canyon where cold mountain air and seasonal waterfalls flow beneath massive cliff walls.

hikingTrails.name: Keystone Thrust Trail
hikingTrails.description: Leads to one of North America's most famous geologic fault lines where older grey limestone was thrust over younger red sandstone.

scenicDrives.name: Red Rock Scenic Loop Drive
scenicDrives.description: Paved, one-way scenic drive with multiple trailheads, scenic overlooks, and interpretive pullouts along the red rock escarpment.

visitorCenter.name: Red Rock Canyon Visitor Center
visitorCenter.info: Award-winning LEED-Gold certified visitor center with interactive outdoor desert exhibits, live desert tortoises, bookstore, and weather reports.

nevada.campingInfo: Red Rock Canyon Campground is located 2 miles east of the Scenic Loop on Moenkopi Road (72 individual sites, vault toilets, water faucets). Closed during summer heat.
bestViewpoints: High Point Overlook (Highest Elevation on Scenic Drive)
nevada.entranceFees: $20.00 per car / vehicle entry fee (NPS America the Beautiful pass accepted). Timed Entry Reservation required Oct 1 – May 31 ($2.00 reservation fee via Recreation.gov).
nevada.hours: Scenic Loop open daily: Nov–Feb: 6:00 AM – 5:00 PM; Mar & Oct: 6:00 AM – 7:00 PM; Apr–Sep: 6:00 AM – 8:00 PM.
nevada.address: 1000 Scenic Loop Dr, Las Vegas, NV 89161
nevada.bestTimeToVisit: October through April for comfortable hiking temperatures; summer brings extreme 100°F+ heat.
nevada.accessibilityInfo: Visitor Center exhibits, restrooms, and several paved overlook platforms along the Scenic Loop are fully ADA accessible.
travelTips: Timed Entry System: Timed entry reservations are mandatory for driving the Scenic Loop between 8:00 AM and 5:00 PM from October 1 through May 31 (book on Recreation.gov).
Wet Sandstone Climbing Rule: Never climb on sandstone for at least 24–48 hours after rain; wet sandstone becomes brittle and breaks easily.
Proximity to Strip: Located only 25 minutes west of Las Vegas Boulevard; ride-shares (Uber/Lyft) can drop off at Visitor Center, but return cell service may be weak.
Carry Water: Always carry at least 2 liters of water per person even on short desert trails.

idaho.name: Shoshone Falls Park
idaho.shortDescription: The "Niagara of the West" – a thunderous 212-foot waterfall spanning 900 feet across the basalt Snake River Canyon.
idaho.fullDescription: Shoshone Falls, famously heralded as the "Niagara of the West," is a majestic waterfall on the Snake River located near Twin Falls, Idaho. Plunging 212 feet over a rim nearly 900 feet wide—standing 36 feet higher than Niagara Falls—the waterfall roars into a rugged volcanic basalt canyon. Fed by melting snowpack from the Rocky Mountains, the falls reach their most thunderous power in the spring before seasonal agricultural diversion.
thingsToDo: Stand on the Multi-Level Observation Decks Overlooking the Roaring Waterfall
Walk the Paved Snake River Canyon Rim Trail to Dierkes Lake
Swim and Paddleboard at the Shaded Beaches of Dierkes Lake Park
Experience the Dazzling "Shoshone Falls After Dark" Light Show (May)
Kayak the Snake River Canyon to Pillar Falls and the Base of Shoshone Falls

hikingTrails.name: Canyon Rim Trail (Shoshone Falls Section)
hikingTrails.description: A paved, scenic multi-use path along the volcanic canyon rim offering continuous views of the Snake River and falls.

hikingTrails.name: Dierkes Lake Walking Trail
hikingTrails.description: A scenic trail looping around the clear spring-fed waters of Dierkes Lake with swimming areas and hidden rock alcoves.

scenicDrives.name: Shoshone Falls Grade Scenic Road
scenicDrives.description: Descends the steep basalt canyon grade from Twin Falls city directly to the waterfall overlook plaza and riverbanks.

visitorCenter.name: Shoshone Falls Information Kiosk & Park Office
visitorCenter.info: Staffed City of Twin Falls Parks & Recreation kiosk with trail maps, gift shop, restrooms, and flow rate monitors.

idaho.campingInfo: No overnight camping in Shoshone Falls Park. RV and tent camping available nearby at Twin Falls 93 RV Park and Rock Creek Park (6 miles).
idaho.entranceFees: $5.00 per vehicle entry fee (charged March 1 through September 30; free during fall/winter). City of Twin Falls municipal park (NPS passes not valid).
idaho.hours: Open daily from dawn to dusk (gates open 7:00 AM to 10:00 PM in summer).
idaho.address: 4155 Shoshone Falls Grade, Twin Falls, ID 83301
idaho.bestTimeToVisit: Spring (April through June) when mountain snowmelt produces peak water volume (often exceeding 10,000–20,000 cfs).
idaho.accessibilityInfo: The main parking lot, concession area, restrooms, and upper viewing platforms are fully ADA wheelchair accessible.
travelTips: Peak Water Flow Timing: Check the live Snake River flow rate online before visiting; spring offers peak cascades, while late summer water is diverted for regional irrigation.
Shoshone Falls After Dark: In May, the falls are illuminated in dynamic multicolored LED lights with choreographed music.
Combine with Perrine Bridge: Visit the famous Perrine Memorial Bridge in Twin Falls (5 miles west) to watch year-round BASE jumpers leaping 486 feet into the canyon.
Gateway Town: Twin Falls is 5 miles away with complete dining, hotels, breweries, and gas stations.
nearbyAttractions: Perrine Memorial Bridge & Canyon Rim Trail
Craters of the Moon National Monument
